item.title: How to Nurture Healthy Communication in Marriage
item.description:
Good communication is so important to the health of a relationship. It’s not overstating it to say that communication in marriage is the lifeblood of that marriage. When good communication ceases to be the hallmark of the relationship, it’s a good sign that there’s marital dissatisfaction, and it’s a warning bell signaling the possibility of eventual breakdown.

What Is Communication?

It seems important to make a distinction between good communication and unhealthy communication. Even when couples are silent toward one another, that is still a form of communication; it just isn’t a healthy form of communication. We’re always communicating in one form or another, but what we’re communicating isn’t always the kind of thing that builds others and the relationship up (Ephesians 4:29).

One of the more common refrains in couples or marriage counseling is, “We just can’t communicate with each other”. This doesn’t mean that the couples aren’t talking; in fact, a good number of the couples that say this are almost never silent. The dynamics of their relationship will often include defending, explaining, persuading, and much else. A lot of talking is going on in that situation.

What the couple likely means isn’t that they aren’t talking to one another. It’s more that they simply cannot hear each other. They are saying that even when we talk, we seem unable to speak in ways that make us feel heard and understood. We keep talking around the same things, arriving at the same impasse, and having the same bruising conversations. Even though we’re talking, we still feel fundamentally alone in each other’s presence.

Communication isn’t the same thing as talking or exchanging information. It’s much more than that. Communication is about being heard and understood, and doing that for the other person, too. How you express yourself matters, as it can mask what you truly mean. There are important skills to learn to help you improve in this regard, just as there are important skills to grow in so that you’re a better listener.

In a marriage, communication is the main way that intimacy is either eroded or built up. This is how people either grow farther apart or draw closer to each other. Poor communication in marriage hinders meaningful intimacy. It’s more than an inconvenience; it’s a significant challenge to the health of the relationship. Poor communication points strongly to a future where the marriage breaks down entirely.

4 Unhealthy Patterns of Communication in Marriage

After decades of research on couples, organizations such as the Gottman Institute have identified certain unhealthy patterns of communication that can have a particularly devastating effect on marriages. These destructive patterns have been named the Four Horsemen, after the figures depicted in the book of Revelation that are harbingers of the end. These harmful communication patterns may point to the end of a marriage.

The Four Horsemen, the main damaging patterns of communication, are criticism, contempt, defensiveness, and stonewalling. Let’s break these down in turn:

Criticism includes attacking your partner’s character rather than raising a specific instance or behavior that you have an issue with. It’s the difference between saying your partner did a thoughtless thing and saying that they are a thoughtless and selfish person.

The second pattern is contempt. This is when you communicate a sense of superiority and are disrespectful to your partner. This can happen in several ways, including mocking and ridiculing, being sarcastic, scoffing, rolling your eyes at them, calling them names, or mimicking them. The person who’s the object of contempt will often feel worthless and despised. This pattern is one of the single strongest predictors of divorce.

The third pattern is defensiveness, which is when you respond to complaints from your partner with counter-complaints and deflection. Defensiveness looks like reversing blame, or fishing for excuses and self-justifications so that one’s partner backs off from any legitimate concerns they raise. Being defensive is a way of not taking responsibility for our actions, and it also communicates that you don’t take your partner’s concerns seriously.

Lastly, there’s stonewalling, which is when a partner shuts down and withdraws emotionally. Instead of engaging in the conversation, they turn away, act busy, tune their partner out by turning the TV up or putting on headphones, or they engage in distracting behaviors to shut the conversation out. Sometimes, stonewalling is a response to other unhealthy patterns of communication, a way of dealing with being overwhelmed.

If you take a look at your marriage, do you see any patterns that remind you of these four horsemen? Taking that first step of recognizing the kinds of patterns you get locked into in your communication heralds the possibility of change. If you’ve been reacting to one another without necessarily thinking about it, that greater awareness can prepare you to do things differently going forward.

Nurturing Healthy Communication in Marriage

The various horsemen that damage a marriage have an antidote. Just because you’ve related to each other in specific ways in the past, that doesn’t mean you’re doomed to repeat those patterns until the marriage falls apart completely. You can begin to undo those patterns by learning new ways to communicate with your spouse.

Some of the ways to nurture healthy communication in marriage include the following:

A gentle start-up To step beyond criticism, it may be helpful to replace it with a gentle start-up, which is when you raise your concerns without attacking your spouse. Concerns ought to be raised and dealt with; the problem is when addressing the concern becomes an attack on the other person’s character.

More appreciation When you’re contemptuous of another person, you’ve likely stopped seeing them as a beautiful creature made in God’s image. This is God’s beloved son or daughter, and He loves them with a love that is hard to fathom. You can start dealing with contempt by recovering this view of them, and by building a culture of respect and appreciation in the relationship.

Instead of focusing on what they haven’t done right, you can consider the things they do well and appreciate them for it. This doesn’t resolve every issue, but it helps you begin to reframe your posture toward them.

Take responsibility Defensiveness can be addressed by taking responsibility, even partial responsibility, for the issue or concern at hand. Often, defensiveness is fueled by the notion that to be accountable and admit when you’ve messed up is the same as losing.

There’s a scorecard that’s shaping your interactions, and to say “I’m sorry” feels unthinkable. It’s not a contest, and your spouse isn’t the enemy; the issue is.

Take a pause Often, stonewalling is a response to feeling overwhelmed, or even emotionally overstimulated. One way to deal with this is to try self-soothing before attempting to reengage the issue. Take a walk, go for a run, or listen to calming music; if this helps you to feel calmer and better able to engage, do that, and then come back to the table to have the conversation.

Using ‘I’ language Healthy communication rests on learning to express your concerns honestly but without weaponizing them. Using ‘I’ language can help you express your experience without making pronouncements about your partner. “I feel dismissed when I’m interrupted” creates space for conversation, but “You never listen!” shuts conversation down.

Practice active listening Sometimes, we listen not to understand, but just long enough to make a rebuttal. While your spouse is speaking, you’re not really listening; you’re preparing your response to that thing they just said. Being a good listener means pausing that process, allowing yourself to be genuinely and fully present so that you can hear what they’re saying, and you grasp what they are feeling.

Seek Christian marriage counseling Counseling will often focus on communication because that is the way we express and begin resolving issues plaguing the marriage. Communication is more than a relational skill; it’s where we love the other person well, where we get to know them and allow ourselves to be known. This requires huge amounts of trust, and trust is a mark of what love is (1 Corinthians 13:4-7).

Through therapies such as Cognitive Behavioral Therapy and Emotionally Focused Therapy, your counselor can help you and your spouse to identify the specific patterns of unhealthy communication in your marriage.

They can guide you within a safe environment to nurture new skills so that you can recover a refreshed capacity to be honest, empathetic, and tender toward each other.

A different, healthier, and more joyful marriage is possible. You can contact our reception team today to schedule an appointment with a Christian counselor to begin a nurturing and healthy marriage.

item.title: Adult Therapy: Grace for an Imperfect Life
item.description:
There’s a mentality that often takes root in the middle of overwhelm. Maybe you’re familiar with it because you live in that constant state of urgency. It’s the inner need to fix everything wrong in your life right now.

Part of adult therapy is learning that this type of pressure, which is often self-inflicted, is linked to a false all-or-nothing thinking and mentality. You believe that you’re failing because you haven’t had time to clean the house or because your finances aren’t where you want them to be.

But that pressure for immediate perfection isn’t biblical. The God of Scripture tells you in the Gospel of Matthew that today’s burdens are already enough to carry. God doesn’t intend for you to fix your whole life in a single day and with perfection. He calls you to be faithful in being present in the life you’re currently living.

Responsibility or Control?

Perfectionism doesn’t always exhibit itself outwardly with a perfectly manicured lawn or nails. Having these outward benchmarks completed to perfection might make you look responsible, mature, and organized. It not only makes others view you in these positive ways, but it feeds your own self-esteem because of the positive reaction you receive from others and your own sense of accomplishment.

Being able to present yourself in a healthy and positive way isn’t bad, but it can add a lot of undue pressure on yourself. Perfectionism is often seen as a trait of high achievers, like the person with the color-coded planner and spotless kitchen. For many people, perfectionism looks rather disorganized and disjointed.

Even if your public-facing life looks imperfect, you can still be battling constant mental pressure to look or be perfect. That’s because perfectionism exhibits itself as an internal standard that demands attention. And that internal dictator can be relentless.

It can tell you that if you’re not doing all you need to do perfectly, you’re doing nothing at all. Instead of this need to achieve being a positive force for healthy change, it becomes a ruthless bully that forces you into unnecessary and reluctant action. This even happens when you’re already exhausted and overwhelmed.

When this happens, your need to meet a high standard is paramount. This can be for yourself or from outside pressure. It becomes the measure of success and a tool for controlling an environment that feels unpredictable.

High Standards, Anxiety, or OCD?

You might feel like you have an internal dictator that demands immediate and perfect action. A therapist might describe that experience as a neurological loop that could be tied to high-functioning anxiety or Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD).

The cultural belief about OCD is that someone with this type of brain insists on symmetry or engages in excessive handwashing rituals. But therapists know that OCD is much more than that and can manifest itself in different ways.

OCD makes you doubt everything. It’s a relentless cycle of intrusive thoughts (that’s the obsessive part) followed by a desperate need to perform a mental or physical act (the compulsion) just to make the discomfort go away.

Within that cycle is a sense of urgency. The urgency that if you don’t perform this task, something truly bad will happen. This leads you to do it. And you do it without delay because you feel threatened. Doing that compulsion offers you some mental relief. And this is exactly where the pressure to fix everything immediately becomes unsustainable.

When you live in this state of high-stakes urgency, you lose the ability to see the middle ground or even the progress. In the midst of the perfectionism, you’re struggling with doubts. These doubts can manifest in one of two opposite states of mind.

  • Reinforcing Compulsions: You might feed your intrusive thought and compulsion loop by “fixing” everything that’s out of order in your life with fervor and urgency because perfection makes you feel temporarily safe.

While there’s nothing wrong with proactively curating your life, the pressure can be excruciating. The urgency and the disproportionate punishment for imperfection can keep you from recognizing that most of life is actually lived somewhere between progress and imperfect completion.

  • Paralysis: On the flip side of that fervor is the second state of mind, paralysis. When your internal dictator tells you that anything less than perfection is total failure, your brain decides that it might be safer not to try at all.

In these cases, while your outward behavior looks like laziness, complacency, or maybe even avoidance, your internal experience feels a lot more like OCD compulsions, failure, and fear.

No Room for Growth

With an all-or-nothing mentality, there is no room for being a work in progress or for the beautiful reality of growth. Because the internal dictator demands immediate results, you might find yourself disproportionately pressured or rendered paralyzed. Neither reaction is healthy nor productive.

This can even spill into your spiritual life. If your self-worth is measured in the number and the quality of accomplishments, what you’re telling yourself is that you’re only acceptable when your to-do list is completed to perfection. Not only is that distorting to your own self-identity, but it can turn your spiritual relationship with God into a transaction.

You might begin to view the Bible as a list of unattainable standards that you’re failing to meet. While there’s truth in the fact that you’re never going to attain the perfection needed to circumvent the Plan of Salvation, an all-or-nothing mentality also removes the beauty of progress, redemption, and God’s grace.

The Fear of Being “Under Construction”

The reason you might cling to this transactional view of yourself and of God is often rooted in a desire to avoid the vulnerability of being unfinished or with obvious, tangible faults.

Maybe you’re only fixing the most publicly facing parts of your life because you’re afraid people will see your faults. Or maybe you have chosen to hide your insecurities behind your failures. If you convince yourself and the world that you’re not trying, then you don’t have to face the terrifying possibility of trying your hardest and failing.

In either case, whether you’re hiding behind a manicured lawn or a mountain of unfinished laundry, the root is still the same. It’s the fear of being seen in the in-between.

The in-between is a vulnerable place because it’s where you lack both the shield of perfection and the excuse of apathy. It’s a raw, unpolished reality that tells everyone that you’re human and that might feel like a threat to your safety.

Adult Therapy

Part of the healing process in adult therapy with a Christian mental health expert is learning to exist peacefully and confidently in the mess. Therapy can provide a structured environment to overthrow that pesky internal dictator by addressing the psychological roots of the pressure you feel.

If you’re trapped in an OCD or anxiety loop, your brain might get addicted to the relief of the immediate fix. Through exposure and response prevention (ERP), you will learn how to sit with the unfinished parts of your life without panicking. It will help you prove to your nervous system that you’re safe, even with the dishes in the sink.

Using Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) will help you learn to cross-examine the voice that equates imperfection with worthlessness. It will help you replace that all-or-nothing mentality with a more realistic mindset. You can have a new mindset that allows for human limitation and God’s grace.

Your human frailty is what shifts the burden of completion from your shoulders to His. God is faithful to you with a promise of persistence. Philippians 1:6 says, “Being confident of this, that He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 1:6, NIV)

This is perhaps the most direct answer to your need to fix it today or abandon it altogether. It reminds you that you’re a work in progress, and it establishes a lifelong timeline for your completion.

If you’re struggling with finding the middle ground between perfectionism, apathy, and self-inflicted pressure, call one of our capable counselors to schedule adult therapy. They are here to help.

item.title: How Christian Premarital Counseling Can Save Your Marriage Before It Starts
item.description:
Using the SYMBIS Assessment to Build a Christ-Centered Foundation

Tom and Tina met at a gathering of mutual friends and quickly hit it off. After spending time in a group setting getting to know one another, Tom asked Tina out on their first date, and the rest is history. Tina believes Tom is “the one” because they have so much in common and have fun together – a perfect fit. Tom adores many qualities of Tina; she is beautiful, funny, and easy to be with.

They soon became engaged, and everything became focused on venues, menus, invitations, and preparations. So far, planning the wedding has been exciting and fun. They can’t wait to start their life together – it is going to be great.

Many couples spend months preparing for a wedding but little time preparing for marriage. By participating in Christian premarital counseling, couples will be guided to identify strengths, address challenges, develop tools, and gain insights. One of the most successful premarital tools available is the SYMBIS (Saving Your Marriage Before It Starts) Assessment developed by Drs. Les and Leslie Parrott.

Why Premarital Counseling Matters

According to research, couples who complete premarital counseling are 31% less likely to divorce and report higher marriage satisfaction. As couples are unique individuals created by God with their own stories from their family of origin, expectations and assumptions, family backgrounds, habits, and beliefs should be explored before the vows are exchanged. This will help to significantly improve marital outcomes.

Marriage is the uniting of two broken, sinful people in a fallen world. It takes work and intentionality to have a fulfilling and joyful union. As stated in Prov 24:3-4, “A house is built by wisdom, and it is established by understanding; by knowledge the rooms are filled with every precious and beautiful treasure.” (CSB)

Marriage is a sacred covenant and should not be entered lightly. According to the Cambridge Dictionary, “covenant” is defined as “a formal agreement or promise between two or more people.” A covenant is a lifelong binding, because as stated in Genesis 2:24, “two are united into one.” (NLT), thus, the importance of learning about one another before going down the aisle.

Exploring common areas of hidden conflict or expectations helps to promote a healthier union. The SYMBIS assessment areas include communication, conflict resolution, finances, roles and responsibilities, intimacy, spiritual life, and family relationships.

What is the SYMBIS assessment?

SYMBIS is a research-based premarital tool developed by Dr. Les and Leslie Parrott. It is specifically designed for engaged and seriously dating couples. The couples complete the assessment individually online, and then a report will be sent to their counselor to then go over in session. Personalized feedback is provided, along with identification of strengths and growth areas.

Areas Assessed by SYMBIS

Better Understanding of Personality styles assists couples in discovering habits that could create future conflict. By revealing blind spots, the assessment gives couples insight into potential challenges, allowing them to work together and better understand one another. God has created each one of us uniquely.

There are differences in sex (male/female), personality, and family background. These differences are what draw us together and complement one another. The assessment promotes growth individually and as a couple.

Search me, God, and know my heart.– Psalm 139:23

Improving communication by helping couples identify their communication strengths and weaknesses so that they learn how to hear and understand one another, thus encouraging healthy conversations about difficult topics and avoiding miscommunications.

Couples learn communication skills to help them listen with curiosity and reflect what they hear so their spouse will feel understood. Often, couples allow the busyness of life to affect their relationship. It is important to set aside time to meet and stay connected.

Can two walk together unless they are agreed? – Amos 3:3

Learning to navigate conflict by developing skills to work through challenging issues. It is not a matter of if conflict will occur but when. Even issues that seem small or inconsequential to one may be important, or an unmet need, to the other and, if left undiscussed, can lead to larger issues. Undiscussed issues can build up, causing couples to get defensive, shut down (stonewall), or respond poorly, so it is imperative to learn and use skills to resolve conflict.

Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to become angry.– James 1:19

Understanding financial attitudes is crucial for a harmonious marriage. Discovering who is the spender and who is the saver, and how finances will be managed, are important things to know. It is also crucial to be on the same page and share the same goals. Finances can cause tension and allow for many misunderstandings, which can be eliminated or more easily worked out with greater understanding of one another’s views and opinions of money.

The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance. – Proverbs 21:5

Finding family-of-origin influences by examining how childhood experiences shape adult relationships through exploring and understanding inherited patterns.It is common to get comfortable with the way we do things.

For example, a woman thought that to cook a ham, you must cut off the ends. When questioned by her husband about this practice, she responded, “It is how my mother taught me to cook a ham.” Not really understanding why, she asked her mom, who explained that the ends were cut off because she didn’t have a pan large enough to fit the entire ham. This is an example of how we learn things from our family of origin and continue doing what we know.

Creating realistic expectations for marriage by encouraging healthy discussions about future goals and dreams and addressing myths about marriage. It is important for couples to head in the same direction regarding their marriage because unrealistic or uncommunicated expectations become a source of conflict and disappointment.

Couples will learn to see the big picture and to consider the needs of their future spouse, taking their eyes off themselves, in an attempt to understand and compromise. Expectations are good, but high expectations can be unhealthy, putting a strain on the relationship.

Exploring spiritual compatibility by encouraging conversations about faith, church involvement, prayer, and discipleship. Helping couples establish a shared vision for a Christ-centered home where it is a marriage of three – husband, wife, and Christ at the center.

Though one may be overpowered, two can defend themselves. A cord of three strands is not quickly broken.– Ecclesiastes 4:12

Counselor’s Role

The counselor’s role in the SYMBIS process is to interpret the assessment results, help couples apply God’s truth to relationship challenges, and encourage spiritual growth alongside relational growth. The counselor also creates a safe place for honest conversations that address difficult issues by encouraging vulnerability and transparency and helps couples develop healthy problem-solving skills.

Speaking the truth in love.– Ephesians 4:15

By participating in premarital counseling, couples will benefit from

  • greater confidence (entering marriage with clarity and understanding
  • feeling prepared for future challenges)
  • stronger communication by learning practical skills to resolve conflict and developing healthy communication skills
  • developing a deeper emotional connection by gaining better understanding of one another
  • building trust and intimacy
  • gaining a stronger spiritual foundation where Christ is the center of the relationship
  • developing shared spiritual goals

Unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labor in vain.– Psalm 127:1

Conclusion

Marriage is one of God’s greatest gifts and one of the most important commitments. Christ-centered premarital counseling provides couples with tools, wisdom, and biblical guidance before marriage begins. The SYMBIS Assessment offers valuable insights that help build a strong and lasting relationship. Invest today.

Are you engaged or seriously considering marriage? Discover how the SYMBIS Assessment and premarital counseling can help you build a strong marriage. Schedule your session today and begin building your covenant foundation.

Above all, love each other deeply, because love covers over a multitude of sins. – 1 Peter 4:8

The post How Christian Premarital Counseling Can Save Your Marriage Before It Starts appeared first on Texas Christian Counseling.

item.title: ADHD and Emotional Regulation: Why Feelings Hit Harder and What Can Help
item.description:
Emotional regulation is not a matter of just choosing to calm down. For people with ADHD, emotional regulation is the hardest part of the day. The distraction and impulsivity affect how emotions are felt, processed, and expressed.

Feelings hit hard and take longer to settle in this pattern of constraint, relationships, and derailed focus. ADHD and emotional regulation are tough when the brain works differently.

What ADHD and Emotional Regulation Actually Look Like

ADHD is often described as a focus problem. Focus is part of it, but the ability to regulate emotions also plays a big role. A significant number of people with ADHD find it difficult to manage the intensity and duration of their emotional responses.

Emotional regulation includes rapid mood shifts, low frustration tolerance, and a heightened sensitivity to rejection. These reflect real neurological differences in how the ADHD brain processes information.

Part of the brain that handles impulse control and emotional braking works differently in those with ADHD. The signal to slow down often arrives late or not at all. It’s just the biology of an ADHD brain.

Understanding this distinction is important because those with ADHD believe they are too emotional, reactive, or too much. Narratives like this do more damage than expected. The reality of the situation is that the brain is doing something specific and identifiable, which means it should be addressed as such.

Research suggests that there is an increase in the number of adults with ADHD who experience a degree of emotional dysregulation. This indicates that the experience is increasingly common. When individuals understand that what they experience has a neurological basis, it shifts the way they relate to themselves. This is one step toward real change.

Why Rejection Feels So Devastating

One of the most talked-about emotional experiences in the ADHD community is known as rejection-sensitive dysphoria. This is an intense emotional response that occurs with criticism, rejection, or failure.

Individuals without ADHD rarely take a critical comment to heart. However, an individual navigating ADHD with emotional regulation handles it differently. Challenges may be met with shame, anger, and withdrawal. What is labeled as drama is simply the nervous system registering something more intense than what most people experience.

Emotional sensitivity of this intensity can make everyday interactions seem exhausting. Social situations may carry extra weight when there’s a low level of awareness of something being said or done that may land the wrong way. When this happens, the fallout feels enormous, and some individuals with ADHD will begin to avoid similar situations where rejection is possible. This results in missed opportunities and isolation.

A pattern of avoidance can quietly reshape a person’s world. Friendships may thin out, and professional opportunities are left unpursued. The individual may not even realize there’s a connection between avoidance and sensitivity.

This is a cycle that requires recognition in order to understand the devastation of rejection. Recognizing this cycle requires an outside perspective from someone who can name the pattern and help the individual see it clearly. Finding this type of clarity is hard, and for many, it may become a turning point that moves them toward seeking help.

Scripture addresses this deep, emotional pain honestly. The book of Psalms contains many instances of raw and unfiltered cries from people who were overwhelmed and not pretending. (Psalm 22, 34, 55). God does not see this type of honesty as weakness. It is a model for processing what is real rather than burying it.

ADHD and Emotional Regulation Strategies That Help

Emotional dysregulation and ADHD respond to intervention. Different approaches have shown real promise, and most people find a combination that will work better than any single strategy.

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy helps people identify thought patterns that may intensify emotional responses. After these patterns are identified, individuals can build accurate interpretations of triggering events. It is a process that takes time, but it does produce lasting change.

Mindfulness-based practices such as breathing exercises may create small but meaningful pauses between a trigger and a reaction. The pause creates a different outlook for those whose emotional brake pedal is slow. Core ADHD symptoms may be addressed through medication that reduces emotional intensity.

Structured daily routines are important to a regulated nervous system. When the body is depleted, a small lifestyle adjustment can make a big difference in emotional stability.

In Scripture, Paul addresses what it means to be content in all circumstances. He didn’t do this because it came naturally. He discussed it because it was something practiced and developed over time. This resonates deeply with people working on emotional regulation. It reduces the expectation of perfection and builds a skill, one day and one situation at a time, with patience for the process. (Philippians 4:11).

When patience extends to the tools, the right combination of strategies can be developed over time. There are no two people with ADHD who are exactly alike. This means that strategies will look different for each one. This is what makes the process worth pursuing. By approaching this process with honesty and support, the result is a meaningful and lasting change.

How Christian Counselors Can Support ADHD and Emotional Regulation

There is an added layer of shame that comes with the emotional intensity for Christians who struggle with ADHD. These individuals feel they should be more patient and more self-controlled. Christian counselors are trying to address the clinical and spiritual dimensions of this experience.

They help individuals separate biology and spirituality. What is a neurological reality versus a moral failure? This is valuable because these two things are not the same. The distinction can create freedom for someone who has spent years feeling like a spiritual failure because of how their brain works.

Christian counselors understand neurodevelopmental differences, which helps develop practical coping skills and hold space for grief, frustration, or other spiritual questions. Many adults are not diagnosed until their thirties or beyond. Discovering this brings up questions about what they experienced over the years, such as grief and anger. Being able to work through these discoveries with a counselor who integrates faith means the conversation doesn’t remain surface-level.

The integration of faith and practical coping skills matters more than one may think. They should not be separate from mental health. Many people use the lens of faith to understand various situations in life. A Christian counselor who understands this lens may offer clients a way to make sense of their diagnosis that will deepen their faith rather than challenge it.

Finding Steadiness When Emotions Run High

Moving forward with emotional regulation and ADHD doesn’t mean the individual is at the mercy of every feeling that arrives. There is a steadiness that comes from understanding what’s actually happening in the brain. When the individual stops suppressing or pretending that emotions are fine, they build skills that work with the ADHD nervous system. This is the awareness that changes things.

This process can also involve faith, which will create a foundation of knowing they are not defined by their worst emotional moments. Faith communities help them understand they are not alone in navigating these situations.

A Christian counselor who understands the spiritual and clinical aspects offers a framework of tools and perspective that will hold both without forcing a choice between them. This type of support is essential to making a difference for those who struggle with ADHD and emotional regulation.

If emotional dysregulation is affecting your daily life, your relationships, or someone you care about, you don’t have to figure it all out on your own. Reaching out for support isn’t a sign of weakness – it can be an important first step toward better understanding yourself and developing healthier ways to respond to difficult emotions.

In my work as a therapist, I help individuals better understand the connection between ADHD, emotions, relationships, and the patterns that can leave them feeling overwhelmed or stuck. If any of this sounds familiar and you feel counseling might be helpful, please consider reaching out to me – Joseph Bennett, LPC – to talk about what you’re experiencing and what your next steps might look like.

item.title: Breaking the Hold: Social Media and Teens
item.description:
Social media is a great way for your teen to keep in touch with extended family and friends, check in with school and church organizations, and learn more about local employment and education opportunities. Social media can also present dangers in the form of an increased likelihood of anxiety and depression, shorter attention spans, exposure to things outside of your beliefs and values, and targeted behavior from bullies and predators.

We don’t want to scare our children away from technology, but we should consider social media and teens when thinking about the best ways to keep children safe.

The following are suggestions for breaking the hold and prioritizing safety when it comes to social media and teens.

Make Your Teen Aware of Their State of Mind When Using an App

The link between social media and teens can be emotional. The behavior can become compulsive when they take a break, need to check what friends are doing, or feel overwhelmed. Talk with your teen about how they feel before, during, and after using an app to uncover triggers.

Limit Social Media Access

Most apps include a setting that lets you or your teen check app usage. This number can be enlightening. Are they spending a few minutes a day checking in with friends, or are they scrolling for hours? Set app limits or specific rules for when your teen can use the platform.

Help Your Teen Find Safe Online Groups for Their Interests

As adults, we know that not all groups are created equal or are safe for minors. If your child wants to find an online group for their interests, help them look for legitimate groups. Teach them proper etiquette and safety protocols, such as never sharing their address or personal details.

Discuss Who to Follow and Unfollow

Some profiles lead to comparison, discontentment, and feelings of unworthiness. Help your teen identify negative accounts and unfollow them. Look for accounts with Christian values, positive body image messages, and good role models.

Put Away All Phones at the Dinner Table

Get back to the 1990s by implementing a device-free table. Ask the family to leave all phones on the counter or in their rooms during meals, or during movie or game nights. While traveling in the car, focus more on the conversation, music, podcasts, or audiobooks as a family than on social media.

Disconnect From Phones Yourself

Be a role model for your children by distancing yourself from your phone at specific times during the day. Let your teen see that phones should be put away while working, if possible. You may want to choose one day a week when phones are checked only once in the morning and again in the evening, such as Sundays.

Choose One Screen at a Time

How often have you sat down to watch a movie or stream a show and find yourself scrolling your phone? Teens do this as well, including while watching something on their computer or TV or trying to do homework on a tablet or laptop. Teach your child to choose one screen at a time, and to put the other away.

Teach Your Teen to Decide Why They Are Opening an App

Online and social media addiction is real and can lead to anxiety and depression. Teach your teen to have an objective before opening an app. Do they want to message a friend, post a picture, make a video, or watch a particular post? Social media is not inherently evil, but children have to be taught discernment. If they do want to scroll, have them set a timer.

Get Offline

Remind your teen that life exists offline. Encourage them to hang out with friends, play sports, join clubs, and go outside and play. Teens are not too old to go outside and ride bikes and skateboards, swim, or play ball. Consider joining in on the fun without devices.

Consider Counseling If Your Teens Show Signs of Anxiety or Depression

Too much social media can lead to signs of anxiety and depression, including:

  • Feeling on edge
  • Compulsive behaviors
  • Unable to cope without leaning on social media
  • Withdrawing from friends and family
  • Sleeping too much or too little
  • Appetite changes
  • Rapid weight changes
  • Talk of self-harm or suicide

Important: If your teen is harming themselves or has suicidal ideation, seek help immediately.

Virtual and In-Person Christian Counseling Sessions for Teens

It is normal to be concerned about social media and teens. Good mental health is critical for a child’s overall well-being. Our Christian counseling center matches clients with counselors, including those specializing in social media and teens. Contact us today to schedule an in-person or virtual session.

item.title: What is EMDR Therapy? Is it the Right Course of Treatment for You?
item.description:
You may have heard of the term EMDR. Lately, EMDR has grown in popularity as an effective mental health treatment to resolve deeper wounds, memories, and/or experiences from your past. Simply put, Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) is known for its unique holistic body and mind approach that aims to help you process trauma.

Continuing to evolve within psychology and mental health, EMDR is acknowledged as an evidence-based practice designed to alleviate distress using a bilateral stimulation method.

What makes EMDR different from traditional therapy is that EMDR involves less talking. In fact, by following the guidance of the bilateral stimulation of the back-and-forth, side-to-side alternation, your body and brain are healing naturally on their own from this motion, making reactions less intense.

By focusing on this method, you are processing the way your mind and body want you to at your own pace. Talk therapy asks you to reiterate the details of your trauma to your therapist.

Although it may make sense that you would need to know what happened in order to help, resharing every detail of the trauma can often be retraumatizing simply by recounting the story. Your mind and body will inadvertently react as if the danger from the trauma is happening all over again.

What is EMDR? A look back to where it all began

EMDR was developed by psychologist Dr. Francine Shapiro in 1987. She realized while walking in the park that her rapid eye movements from one point to another decreased the negative emotion associated with her distressing memories. The intensity of her thoughts and emotions lessened.

This led her to do her own research through case studies to evaluate the effectiveness of this treatment approach. Shapiro developed her model and approach to EMDR treatment, and within a few years of controlled studies and investigation of the treatment of PTSD, EMDR was found to have “significant decreases in ratings of subjective distress and significant increases in rating of confidence in a positive belief.”

In 1990, Shapiro conducted her first EMDR training for licensed mental health professionals. Since then, there have been hundreds of case studies that have shown the effectiveness of cognitive changes, and it is recognized as an effective PTSD treatment.

Though EMDR has been surrounded by controversy as a newer approach to psychotherapy that was established and taught through experimental procedures, EMDR and Shapiro have been recognized for providing relief from negative-shaped thoughts, beliefs, emotions, and images stored from unprocessed memories.

Shortly thereafter, the EMDR Institute was created, now known as EMDRIA (EMDR International Association), and has since held conferences and trainings across the world.

So how does EMDR work?

EMDR follows an Adaptive Information Processing (AIP) model that accesses and processes the traumatic memories or experiences you have had. This model looks at how your brain stores traumatic memories from your past differently than a more normal memory. When a disturbing or distressing event occurs, your brain doesn’t store memories smoothly.

There is a disconnection between what you experienced and what your brain remembers. Because your brain remembers the experience a certain way and hasn’t healed or processed it, your brain doesn’t understand that the danger it felt from it is over. Your brain and body are sensitive to the danger, pain, and injury it experienced from the memory, whether remembered or suppressed.

By looking at your past, present, and future, EMDR therapy addresses your full lifespan, knowing that by processing your past, it will provide you with the ability to be less activated by a present trigger that’s connected to your past. EMDR aims to relieve you of your distress, shift negative beliefs, and help you move past the things that caused you to be stuck.

What does EMDR therapy involve?

EMDR consists of eight phases that occur over multiple therapy sessions. The exact length of EMDR treatment varies person to person based on their needs and how the processing of the eight phases goes.

Typically, most people do a standard 55-minute therapy session once a week, taking time between therapy sessions to give their brain and body rest. However, some prefer doing a lot of work in a shorter amount of time in an EMDR therapy intensive (full-day, multi-day therapy session).

The Eight Phases

History and Information Gathering

This phase begins with an intake, gathering information about your past and what brings you to therapy. Additional information gathering may include checking for your level of dissociation, substance abuse, any suicide or self-harm risk, and medical issues that could impact your EMDR reprocessing.

Your therapist will see if EMDR treatment is a fit for what your goals are, assess your readiness, and will develop a treatment plan for the selected traumatic events you’ve shared.

Preparation

Your therapist will explain any necessary EMDR information, terms, and what you can expect. Your internal and external resources will be assessed and strengthened to prepare for coping with and handling any emotional disturbance that comes up during and in between therapy sessions. The next four phases (3-6) often happen together to reprocess an event or memory.

Assessment

The assessment phase looks deeper into an image, negative belief, emotions, and body sensations, and is measured using the Subjective Unit of Disturbance (SUD) scale and the Validity of Cognition (VOC) scale.

Desensitization

Desensitization occurs while focusing on the traumatic event while simultaneously engaging in side-to-side Bilateral Stimulation (BLS) through eye movements, sounds, taps, or buzzers. This continues until your SUD number reduces to zero. During this phase, new thoughts, sensations, images, and feelings may arise, which is part of the desensitization and reprocessing of the memory.

Installation

When desensitization is done, installation begins, where you strengthen a positive belief with the memory you were processing.

Body Scan

In this phase, you are asked to imagine the memory or event in your mind with the negative belief shared during the assessment phase. Then you are to scan your full body to see if any lingering body sensations are still present.

Closure and Stabilization

In every session that entails phases 3-6, your therapist will end it with phase 7 closure. With guidance from your therapist, you will return to a state of calmness and bring your awareness back to the present, whether you have completed the reprocessing of the memory or not. This allows you to be clear of any disturbances in your mind and body so you can go back to your typical day-to-day life.

Reevaluation and Continuing Care

At the beginning of each therapy session, you and your therapist will briefly check in and discuss your last processed memory and where the distress level is with it. If there appears to be residual distress, you may need to go back to phases 3-7 of the same memory. But if the distress remains low and the positive belief is strong, you may proceed to a new memory and continue your treatment plan and/or process future events related to the memory worked on.

Is EMDR the right course of treatment for you?

EMDR emphasizes that your distressing memory will not go away, as we cannot erase our past. But what EMDR helps do is shift the way your brain recalls it from something that once felt distressing or in control of you into a memory that knows that the event occurred, it does not impact you, and it is something that occurred as part of your story.

EMDR calms your nervous system, brings you from survival mode to thriving, and gives your brain the message that you are not in danger anymore. When you have something that triggers you in your present, and the trigger feels similar to the memory you processed, your reaction will be minimal and less negatively impactful due to the time you took to process and reshape the way your brain and body remembers it.

After reading all of this and you still are not sure if EMDR is the right type of therapy treatment for you, contact us and talk to an EMDR therapist who can answer your questions directly. I provide EMDR to both adult individuals and couples seeking relief from areas where they feel stuck.

item.title: 3 Major Causes of Relationship Problems
item.description:
If you have the joy of being in relationships with other people, like siblings, parents, romantic partners, friends, neighbors, and colleagues, then you know that those relationships can be fulfilling. Sometimes, however, there’s an issue that spoils things, putting a strain on the relationship.

Every relationship has its problems, and some of those persist over time. Sometimes the problems in our relationship are nothing we’ve created. They are simply the seasons that we go through in life, combined with our reactions to those seasons. Other times, there are problems we contribute to that cause issues in the relationship.

Some of the problems in our relationships flow from us and how we are within those relationships. For example, a person who wrestles with controlling their anger may find that it damages their relationships with everyone in their lives.

There are many different kinds of problems that can plague relationships, stemming from a wide range of sources. They can come from poor attachment from our childhood that makes it hard to bond successfully with our significant others. Another source can be addictions that alienate us from our loved ones. Mental health challenges, such as major depressive disorder or Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, can make maintaining relationships difficult.

There are different kinds of relationships, and something that’s an issue in one may not be in others. For instance, struggling with physical intimacy may not be an issue with your colleagues or friends, but it can affect a marriage. In this article, we’ll focus on 3 areas where relationship problems can come from, regardless of the kind of relationship it is.

Relationship Problems from a Lack of Empathy

Empathy is our capacity and ability to understand what other people feel and go through. Empathy allows us to see things from another person’s perspective, and it enables us to imagine ourselves in their situation. While they all relate to this, empathy has different forms.

Somatic empathy involves having a physical reaction in response to another’s experience, such as turning away or blushing when we see someone else feel embarrassed. Affective empathy is our capacity to understand what another person is feeling and being able to respond appropriately to those emotions. Cognitive empathy focuses on understanding another person’s state of mind and what they might be thinking in response to a situation.

Whatever form it takes, having empathy is key to having successful relationships. If we cannot understand what the people around us are feeling, or we cannot fathom what they are thinking and the appropriate response to those thoughts and feelings, that makes relationships incredibly difficult and awkward. Relationships are all about seeing one another and appropriately responding through love.

If you can’t understand what the other person is feeling or experiencing, it’s easy to dismiss their feelings without paying them any mind. It’s our empathy that allows us to ‘read the room’ and know it’s not appropriate to carry on celebrating when we can see that our spouse has had a rough day.

Empathy enables us to see that a person is hurt by what we said and moderate our words and actions carefully. Empathy is what allows two people in a relationship to meet one another in their frail humanity, offer support, and care for each other in ways that are appropriate and meaningful to the situation. Without empathy, relationships are frustrating, and you don’t connect because you’re simply not on the same page.

Empathy helps with forgiveness and is instrumental for humanizing others so that we offer them the same grace we offer ourselves. In any relationship, people will do and say things that hurt or disappoint us. How do we receive that? Empathy helps us to look at the situation from their point of view, even while we feel hurt because our point of view was disregarded.

We might not agree with the perspective and reasons a person has, but if we can at least see it from their side, we can understand it. Understanding something is not the same as excusing it. Empathy helps us on the path to forgive the inexcusable. When we see others as human, just as we are, we can see how we are capable of the same things.

Looking to Our Needs Before Those of Others

The second main cause of relationship problems is that we tend to consider ourselves first before other people. We are in our own bodies, and we inhabit our own minds. This makes us aware of what we need and desire, more so than we can see the needs of others. And sometimes, we might see the needs of others but feel our own needs. There is an immediacy to feeling our own needs.

We have a deep bias toward ourselves. That is reflected in the ways we can excuse our own behavior while holding others to a stricter standard, or how we will try to meet our needs first before we meet those of others. Of course, there’s a place and time to meet your own needs first because not doing so is detrimental to yourself and the people around you.

Parents need their sleep so that they can function well for their kids. Each spouse needs time and space to rest and refresh themselves so that they can give their marriage the best they’ve got. Friends need to meet their obligations outside the friendship, and that means they aren’t always available. This is as it should be.

The problem is that our desire to meet our needs goes beyond this. Often, we might not be willing to extend others the same courtesies we desire when our needs are the ones on the line.

Relationships require people to think of others, and quite often to put the interests of others before their own (in healthy ways). The sacrifices of time, energy, resources, and allowing ourselves to be vulnerable that we make for one another are what relationships are built upon. If we look mainly or only at what we want, that will lead to disaster.

Even within the church, it’s easy to look out for ourselves and not at what can benefit others. Paul says in Philippians, “…not looking to your own interests but each of you to the interests of the others.” (Philippians 2:4, NLT) In his letter to the Christians in the city of Ephesus, he writes, “Do not let any unwholesome talk come out of your mouths, but only what is helpful for building others up according to their needs, that it may benefit those who listen” (Ephesians 4:29 NIV).

I might want to crack a joke that makes me chuckle, but I need to consider whether what I’m saying will benefit the people listening. I have my needs and desires in that moment, but so do others. Instead of considering my own needs as paramount, I need to do what will benefit others.

In that moment, you lose the chuckle and the opportunity to get something off your chest. What you gain by keeping silent or by choosing to say something else that benefits the other person is that you’re contributing to their well-being. It requires a mind and heart that God is reshaping to look more and more like Jesus Christ for you to consider others before yourself.

Relationship Problems from Not Listening Well

Lastly, a major cause of relationship problems is not listening well to others. We are not the great listeners we think we are, and that’s something we all need to grow in. Some of this was mentioned already in the points about empathy and the needs of others. When we don’t listen well to others, we don’t know where they’re at, what they need, and what their concerns are. If we are not on the same page, that can cause a lot of conflict in a relationship.

We need to listen well to others so that we can know what they need. That’s how we can know in what ways to be there for the people we’re in relationship with. Sometimes we don’t hear the people in our lives, understand their concerns, and allow them to know that we understand them. It can create the impression that we don’t care about them.

One of the best gifts you can give someone is to listen to them, and to listen well. It takes time and skill to be a good listener, and every relationship can benefit from it. There’s probably no greater help to a relationship than being a good listener. If you do that for one another, that is absolutely priceless.

Listening well helps you avoid conflict because you know the areas of concern and what the actual needs are. It also allows you to chart a course that helps you meet those needs effectively. Being a good listener allows you to make effective decisions because you’re working from knowledge and not supposition.

When we fail to listen, that undermines emotional intimacy. This creates room for conflict and often escalates it. With time and intentionality, we can grow in learning to listen well, show empathy, and care for the needs and interests of others. This is how we cultivate healthy relationships that last.

Help for Relationship Problems

If you want to have stronger, healthier relationships, help is available. Consider working with a Christian therapist on this site to learn more about fostering the relationships you long for. Reach out to the office by calling or filling out the online form for more information.

item.title: Journeying Through Loss: Understanding the Grief Process
item.description:
Despite our sometimes-stark differences, some things are common to us all. One of those things that we have in common with each other is that we grieve losses of various kinds. Grief is indeed one of the more universal human experiences, but it is also true that it remains poorly misunderstood and inadequately supported. Understanding the grief process can help you as you try to make sense of life after loss.

The Need to Pause After Loss

What is grief, and why do we need to grieve when we’ve experienced loss? Grief is the process we go through to come to terms with the fact that we’ve experienced a loss of some kind. Grief is how we adjust to no longer having a partner, whether because they’ve died or because you’ve undergone a divorce. Grief is the way you process having lost your community or sense of safety because you’ve moved or because of being a victim of crime.

When we experience loss, it comes with a swathe of emotions and the need to adjust to a new reality. You may experience feelings like shock and disbelief. Some experience deep anger, at themselves, at the person who left them, or at the Lord. Others feel a paralyzing fear as they contemplate what life will look like in the coming days, and others are numb. The question that faces a person who has experienced loss is usually, “What now?”

The many questions, doubts, emotions, and challenges that loss stirs up aren’t easy to come to terms with. For one thing, they imply that things are changing, and that what once could be counted on – the things that once made up your life as you knew it – are no longer the same. Now, you’ll have to adjust and figure out how to live without that loved one, without that same sense of place, or without the resources that you once could count on.

Our culture prizes forward movement, looking to the future, being productive, and possessing emotional composure. That often means that grief is treated as though it’s a temporary state that the individual should simply move through and get over as quickly as possible. Instead of seeing it as a deep wound that requires sustained, wise, and patient care, grief and loss are often treated like a superficial wound that you quickly dress and then forget about.

One of the tragedies of how our culture deals with loss and grief is that many people are left to grieve alone and in silence. If their grief shows, it sometimes invites reprimand, leading to an added sense of shame about the depth and duration of their grief and pain. In this way, grief is sometimes shuttered away and not given the chance to be dealt with properly. That grief doesn’t go away; it’s there, beneath the surface, and it affects your well-being in the long run.

There is a need to pause after loss, to give yourself time to grieve, to process things, and to begin rebuilding again. Grieving well doesn’t mean everything has to come to a standstill; life doesn’t afford us that luxury, as houses need to be cleaned, children need to be clothed, work needs doing, and bills need paying. Grieving does mean giving yourself space to work through the loss in the midst of everything else that may be happening.

How Grief Affects You

While grief is itself a process, going through that process has an impact on you. Facing your anger, sadness, sense of relief, or confusion about your loss isn’t easy. Often, people would rather avoid dealing with these complex and heavy emotions, and so it’s easier to bury these feelings, deny they exist, or simply find ways to not engage with them.

Grief affects you physically, emotionally, spiritually, and mentally. When you’ve experienced significant loss, it affects you spiritually, as you ask questions such as “Why did this happen?” “Where is God in the midst of all this?” or “What does this mean?” Loss and the grief that follows can leave you asking these deep, existential questions about meaning, purpose, and God’s presence in the darkest valleys.

Physically, your grief can manifest as disruptions in your sleeping patterns. Some people struggle to fall and stay asleep, while others find themselves sleeping far more than usual. You may also find that your appetite changes, you feel tired quite often, your immune system feels like it’s weakened and under constant attack, and you carry a sort of heaviness that weighs on you in ways you struggle to describe.

Grief also affects you cognitively in various ways. Some people find it harder to remember things; it feels like your mind is losing grasp of things like names, places, faces, and other details. Grief also affects your ability to concentrate, and it can also make it harder to make decisions, even about simple everyday matters like what to wear and in what order to perform daily chores.

In terms of your emotions, grief surfaces a variety of feelings including sadness, guilt, anxiety, longing, confusion, relief, and anger. These emotions point to the fact that you’ve lost something or someone that mattered to you, and when that bond is severed, it produces a variety of emotional responses. Even complicated relationships, like with an estranged parent, can manifest in these emotions.

Grief will often run its natural course. That’s not to say that grief is a linear process, or that it comes to an end. Rather, it’s to say that you learn to live with the loss, to carry on. However, grief can also become complicated, whether by being intensified, prolonged, or leaving you feeling stuck in such a way that you’re not carrying on with the business of living.

This complicated grief is marked by an intense and persistent yearning for what you’ve lost, having difficulty accepting the loss, feeling bitter or emotionally numb, and being unable to engage with life again. This kind of complicated grief happens when a person experiences sudden or traumatic loss. It also occurs when a person doesn’t have adequate social support to help them grieve, or when they are ambivalent toward the loss.

Looking Beyond the Five Stages of Grief

Grief is, at its heart, how we come to terms with loss. One of the more common ways to understand grief is through the Kübler-Ross model of grief, which has five stages. These stages are denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance. What this model has done is help people understand that grief is a process, and not a single event. This is helpful, especially in those circumstances where people are too quick to move on from loss.

Having said that, the Kübler-Ross model of grief is also often misunderstood by people. Some people assume that the five stages name a neat progression from one emotional state to the next, and then out the other side with acceptance. Grief isn’t a linear journey that takes you from denial to acceptance in an orderly fashion. These stages don’t occur in order; they also don’t occur once, and they don’t apply to everyone or every kind of loss in the same way.

Grief often occurs as waves, and you could find yourself feeling anger and depression on the same day. Sometimes a particular experience surfaces a specific feeling, like when you walk in a familiar park and find it hard to accept that your loved one is just gone.

Another way to understand grief is through what’s known as the dual process model of grief, which describes how people experiencing loss will go between loss-orientation, which is when they’re engaging directly with the memories, the grief, and the pain of loss, and restoration-orientation, which is them attending to new roles they take up, life changes that the loss necessitated, and looking to the future.

Dealing with loss in a healthy way means moving between both orientations. Life won’t look like a steady progression through the various stages of grief; rather, it’ll be more of a non-linear, dynamic process that doesn’t look the same for any two people dealing with loss.

As you journey through grief, you don’t have to do it alone. Whether the grief and loss that you’re dealing with is old or more recent, whether it’s clean-cut or complicated, and whether you’ve even named that grief for yourself, you can have respectful company along with you on the journey. Christian counseling offers you a structured and safe place to be honest about what you’ve lost, how you feel about it, and what you need to help you go on.

If you want to unpack your grief and loss, you can browse our online counselor directory or reach out to our office today to schedule an appointment with a Christian counselor. Your counselor will journey with you, without placing you under the pressure of a timeline or a cultural script that you should follow in dealing with your grief.

Reach out today to learn more.

item.title: Finding the Right Help: The Value of Naming Addictions Like Chemical Dependency
item.description:
When someone starts looking for mental health support, they expect clear answers. Instead, most likely, you’ll hear a mix of terms that leave you wondering what applies to you, especially when it comes to addiction therapy.

You reach out for help because something doesn’t feel right. You’re tired, anxious, and using substances to get through the day. Yet most people say they don’t really know which category they fall into.

Is it addiction? Is it chemical dependency? Substance abuse? Use Abuse? Drug Abuse? Or something else entirely? The truth is, the words used to describe your struggle can shape the kind of help you receive, and whether that help truly fits your needs.

It’s easy to assume they all mean the same thing, but those terms point to different realities. When the wrong one is used, the treatment plan can miss the real issue. You might end up addressing symptoms instead of causes, or focusing on behavior when the body itself is dependent.

Understanding which one describes what you’re facing is the first step toward getting help that works for you.

Why Language Decides the Direction of Your Recovery

Language in mental health and recovery isn’t just technical; it’s also directional. The words professionals use determine what kind of support you’ll be offered, what insurance covers, and how your progress is measured.

If someone treats chemical dependency as general addiction, they may overlook the body’s physical need for the substance. If they treat substance abuse as chemical dependency, they may over‑medicalize what’s primarily behavioral.

When the terminology doesn’t match the reality, recovery becomes harder. You might feel like you’re doing everything right but still not improving, because the treatment isn’t addressing the right layer of the problem.

How These Terms Came to Be

The confusion around addiction language didn’t happen overnight. The words used to describe addiction didn’t appear all at once. They grew out of different moments in history, each shaped by how society viewed substance use at the time.

Moreover, these shifts weren’t just linguistic; they changed how people were treated and perceived.

Alcoholism became common in the 1930s and 1940s. In the early 1900s, people struggling with alcohol were often seen as weak or immoral. When Alcoholics Anonymous began in the 1930s, the term alcoholism reframed drinking as a disease rather than a failure of character.

Drug abuse entered the public vocabulary in the 1960s and 1970s when public concern shifted toward drugs. Governments and health agencies started using the phrase drug abuse, which focused more on control and legality than healing. The word abuse carried judgment, and many people were treated as criminals rather than patients.

Chemical dependency appeared in the 1970s and 1980s, when treatment centers introduced the concept of chemical dependency to highlight the body’s physical reliance on an actual substance. This helped professionals separate biological dependence from emotional or behavioral addiction. It also made space for medical detox programs and more structured rehabilitation.

Substance abuse became a clinical term as research expanded in the 1980s and 1990s. Substance became a broader clinical term, covering alcohol, prescription medication, and other substances.

Substance use disorder replaced older labels in the DSM‑5. This newer language recognizes that addiction exists on a spectrum, from mild misuse to severe dependency, and aims to reduce the shame of the word ‘abuse’ while improving accuracy.

Each transition reflected a growing understanding of addiction as both biological and psychological. But it also created overlap, and sometimes confusion, between terms that sound interchangeable but aren’t.

Understanding the Differences

To make sense of these words, it helps to see how they relate to one another.

  • Addiction describes a pattern of compulsive use despite harm. It’s broad and behavioral
  • Chemical dependency focuses on the body’s physical reliance on a substance. It’s biological and measurable
  • Substance abuse refers to harmful or risky use, not necessarily dependence
  • Alcoholism is specific to alcohol and includes both physical and emotional dependence
  • Substance use disorder is the modern diagnostic term that covers all levels of severity

When you understand these distinctions, you start to see why treatment plans differ. Detox addresses chemical dependency. Counseling addresses addiction patterns. Support groups address emotional recovery. Each piece matters, but only if it matches the real issue.

The Emotional Side of Getting the Words Right

There’s also a personal reason to understand these terms. When you know what you’re facing, you stop blaming yourself for not “trying hard enough.” You begin to see that recovery isn’t a test of character, but a process of healing both body and mind.

Accurate language helps you talk to loved ones, counselors, and even yourself with more clarity. It turns vague frustration into specific understanding. Instead of saying, “I can’t stop,” you start saying, “My body has adapted to this substance, and I need help to reverse that.” That change of mindset changes everything.

If you’re unsure which term fits your situation, start by noticing what’s happening in your body and emotions.

Why Chemical Dependency Deserves Its Own Attention

Chemical dependency is unique because it involves the body’s chemistry adapting to a substance. The brain and nervous system begin to rely on it to function normally. When the substance is removed, the body reacts, sometimes severely.

That’s why treating chemical dependency requires medical oversight and gradual stabilization. It’s not just about willpower or mindset. It’s about helping the body relearn balance.

Ignoring this distinction can be serious. Without proper medical support, withdrawal can be dangerous. Without emotional support, relapse becomes more likely. Both sides need to be addressed, but in the right order.

How to Tell What Kind of Help You Need

Ask yourself:

  • Do I feel physically unwell when I stop using a certain substance?
  • Do I rely on it to feel normal or calm?
  • Do I use it to manage emotions rather than physical cravings?
  • Have I tried to quit but found my body reacting strongly?

If your body reacts to a specific chemical component, then that points toward chemical dependency. If the struggle feels more emotional or behavioral, it may be addiction. Either way, clarity helps professionals guide you toward the right combination of medical and therapeutic support.

Once you have a clearer sense of what’s happening, you then need steps to make sure you’re getting appropriate care.

Getting the Right Help

Ask for definitions: When a counselor or doctor uses a term, ask what it means and how it applies to you.

Describe your symptoms clearly: Include both physical and emotional experiences.

Seek integrated care: Look for professionals who address both body and mind; medical detox paired with counseling or faith‑based support.

Avoid self‑diagnosis: Online definitions can help you learn, but professional evaluation ensures accuracy.

Keep language consistent: When talking to different providers, use the same term so your care stays aligned.

These steps may sound simple, but they prevent confusion that can delay recovery. They also help you feel more in control of your healing process.

Faith communities sometimes use different words, such as bondage, brokenness, or deliverance, to describe addiction. Those words carry emotional truth, but they don’t replace medical understanding.

Bringing both perspectives together creates a fuller picture. Faith offers hope and meaning; clinical language offers precision and safety. When both are respected, recovery becomes more holistic and sustainable.

Getting the right help starts with being understood. When professionals use the right term, treatment becomes targeted. When you understand those terms yourself, you become an active participant in your healing.

Chemical dependency isn’t just another word for addiction; it’s a specific condition that requires specific care. Knowing that difference can protect your health, your relationships, and your sense of hope.

If you’re unsure which term fits what you’re facing, reach out to a professional therapist who is trained to help you sort through it. The right words lead to the right kind of help, and that help can change your life.

Consider connecting with a counselor listed on this site or calling the numbers on the screen to start that conversation today.

item.title: Finding Common Ground in the Stepfamily
item.description:
For many people, a blended family can be both exciting and scary. New rules and clashing personalities can turn a home into a war zone if not properly handled. Learning how to find common ground in a step family can help you bypass some of those learning curves and embrace the new living arrangement so you can really become a family.

Common Ground in a Step Family

Connecting with others in a step family can be a challenge, especially the first few weeks and months. Learning to live in the same household, work with each other’s schedules and likes and dislikes, while remaining patient can begin to wear thin.

The following list of tips for finding common ground in a stepfamily can help you make the transition smoother. Keep in mind that building trust, confidence, and loyalty towards others can take years.

Think of it as a New Family

Accepting that the new family structure will be different than what you had before can help you change your perspective. Everyone entering the stepfamily will need a period of adjustment. For some family members, this adjustment may be minor. For others, expect weeks or months for them to adjust to the new living arrangement and rules.

Become a Reliable and Steady Presence

Stepfamily members may feel wary about someone suddenly trying to be their best friend or a replacement for their biological mother or father. Instead of pushing for everyone to get along, try to be a reliable and steady presence in the home. Become someone they can count on to be there for them no matter what. Demonstrate consistent love and actions towards every family member.

Clearly Communicate Expectations

Each family has their own set of rules. What one parent permitted in their household may cause friction in the new step family. Be clear about expectations in the household and allow family members to ask questions and offer opinions and insight. At the same time, remain open to new ideas. Be willing to adopt or compromise on certain rules.

Set Boundaries

Set boundaries and respect the boundaries of others, and teach this concept to your children. A stepfamily can become cramped very quickly as they run out of space, or when new step-siblings need to room with each other. Teach everyone to honor each other by respecting privacy.

Find a Common Interest

Bonding over a common interest can lead to open lines of communication. Movie and game nights, day trips, or vacations to much-loved destinations could help family members feel like they belong. Many people question their roles and positions in a blended family. Tear down this barrier by talking to each member to learn their hobbies and interests, and scheduling movies, games, trips, and events that include everyone.

Co-Parent with Similar Rules and Expectations

If you are in a co-parenting relationship with your ex or your new spouse co-parents with their ex-spouse, consider working hand in hand with them to agree on a few expectations and rules. This makes the transition less jarring. Of course, each household is run differently, and you will not see eye to eye, but having a similar structure will be less daunting for a blended family.

Help for Step Families

Christian counseling provides help for blended families easing into the stepfamily lifestyle. Your counselor is familiar with the obstacles of bringing two families together, including loyalties and personalities. Call our center today to schedule a session with a counselor for family counseling. Let us help you build your new family with a strong foundation.
