item.title: Mental Health Crisis: How to Know You’re in One, and What to Do
item.description:
Life can hit hard at times. Despite our best laid plans and our most cherished hopes, we can find ourselves discouraged by life in ways we may never have expected. What do you do, for instance, when you find yourself in a mental health crisis?

Some say that health is everything, and your mental health certainly affects how you experience the world and the ways you contribute to it. Experiencing a crisis can be a significant roadblock. Just as you need to pay attention to your physical health, you also need to keep tabs on your mental health.

What Is a Mental Health Crisis?

The word ‘crisis’ might convey a situation where everything is falling apart in a rather dramatic fashion. If this is how you understand or experience a crisis, that can potentially stand in the way of you taking the necessary steps to look after yourself. A crisis can be when things simply seem overwhelming, and that includes those moments and seasons of quiet desperation that could be easy to miss.

We all have our hard days, and we sometimes have entire seasons of hardship and stress. Talking about a mental health crisis isn’t referring to this. Rather, when a person is experiencing a crisis, they are at the point where their psychological or emotional pain has become overwhelming. They struggle to care for themselves, function properly, or make safe decisions that promote their wellbeing and that of others around them.

A mental health crisis doesn’t necessarily happen all at once in a dramatic fashion. Sometimes it does, in the wake of experiences such as loss, trauma, or prolonged suffering. At other times, the crisis happens on the back of long seasons of struggle, building up slowly until the weight becomes too difficult to bear.

Believers are not immune to such challenges, as we find story after story in Scripture where individuals are deeply distressed and crying out to the Lord in anguish. Think of Elijah and what might be described as spiritual burnout and suicidal despair after his contest with the prophets of Baal. Collapsed under a broom tree, he begs the Lord to take his life (1 Kings 19:1-18).

There are other examples, like Job’s deep despair and grief after his severe losses, when he no longer sees meaning in his life. He curses the day of his birth (Job 3:1). Or Hannah, whose longing for a child and the mockery from her husband’s other wife led her into deep distress and bitter weeping. We read that she didn’t eat and, “In her deep anguish Hannah prayed to the Lord, weeping bitterly” (1 Samuel 1:10, NIV).

These moments of crisis come to all of us at one point or another. They can be overwhelming to the point where we despair of life itself, but they are not signs that the Lord has abandoned us. The Lord meets us in those spaces of darkness, comforting us (2 Corinthians 1:3-7, NIV). It’s important to be able to recognize those moments of a mental health crisis so that we can receive the necessary help and support.

Signs of a Mental Health Crisis

Pinpointing when you’re going through a mental health crisis can make a huge difference. If you know what’s going on and you take early steps at intervention, you can start moving toward better health and wellbeing, preventing the situation from deteriorating further. If you want to know if you or a loved one is in a mental health crisis, some of the signs to look out for include:

  • Inability to cope: This might look like feeling overwhelmed and unable to manage day-to-day decisions or tasks.
  • Overwhelming sense of hopelessness: A persistent and deep belief or feeling that your situation will never improve and that life is not worth living could be a sign of a mental health crisis. This might also manifest as a person saying that others would be “better off without them.” This is a signal that someone is undergoing crisis, and it shouldn’t be dismissed as a passing thought.
  • Inability to sleep or eat: A severe disruption to basic functioning, such as sleeping or eating, over several days, could point to a person being in crisis.
  • Disconnection from reality: If a person is seeing or hearing things that others around them cannot, or they feel like the world around them is not real, that may also point to a mental health crisis.
  • Reckless or dangerous behavior: Making risky decisions, starting or increasing substance use, or engaging in behaviors that seem self-destructive, like unprotected sex with multiple partners, gambling, or reckless driving, are all signs to take note of.
  • Intrusive or racing thoughts: Another sign to look out for is thoughts that are impossible to quiet or having thoughts that are frightening to you or feel out of control. These thoughts may pop up at random moments, and they cause significant distress.
  • Extreme withdrawal: We all need moments and space to ourselves, but when a person drastically reduces their interactions with friends, family, their church community, or they steer clear of activities that brought them joy or meaning, that could signal a mental health crisis.
  • Giving away possessions: A person giving away the things they own and reasonably need for everyday life could be a sign that a person is in crisis and preparing to end their life.
  • Talk or thoughts of suicide or self-harm: When a person thinks about, expresses a desire to, or attempts to harm themselves or end their own life, that indicates they are in crisis. This must be taken seriously, and steps should be taken immediately to seek the appropriate help, whether by dialing 911 or a crisis hotline.

Dealing with a Mental Health Crisis

What should you do if you or a loved one is experiencing a mental health crisis? Depending on the situation, you can take steps that help to stabilize the crisis and start to move the needle toward safety and healing. For instance, if there is a risk of harm or suicide, call for help immediately, whether that’s 911 or a suicide and crisis lifeline. Don’t hesitate to take active steps to seek help.

If there is a risk of self-harm, it’s important that you safely secure or remove dangerous items such as weapons, medications, or other items that can be used in this manner. Call on someone who can help with this.

Other steps that you can take would include not seeking isolation but instead reaching out to a trusted person. That could be your pastor, a wise friend, or a family member who can be physically with you and work through the crisis. When in crisis, it’s often tempting and easier to simply retreat into yourself. This only serves to deepen despair. It’s important to connect and stay connected, even though that may feel uncomfortable.

If you already have and are working with a psychiatrist or therapist, you can also reach out to them directly so that they can walk with you through the crisis. Many practices have their protocols for dealing with established clients in crisis.

Accept help from your mental health provider and allow others to care for you. Opening up space for others to care for you isn’t a sign of weakness or faithlessness. It’s wisdom that recognizes that we need each other, and that’s how the body of Christ functions (Romans 12:15-16).

You can also take time to ground yourself in the present, whether that’s through breathing slowly, placing your feet flat on the floor or on the grass, or naming five things you can see. In the moment, this can disrupt panic or anxiety, giving you room to seek help. Do this instead of using substances like alcohol or drugs to cope, as these only serve to impair your judgment and increase the risk of making damaging decisions.

As you experience the crisis, don’t minimize what you’re feeling or tell yourself to just push on without seeking help, especially if you’re having suicidal thoughts. Pray and invite the Lord into the season or moment, but reach out for help from others. The Lord uses community, doctors, and counselors as instruments of healing, and wisdom means making use of these gifts.

Lastly, don’t make major life decisions during a crisis, and don’t carry this struggle alone. You must wait until you’re stable and supported before you make major decisions like quitting your job, ending a marriage, moving house, or making other kinds of irreversible choices. You don’t have to go it alone. The journey of long-term healing will take time, and you need others along the way.

Your path toward healing and wholeness might include a combination of professional therapy, medication, and lifestyle changes to help support your wellbeing. Your counselor can walk with you through every stage of that journey. You can contact our reception team to schedule an appointment and begin that journey today.

“Small plant,” courtesy of Matt Baron-Thompson, Unsplash.com, CCO License

The post Mental Health Crisis: How to Know You’re in One, and What to Do appeared first on Bothell Christian Counseling.

item.title: Christian Marriage Advice: 8 Tips for Married Life
item.description:
The best time to seek Christian marriage advice is probably before the wedding day. However, it is impossible to prepare for everything life may throw at you over the next 30 or 40 years or more. Obstacles and life events have a way of showing up when you least expect them. People grow and go through seasons of their own that can take a toll on a relationship.

But as believers in the Christian faith, you know that your relationship was solidified as a covenant before God and not to be taken lightly. Christian marriage advice can help no matter what anniversary you most recently celebrated.

The Pillars of Christian Marriage Advice

Christians should base their marriage on the foundation of Jesus Christ. Trying to navigate through life without Jesus as the anchor means rough waters and storms that might just take down the ship. Making sure that you have the pillars in place is the best Christian marriage advice you can receive.

The pillars include honoring each other and being quick to forgive and work through issues, committing wholeheartedly to each other and being willing to follow up with sacrificial love, and following Christ as a couple and as the heads of your household. Submissive love is not one spouse ruling over the other; it is loving each other as Christ loved us and being a helpmate to each other.

8 Christian Marriage Tips

Aligning your values and beliefs is the first step in a Christian marriage. Conflict can occur if one of you has strayed from God’s word and guidance. As you read through the following Christian marriage advice tips, keep in mind where you are in your Christian journey. Getting yourself back on track sets an example for your spouse and the rest of your household.

  • Have you lost track of your first love, Jesus?
  • Has day-to-day living and responsibilities taken you away from reading and communing with God?
  • Has it been a long time since you worshipped God, whether at church or in the car?
  • Are there mistakes you have made that you have not brought before God and asked for forgiveness through Jesus?

Take inventory of your heart first. Then discuss with your spouse how you want to get your marriage back on track, with Jesus as the foundational cornerstone. Professional help is available.

Keep God at the center

God should always be at the center of your marriage. If you think back to issues in your relationship in the past, was God at the center of it? Were you treating your Christian faith as an add-on component to your life? Jesus should be the foundation of your marriage.

When you view life through this lens, of becoming more like Christ and obeying God, rather than simply a “religious” lens, decisions become clearer. You and your spouse can choose paths that lead to life and something bigger than just surviving day to day and paying the bills.

Don’t hold a grudge

Carrying a grudge only leads to bitterness and resentment. Is that how believers should act toward others? Yet, we often treat our spouses this way when angry. After all, they should know us better than anyone.

But this is where forgiveness and grace come to the rescue. Jesus forgave you for everything you have thought and done in the past, present, and future as long as you turn to Him. As Romans 8:1 states, “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit.” (NKJV)

If Jesus can forgive us when our hearts plead for forgiveness and yearn to walk right with Him, can we not forgive our significant other?

Honor each other

How you treat your spouse says a lot about how much you respect and honor them. If either one of you badmouths the other, ask for forgiveness and vow never to do it again. Venting to others only plants seeds of discontent. What can others do? Fixing a marriage can only happen when both spouses are involved in the resolution.

Consulting a therapist or another marriage counseling professional is not venting or oversharing. It is asking for professional help from trained counselors to help mend your marriage, not destroy it. It starts with confiding in one another, not friends and colleagues.

Be one

When you marry and come together, you become one flesh. You unite as one and start working as a team. Are you your spouse’s helpmate, or more of a hindrance? Is your spouse your helpmate?

Sometimes, we allow pride and arrogance to get in the way of submissive love. Yet, sacrificial love is a theme in the Bible. Two are better than one. Your spouse can be your support in seasons when you feel weak, and you can be theirs when they need it.

Love each other

We should love each other as Christ loved us. Nowhere in the Bible does it state that the command should exclude our spouse. Yet we readily forgive others while demanding perfection from our spouse. Learn to love each other, even in hard times.

The only caveat is if you are in an abusive relationship. Jesus Christ did not abuse His followers, and if your spouse is abusive, then they are not following Jesus. In this case, seek help immediately. Reach out for help to create an exit plan. Your safety and the safety of your children are important to your Father in heaven.

Communicate with each other

More marriages end due to miscommunication, angry outbursts, and unresolved conflict. How many times have you felt slighted and not said a word? Instead, you allowed the action (or non-action) to simmer until the resentment and bitterness overflowed one day? Do you or your spouse use the silent treatment as a way to punish the other instead of discussing the matter?

Communication skills, anger management, and conflict resolution are learned skills. During marriage counseling, your counselor can equip you and your spouse with the necessary strategies and techniques to cool down, actively listen, and resolve disagreements.

Make emotional intimacy a priority

Physical intimacy and sex are important aspects of marriage. Both bring forth feelings of connection, bonding, and love. However, emotional intimacy is just as critical. The little touches when you walk by are unspoken acts of love, but the eye contact on a bad day with a supportive spouse can give you strength without them ever saying a word.

Investing time in your relationship helps you to make that connection. This is the type of intimacy that will carry you through the later Golden Years when sex may no longer be possible. Nurture your relationship with date nights, either out and about or at home. Take trips to your favorite places, or curl up on the couch, holding each other, and talking about the day, goals, or dreams for your family’s future.

Form friendships with older Christian couples

Sometimes a marriage can hit a snag after several years. The newness has worn off, and the demands of daily and family life can replace the spot where your spouse should be. Learning y means recognizing when it happens and correcting course.

This is easier when you have friends and Christian mentors who can help guide you. Form friendships with Christian couples who have been married for a few decades. Ask their advice on how they have maintained their love and marriage through the years. Everyone has a story (or two) where they thought it was over, but something happened, and they came out stronger than ever.

Christian Marriage Counseling in Your Area

Christian marriage advice is only a phone call or click away. Our Christian counseling center offers guidance from professionals specializing in evidence-based psychology and faith-based principles to help you navigate your relationship and come out stronger on the other side. We arm our couples with strategies and the word of God to overcome and manage anything that life throws at them. Contact us today to see how we can help.

“Engaged”, Courtesy of Derek Owens, Unsplash.com, CC0 License

The post Christian Marriage Advice: 8 Tips for Married Life appeared first on Mill Creek Christian Counseling.

But this is where forgiveness and grace come to the rescue. Jesus forgave you for everything you have thought and done in the past, present, and future as long as you turn to Him. As Romans 8:1 states, “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit.” (NKJV)

If Jesus can forgive us when our hearts plead for forgiveness and yearn to walk right with Him, can we not forgive our significant other?

Honor each other

How you treat your spouse says a lot about how much you respect and honor them. If either one of you badmouths the other, ask for forgiveness and vow never to do it again. Venting to others only plants seeds of discontent. What can others do? Fixing a marriage can only happen when both spouses are involved in the resolution.

Consulting a therapist or another marriage counseling professional is not venting or oversharing. It is asking for professional help from trained counselors to help mend your marriage, not destroy it. It starts with confiding in one another, not friends and colleagues.

Be one

When you marry and come together, you become one flesh. You unite as one and start working as a team. Are you your spouse’s helpmate, or more of a hindrance? Is your spouse your helpmate?

Sometimes, we allow pride and arrogance to get in the way of submissive love. Yet, sacrificial love is a theme in the Bible. Two are better than one. Your spouse can be your support in seasons when you feel weak, and you can be theirs when they need it.

Love each other

We should love each other as Christ loved us. Nowhere in the Bible does it state that the command should exclude our spouse. Yet we readily forgive others while demanding perfection from our spouse. Learn to love each other, even in hard times.

The only caveat is if you are in an abusive relationship. Jesus Christ did not abuse His followers, and if your spouse is abusive, then they are not following Jesus. In this case, seek help immediately. Reach out for help to create an exit plan. Your safety and the safety of your children are important to your Father in heaven.

Communicate with each other

More marriages end due to miscommunication, angry outbursts, and unresolved conflict. How many times have you felt slighted and not said a word? Instead, you allowed the action (or non-action) to simmer until the resentment and bitterness overflowed one day? Do you or your spouse use the silent treatment as a way to punish the other instead of discussing the matter?

Communication skills, anger management, and conflict resolution are learned skills. During marriage counseling, your counselor can equip you and your spouse with the necessary strategies and techniques to cool down, actively listen, and resolve disagreements.

Make emotional intimacy a priority

Physical intimacy and sex are important aspects of marriage. Both bring forth feelings of connection, bonding, and love. However, emotional intimacy is just as critical. The little touches when you walk by are unspoken acts of love, but the eye contact on a bad day with a supportive spouse can give you strength without them ever saying a word.

Investing time in your relationship helps you to make that connection. This is the type of intimacy that will carry you through the later Golden Years when sex may no longer be possible. Nurture your relationship with date nights, either out and about or at home. Take trips to your favorite places, or curl up on the couch, holding each other, and talking about the day, goals, or dreams for your family’s future.

Form friendships with older Christian couples

Sometimes a marriage can hit a snag after several years. The newness has worn off, and the demands of daily and family life can replace the spot where your spouse should be. Learning y means recognizing when it happens and correcting course.

This is easier when you have friends and Christian mentors who can help guide you. Form friendships with Christian couples who have been married for a few decades. Ask their advice on how they have maintained their love and marriage through the years. Everyone has a story (or two) where they thought it was over, but something happened, and they came out stronger than ever.

Christian Marriage Counseling in Your Area

Christian marriage advice is only a phone call or click away. Our Christian counseling center offers guidance from professionals specializing in evidence-based psychology and faith-based principles to help you navigate your relationship and come out stronger on the other side. We arm our couples with strategies and the word of God to overcome and manage anything that life throws at them. Contact us today to see how we can help.

The post Christian Marriage Advice: 8 Tips for Married Life appeared first on Bothell Christian Counseling.

item.title: Learning to Rest in the Lord
item.description:
Rest in the Lord, and wait patiently for Him; do not fret… – Psalm 37:7, NKJV

Recently, a group of women at my church were gathered around someone who was struggling. One of the women gently observed that she was struggling – striving, pushing, fighting, trying to fix everything – when what she truly needed was rest. The comment gave me a vivid picture of a tired swimmer who needs to flip onto his/her back and float.

My husband once trained for a triathlon, and during his swimming instruction, his coach taught him something essential: when you get tired in the water, the safest thing you can do is flip onto your back and rest. Back-floating is a survival skill. It conserves energy, slows panic, and keeps you stable until you’re ready to swim again.

When swimmers panic, they burn through oxygen and strength at an alarming rate. Their arms flail, their breathing becomes erratic, and their bodies tense. Panic makes drowning more likely, not less. But back-floating interrupts that cycle. It signals to the body, “You’re safe. You can breathe. You can rest.”

Many of us have experienced seasons where we feel like we’re drowning emotionally or spiritually. The circumstances may differ – financial stress, relational strain, health challenges, grief, burnout – but the sensation is the same. You feel like you’re kicking and kicking, trying to stay afloat, but the water keeps rising, and you’re barely staying above water. You’re exhausted, overwhelmed, and unsure how much longer you can keep going.

Years ago, that was me. My husband and I were struggling financially, and instead of praying or pausing, I went into overdrive. I took on a second job. Then I signed up with a direct-selling company to earn extra income. I was constantly running from one responsibility to the next, convinced that if I just worked harder, I could help fix everything.

I was so stressed, I would take something for my upset stomach, put on a comedy, and simply permit myself to stop thinking about everything for a while. One afternoon, I sat down for a moment and turned on a talk show.

A woman on the screen said she felt like she was drowning emotionally. Her words hit home and spoke directly to what I was feeling. I was physically, emotionally, and spiritually depleted. I realized I had been trying to survive on my own strength, and it was pulling me under.

I repented. I prayed and told God I was sorry for relying on my own strength instead of His. I asked Him to help me rest instead of strive. Years later, when I felt that drowning sensation again, God placed this on my heart: “If you feel you have hit rock bottom, stand on the Rock. If you feel you are drowning, let My peace like a river sweep over you.”

Psalm 62:2 says, “He alone is my rock and my salvation; He is my fortress, I will never be shaken.” And verses 5–6 remind us, “Yes, my soul, find rest in God; my hope comes from Him. Truly He is my rock and my salvation; He is my fortress, I will not be shaken.”

In practical terms, I knew I couldn’t keep living at the pace I was going. I let go of the extra commitments. The second job ended naturally, and I stepped away from the direct-selling business. I began to breathe again. Billy Graham once said, “We must let go of inner tensions that life sends our way, trusting in God moment by moment.” That truth became real for me: whenever we fight for control, we step out of the rest God offers.

Why We Strive When Life Feels Out of Control

As a therapist, I often see this pattern. When life feels chaotic, the brain instinctively grabs for control. It’s a survival response. When we feel powerless in big areas – finances, relationships, health – we hyper-focus on small things we can control.

Suddenly, the dishwasher must be loaded a certain way. The kids must follow instructions perfectly. The house must stay spotless. These behaviors are more about trying to create stability when our internal world feels unstable.

This is part of the body’s stress response. When we’re overwhelmed, our nervous system shifts into fight-or-flight mode. “Fight” can look like striving, overworking, micromanaging, or perfectionism. “Flight” can look like avoidance, shutting down, or withdrawing. Neither response creates peace. Both keep us in survival mode.

Rest, however, activates the parasympathetic nervous system – the part of the body responsible for calm, clarity, and emotional regulation. Spiritually, rest is an act of trust. Physically, rest is an act of regulation. Emotionally, rest is an act of surrender.

How to Shift From Striving to Resting

Below are practices that integrate both faith and mental health principles.

Let go: Release the burden

Cast all your anxiety on him because he cares for you. – 1 Peter 5:7, NIV

Letting go is not passive It is intentional surrender When anxiety rises, pause and say, “Lord, I give this to You.” This simple act interrupts the cycle of striving and invites God into the moment.

Be still: Calm the mind and body

“Be still, and know that I am God…” – Psalm 46:10, NIV

Stillness is difficult for many people, especially Type A personalities or those who grew up needing to be self-reliant. But stillness is essential for experiencing God’s peace. It teaches the nervous system that it is safe. It reminds the soul that God is present.

Trust daily: Build trust through small steps

Trust doesn’t appear overnight. It grows through experience. Trust develops as we take steps of faith and see God’s faithfulness. Each small act of trust quiets fear and brings rest to the soul. Trust is a spiritual muscle  –  the more we use it, the stronger it becomes.

Support your nervous system

These evidence-based practices help regulate the body and reduce overwhelming emotions:

  • Name the emotion “I’m overwhelmed.” “I’m stressed.” Naming reduces intensity
  • Breathe slowly Deep breathing activates the parasympathetic nervous system
  • Use temperature change/cold water Splashing your face or running your hands under cold water stimulates the vagus nerve
  • Reach out for support Connection is protective for mental health
  • Rest physically Tea, a warm bath, quiet time, or simply lying down

Praise

Psalm 22:3 reminds us that God inhabits the praises of His people. Worship redirects our attention from our problems to God’s character. It brings emotional regulation and emotional and spiritual grounding. Singing stimulates the vagus nerve, releases endorphins, and shifts focus from fear to God’s presence.

Praise is not just a response; it is a weapon. Praise doesn’t just calm our bodies; it strengthens us spiritually. Scripture shows that praise pushes back darkness and disrupts the enemy’s lies. When we worship, we align ourselves with God’s truth; we make the enemy flee because it declares, out loud, who is truly in control. Evil will not linger where God is being exalted.

As they began to sing and praise, the Lord set ambushes against the men of Ammon and Moab, and Mount Seir who were invading Judah, and they were defeated. – 2 Chronicles 20:22, NIV

It shifts the atmosphere, strengthens our faith, and reminds our hearts that God is present, powerful, and actively working on our behalf. In 2 Chronicles 20, God told King Jehoshaphat that the battle did not belong to them (him and the men of Judah), but to God, and that they would win without fighting.

Reach out: You don’t have to do this alone

One of the most powerful steps you can take when you feel overwhelmed is to reach out for support. God designed us for connection, not isolation. Sometimes “resting in the Lord” also means letting Him work through the people He’s placed in our lives – friends, pastors, mentors, and trained professionals – who can help shoulder the weight we’re carrying.

If you notice that the feeling of drowning keeps returning, or if you’re struggling to regulate your emotions on your own, it may be time to schedule an appointment with a professional counselor. Therapy is not a sign of weakness; it’s a form of wisdom and stewardship.

A counselor can help you identify patterns of striving, understand your stress responses, and learn practical tools to support your emotional and spiritual well‑being. Many people find that having a safe, confidential space to talk through their experiences brings clarity, relief, and renewed strength.

Reaching out is an act of courage. It’s flipping onto your back in deep water and allowing someone to help you float until you regain your strength. It’s choosing rest over panic, connection over isolation, and healing over exhaustion.

Final Encouragement

Resting in the Lord is not inactivity – it is a posture of trust. It is choosing to float instead of flail, to breathe instead of panic, and to let God’s peace steady your soul. When we stop striving and learn to rest, we make space to receive God’s strength.

“…the joy of the Lord is your strength.” – Nehemiah 8:10, NIV

The Lord is the strength of his people, a fortress of salvation for his anointed one. – Psalm 28:8, NIV

I can do all this through Him who gives me strength. – Phil. 4:13, NIV

…but those who hope in the LORD will renew their strength. They will soar on wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary; they will walk and not be faint. – Isaiah 40:31, NIV

Photos:
“Palette”, Courtesy of Vitaly Gariev, Unsplash.com, CC0 License; “Woman in Spring”, Courtesy of Andrey K, Unsplash.com, CC0 License

The post Learning to Rest in the Lord appeared first on Tacoma Christian Counseling.

item.title: Can a Marriage Survive Infidelity? 10 Christian Principles for Healing and Recovery
item.description:
Discovering that your spouse has been unfaithful can feel like the ground has disappeared underneath you. The person you trusted and built a life with has betrayed that trust. Suddenly, you may find yourself questioning your marriage, your memories, your judgment, and your future. And then comes the big question: “Can our marriage actually survive this?”

The short answer is: “yes.” Marriages can survive infidelity. Some couples even go on to build marriages that are more honest, connected, and intentional than they were before. But that doesn’t mean every marriage should survive infidelity. You do have a choice in whether or not you stay in the marriage. And from a Christian perspective, distinction is incredibly important.

What counts as infidelity?

When we hear the words “affair” or “infidelity,” we often think of a sexual relationship outside of marriage. But this can take different forms.

An emotional affair may involve developing a secret emotional intimacy or romantic attachment to someone outside the marriage. Sexual infidelity that doesn’t become physical can include sexting, explicit photos, sexual conversations, or online sexual relationships. Physical infidelity can range from kissing or sexual touching to intercourse. And some affairs become full romantic relationships involving emotional and physical intimacy over time.

Rather than defining infidelity by one particular act, it can be helpful to look at the boundaries of marriage, secrecy, and betrayal of trust. Ask yourself if a romantic, emotional, or sexual relationship developed outside the boundaries you and your spouse had for your marriage. Was it kept secret because you knew your spouse would feel hurt or betrayed if they knew?

Someone might say, “But we never had sex.” That may be true. But infidelity does not have to involve sex. Emotional or romantic relationships can also cross the boundaries of a marriage and create a deep sense of betrayal.

First: Staying is a choice

As a Christian, you may feel pressure to save your marriage no matter what. After infidelity, you might even wonder, “If I leave, does that mean I didn’t forgive enough? Did I not pray enough? Am I giving up instead of trusting God?”

But the Bible does not tell a betrayed spouse that they must stay in a marriage after sexual immorality. In Matthew 19:9, Jesus says that divorce is permitted in cases of sexual immorality. In other words, Scripture gives the betrayed spouse permission to leave. But permission to leave is not a command to leave.

You may decide that too much trust has been broken and you cannot rebuild the marriage. Or you may decide that you want to stay and work toward reconciliation. This is a deep personal decision that deserves time, prayer, wisdom, and support.

Choosing to stay does not make you weak. And choosing to leave after infidelity does not automatically mean you have failed God. If you choose to stay, though, healing will require more than simply deciding not to get divorced. The relationship itself will need to heal.

Drawing from my work with couples and betrayal trauma, along with principles from Gottman Method Couples Therapy, here are ten important, faith-based principles for recovery.

Come clean

One of the most damaging patterns after infidelity is what we in the field often refer to as “trickle truth.”

The betrayed spouse discovers something; the unfaithful partner may completely deny it or only admit to part of it, until more information comes out later. The person who had the affair may say they were withholding information to “protect” their spouse. But withholding the truth also allows them to control the narrative.

We know that every new disclosure can create another betrayal. This erodes any of the fragile trust that may have been built back since discovery. The hurt spouse may ask themselves: “What else don’t I know? Can I trust anything you’ve told me?” Healing cannot truly begin while significant information is still being withheld. Your spouse needs an intentional disclosure process rather than numerous discovery days.

That doesn’t mean sharing unnecessarily graphic, intimate details that could worsen intrusive images. But the key facts of the infidelity need to come into the light as soon as possible. The simple fact is you cannot rebuild trust on top of secrecy.

Atone and take responsibility

The Gottman approach to healing after an affair describes three phases: atone, attune, and attach. Healing begins with atonement, or taking responsibility for what happened.

If you were the unfaithful partner, this is not the time to say, “I was lonely,” “You weren’t affectionate,” or “We were already having problems.” Those struggles in the marriage may be real, and there will be a time to talk about them. But they do not make your spouse responsible for your decision to cross the boundaries of the marriage.

Atonement means being able to say, “I did this. I hurt you. I am responsible for my choices.” It means showing genuine remorse, answering reasonable questions honestly, and allowing your spouse to be hurt without immediately defending yourself or shifting the blame.

The Bible also connects healing with bringing sin into the open rather than hiding it. Proverbs 28:13 teaches that the person who hides or covers their sin will not prosper, but the person who confesses it and turns away from it finds mercy.

And repentance is more than simply saying, “I’m sorry.” In 2 Corinthians 7:10–11, Paul describes godly sorrow as the kind of sorrow that leads to repentance and produces real change. That distinction matters after infidelity. Your spouse does not only need to hear that you are sorry. Over time, they need to see honesty, responsibility, openness, and changed behavior. They need to slowly begin recognizing that this marriage is becoming safe again.

Understand the trauma and unite against it.

Many people do not understand that betrayal can be traumatic. After discovering infidelity, the hurt partner may feel constantly on guard. They may experience intrusive thoughts or images, nightmares, anxiety, difficulty trusting, or a strong need to know that they are safe.

Triggers can also show up unexpectedly. A phone notification, a certain place, a song, a date, a photo, a sexual experience, or even a random comment can suddenly bring the pain rushing back. The hurt partner may wonder, “Why can’t I just move forward?”

The truth is that some people experience symptoms like post-traumatic stress after betrayal. Their mind and body may continue reacting to reminders of what happened, even when they desperately want to move forward. Understanding this can change the way a couple responds to those difficult moments.

Instead of: “Why are you bringing this up again?”

Try: “This brought the hurt back up again. How can we get through this moment together?”

Ecclesiastes 4:9–10 says that “two are better than one” and describes how one person can help the other when they fall. That can be a beautiful picture of recovery. If you have both chosen to work toward rebuilding the marriage, you can begin learning how to face the pain together instead of turning against each other.

The goal is not for the hurt partner to simply “get over it.” The goal is for both of you to recognize when the betrayal is affecting the relationship and learn how to respond as a team. Instead of fighting each other, you can begin fighting together for the healing of your marriage.

Accept your choice to stay

If you choose to stay, know that staying may be incredibly hard. People around you may have opinions. Friends, family members, pastors, or mentors may tell you what they think you should do. You may even question your own decision at times.

If you have prayerfully chosen to see whether your marriage can heal, there will come a point when you need to radically accept the decision you are making for today. Radical acceptance does not mean saying, “What happened was okay.”

It does not mean excusing the betrayal, minimizing your pain, or promising that you will stay no matter what happens next. It simply means: “This happened. I wish it had not happened, but I cannot change the past. Today, I am choosing to see if healing and reconciliation are possible.”

You do not have to know exactly what your marriage will look like a year from now. You do not need 100% certainty that everything will work out. You can simply take the next faithful step in front of you.

If reconciliation is what you have prayerfully chosen to pursue, there can be something deeply God-honoring in extending grace, seeking healing, and working toward restoration after you have been deeply hurt. That does not make the betrayal acceptable. It means you are choosing to see whether something broken can be rebuilt.

Galatians 6:9 offers encouragement for seasons like this: “Let us not become weary in doing good.” This verse is a reminder that there is a harvest when we do not give up. Healing after betrayal can be slow and exhausting. Permit yourself to take it one day at a time.

Limit third-party influence

Support matters after betrayal, but not all support will help you heal. If you have chosen to work toward reconciliation, surround yourself with people who can support that decision and walk prayerfully beside you through the process.

If every conversation ends with someone saying, “I can’t believe you’re staying,” or constantly questioning your decision, their voice can eventually become louder than your own. That can make an already difficult season even harder.

You are allowed to be careful about who has access to this vulnerable part of your marriage. Proverbs 13:20 tells us, “Walk with the wise and become wise.” During a difficult season, the people walking beside you matter.

Look for a few trusted people who will pray with you, encourage you, listen without judgment, and speak truth when you need to hear it. You need people who understand that supporting you does not mean pretending the betrayal was okay. It means respecting your prayerful decision to pursue healing and being willing to walk beside you as you do.

This does not mean isolating yourself or avoiding healthy accountability. You still need people who will be honest with you and who care about the health and safety of your marriage. But you can choose people who are able to say, “I know this is hard. I’m here. I’ll pray with you. I’ll support you as you seek God’s wisdom and take this one step at a time.”

You do not need everyone to understand your decision. You need a few safe, wise, prayerful people who are willing to walk with you through it.

Be patient with healing

Healing rarely draws a straight line. You may have several good weeks and then suddenly have a really hard day. That does not mean you are back at the beginning, even though it can often feel that way. The betrayed spouse may love their partner and still feel angry. They may forgive and still grieve. They may have a wonderful weekend together and then experience a painful trigger on Monday.

The unfaithful partner needs to resist saying, “We’ve already talked about this,” or “When are you going to let this go?” And the betrayed partner needs to have patience with themselves. Psalm 147:3 reminds us that God “heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.” Healing takes time, and God can be present in the process.

Sometimes recovery feels like two steps forward and one step backward. But one step backward does not erase the two steps you already took.

Replace secrecy with transparency

If secrecy created the hurt, transparency can help rebuild safety. This may mean being more open about phones, communication, schedules, friendships, social media, or contact with certain people. The goal is not for one spouse to become a permanent detective. Transparency simply says: “I understand why you don’t trust me right now, and I am willing to live in a way that helps you feel safe trusting me again.”

Scripture values this kind of honesty. Proverbs 12:22 says that “the Lord delights in people who are trustworthy.” Trust is not something the betrayed spouse owes simply because an apology was given. Trust is rebuilt slowly through honesty, consistency, and repeated experiences of trustworthiness.

Learn to attune to each other again

Eventually, healing needs to become about more than the affair itself. This is where the Gottman concept of attunement becomes important. Can you listen without immediately defending yourself? Can you begin understanding what your spouse is feeling and experiencing? Can you have honest conversations about intimacy, loneliness, stress, sex, faith, resentment, and unmet needs?

James 1:19 encourages us to be “quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to become angry.” That can be an important mindset as you learn how to hear and understand each other again. Your marriage may have had real problems before the affair, and those problems deserve attention.

But remember, relationship problems can be explored without making them responsible for the affair. The marriage belongs to both people. The decision to cross its boundaries belongs to the person who made that choice.

Rebuild trust in small moments

Trust usually does not return in one giant moment. It comes back through hundreds of small ones. After betrayal, it can be tempting to look for the big conversation, apology, or promise that will finally make everything feel okay again. But trust is usually rebuilt much more slowly.

  • You said you would call, and you called
  • You answered the uncomfortable question honestly
  • Your spouse became triggered, and instead of becoming defensive or frustrated, you stayed present
  • You followed through
  • You listened
  • You kept your word
  • And then you did it again tomorrow

Jesus says in Luke 16:10, “Whoever can be trusted with very little can also be trusted with much.” While this passage is not specifically about marriage, the principle of faithfulness in the small things applies beautifully to rebuilding trust.

Faithfulness is not only found in big promises. It is demonstrated in the small, everyday choices to be honest, consistent, patient, and dependable. After infidelity, your spouse may not be ready to trust your words yet. Give them time to experience your actions. You do not rebuild trust by asking someone to trust you again. You rebuild it by becoming trustworthy again, one small choice at a time.

Build something new

After an affair, the goal is not to get your old marriage back. That marriage has been changed by what happened, and in many ways, it is something you will need to grieve. If you choose reconciliation, the question centers around what kind of marriage you want to build now.

Maybe it is a marriage with more honesty, healthier boundaries, deeper emotional intimacy, better communication, and a faith lived out in the difficult parts of marriage- not just on Sunday.

In Isaiah 43:18–19, God tells His people not to remain stuck in the past because He says, “I am doing a new thing.” This passage offers us a beautiful reminder that God can bring something new out of a painful season.

This is where the Gottman concept of “Attach” becomes meaningful. You begin intentionally reconnecting, creating new experiences together, and building a different marriage: one shaped by greater honesty, understanding, and faithfulness.

You are not pretending the betrayal never happened, and you are not trying to recreate what was there before. That marriage is gone. But if you both choose healing, with God’s help, you can begin building something new.

Choosing What Comes Next

If you are standing in the aftermath of infidelity, you may desperately want someone to tell you what to do, but you do not have to make every decision today. You are allowed to grieve, ask questions, establish boundaries, seek wise counsel, and take time.

From a Christian perspective, you may have biblical permission to leave. But you also have permission to stay. Choosing reconciliation does not mean pretending the betrayal wasn’t serious. Forgiveness does not remove accountability. Grace does not require the absence of boundaries.

If you choose to stay, the goal should not simply be keeping your marriage intact. The goal is healing. The healing will not happen quickly or easily. But with time, grace, truth, and intentional work, a couple can build a new marriage where trust can slowly grow again.

Help is out there

If you are trying to make sense of betrayal, rebuild trust, or determine what healing looks like for your marriage, you don’t have to navigate it alone. You can reach out to schedule a counseling appointment for support with infidelity recovery and betrayal trauma.

I have also created two faith-based healing guides available on Amazon:

When Covenant Was Broken is for the betrayed partner navigating the hurt, trauma, questions, and complicated emotions that follow infidelity.

When You Broke Covenant is for the partner who was unfaithful and wants to take responsibility, understand their spouse’s pain, and begin rebuilding trust.

Both combine practical healing tools with Christian faith and biblical encouragement. You don’t have to know exactly what the future of your marriage looks like today to start with the next faithful step in healing.

Photo:
“Fighting”, Courtesy of Getty Images, Unsplash.com, Unsplash+ License

The post Can a Marriage Survive Infidelity? 10 Christian Principles for Healing and Recovery appeared first on Texas Christian Counseling.

item.title: Can EMDR Help When Grief Has Left Me Feeling Empty?
item.description:
For many people, grief doesn’t feel like pain. It feels like nothing at all. A strange emptiness that can last for weeks or years, making it hard to connect with life or hope. You may not notice when your grief turns into emptiness. You just realize one day that nothing moves you anymore.

You may find yourself going through the motions, doing what needs to be done, but feeling disconnected from life. That kind of numbness can be confusing because it doesn’t fit the picture most people have of grief.

Eye movement desensitization and reprocessing, or EMDR, is usually known for helping people recover from trauma. What many don’t know is that it can also help when grief leaves you feeling hollow inside. Many therapists have used it as a practical tool for helping your mind and body reconnect after loss in ways that feel natural and human again.

When Grief Turns into Emotional Numbness

After the loss of a loved one, your body and mind naturally try to protect you. Sometimes that protection means shutting down feelings that seem too painful to face. You may not even realize it’s happening and just notice that you feel numb inside.

  • You stop reacting to things that used to move you
  • You feel detached from people you care about
  • You lose interest in routines that once gave you comfort

This is your nervous system trying to keep you safe. Unfortunately, over time, that safety mechanism can lead to isolation. You start to feel like you’re watching your own life from a distance, unable to step back into it.

Why Emotional Disconnection Happens

Grief doesn’t only affect your thoughts; it changes how your body processes emotion. When pain feels unbearable, your brain may block certain memories or sensations to help you function. That’s why some people describe feeling frozen in time or dead inside.

Action-oriented therapies like eye movement desensitization and reprocessing can help by gently unlocking those frozen responses. Through guided, tiny, deliberate eye movements or other forms of bilateral stimulation, EMDR helps your brain reprocess memories and emotions that were stored in survival mode. The focus is on helping your body recognize that the danger has passed so it can begin to feel again.

What EMDR Does Differently

Traditional talk therapy helps you understand grief through conversation. EMDR works on a deeper level: the part of your brain that holds emotional memory. When you experience loss, your mind stores not just the event but the sensations, thoughts, and physical reactions that came with it.

EMDR helps those memories move from a raw, reactive state into a more integrated one. You may start to notice that memories of your loved one feel less painful and more peaceful. You could also find that eventually the emptiness begins to soften, replaced by small instances of connection: a song that suddenly feels meaningful again, or a memory that brings warmth instead of ache.

When You Feel Empty but Still Function

One of the hardest parts of grief-related numbness is that you can still appear fine. You go to work, take care of responsibilities, and even laugh at times. But inside, there’s a quiet sense of absence.

EMDR helps bridge that gap between functioning and feeling. It gives your nervous system permission to reconnect with emotion safely. You don’t have to force tears or talk endlessly about the loss. The process works gradually, helping your body release tension and your mind rediscover emotional rhythm.

How EMDR Supports Healing Beyond Tears

Healing doesn’t always mean crying or expressing sadness. Sometimes it means learning to feel again in rather ordinary ways. EMDR helps you notice sensations you may have tuned out, like the warmth of sunlight, the comfort of a familiar smell, and the sound of laughter.

These reconnections with ordinary things matter because they remind your body that life still holds meaning.

How Healing Through EMDR Happens

Healing through EMDR may not happen instantly; usually, it works slowly, subtly, and in a deeply personal way. Bit by bit, you’ll start to notice changes like:

  • Feeling more emotionally responsive to everyday life
  • Remembering your loved one with less pain and more peace
  • Experiencing fewer physical symptoms of tension or fatigue
  • Reconnecting with faith, creativity, or relationships that once felt distant

Each session helps your brain reprocess stored emotions so they no longer feel overwhelming or unreachable. Over time, you begin to experience grief as part of your story, rather than as something that defines or drains you.

In time, you begin to find that grief becomes less about emptiness and more about remembrance, the kind that honors what was lost. While EMDR helps on a neurological level, emotional reconnection also grows through deliberate, intentional habits.

Simple Ways to Support Emotional Reconnection Alongside EMDR

Write without censoring: Let your thoughts spill onto paper, not to analyze them, but to give them space.

Practice calm movement: Regular walking, stretching, or breathing exercises help release stored tension.

Learn to enjoy shared silence: Connect with others through shared silence. Sometimes a person’s presence matters more than words.

Allow yourself small joys: You don’t have to feel guilty for moments of laughter or calm. There are signs that your nervous system is healing. None of this can truly replace therapy, but simple, intentional steps like this complement it.

They help you rebuild emotional rhythm in daily life while EMDR works on deeper layers of healing.

Why Feeling Empty Deserves Compassion, Not Judgment

Many people assume grief should look a certain way, with tears, sadness, and visible emotion all the time. Yet, emotional emptiness and the complete lack of those emotions is just as painful. It’s a sign that your body has been through something profound and is in defense mode.

Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing can help you meet that emptiness with compassion instead of frustration. It teaches your mind that feeling disconnected isn’t failure; it’s part of how healing unfolds. When you stop fighting the numbness and start understanding it, space opens for emotion to return naturally.

Relearning How to Feel Safe in Your Own Body

One of the quiet gifts of approaches like EMDR is helping you feel safe again, not just mentally, but physically. Grief can make your body feel foreign, as if you’re living inside someone else’s skin. Through EMDR, you begin to trust your body’s signals again. You notice when you’re tense, when you’re calm, and when you’re ready to feel.

That sense of safety is what allows emotion to return. You don’t have to chase it; it comes back when your body knows it’s ready.

When to Reach Out for More Help

If grief has left you feeling empty for months or years, EMDR therapy is one option among many, but it works gently and effectively for people who feel disconnected after loss. A trained therapist can help you explore whether EMDR fits your needs and guide you through the process at a pace that feels right.

Feeling empty after grief doesn’t mean you’ve stopped caring or forgotten. It means your body and mind are still protecting you from pain that felt too deep to face. Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing offers a way to reconnect: not by forcing emotion, but by helping your nervous system remember how to feel safely again.

If you’ve been living in that quiet space where everything feels muted, don’t hesitate to ask for a professional to help. The team listed on this site can help you explore EMDR and other approaches that support emotional healing in a way that works for you.

You can also call the numbers on the screen to speak with someone who understands what you’re going through. Healing begins when you stop trying to feel normal and start allowing yourself to feel human again.

item.title: Noticing Signs of Autism in Women and Finding Christian Support
item.description:
Signs of autism in women may not always be easy to spot. Often, women learn to mask these symptoms to feel more confident or to blend in with how other women behave at work, church, and social events.

What Is Masking?

Masking is the ability to hide the signs of autism in women by mimicking the behaviors of other women. For example, facial features, behaviors, appearance, and speech are all cues that a woman with autism may adopt from those closest to her.

Since a woman with autism may struggle with communication and social cues, masking her behavior by mirroring what another woman does decreases the risk of being misunderstood by family, friends, acquaintances, and coworkers. However, masking can also make it difficult to recognize the signs of autism in women.

Signs of Autism in Women

Only a professional can make a diagnosis, but knowing the signs of autism in women can help you identify concerns that you may want to address with your doctor or therapist.

The following are several common signs of autism in women. If you notice a pattern, consult with a professional as soon as possible to discuss symptoms and treatment.

Masking to Blend In

A woman with autism may focus on how other women behave and begin dressing like them, using their specific vernacular, or mimicking facial expressions. They may repeat the same phrases and adopt their behaviors. This can leave the woman with autism emotionally exhausted at the end of the day.

Overstimulation

The woman with autism may become overstimulated throughout the day due to large crowds, loud noises or music, too many people talking at once, bright lights, or strong smells. She needs time to filter out her surroundings. She may use headphones, turn off overhead lights and use only lamps, or isolate during busier seasons.

Communication Issues in Social Settings

She may become frustrated when she doesn’t understand social cues. To make matters worse, she may feel alone because she is unsure how to nurture new friendships and connect with others. She may practice conversations alone to feel more confident before facing others. Women with autism often have to force eye contact.

Strict Routines

Routines provide security and emotional relief when a woman with autism feels stressed. She needs predictability in her life and to know what comes next. If events derail her routine, she may have a meltdown or shut down.

Meltdowns and Shutdowns

A meltdown can occur when the woman with autism feels like everything is out of control, she is overstimulated, or her routine has been derailed. She can’t control her emotions. However, some women react in the opposite way, shutting down emotionally until the perceived danger has passed or she can resume her routine.

Do You Suspect Autism?

The signs of autism in women can become more pronounced when a woman is under extreme stress, experiencing hormonal changes, caregiving for a loved one with little breaks, or facing emotional life events.

If the signs of autism in women sound familiar or you recognize a pattern, consider seeking the help of a Christian counselor. Christian counseling combines psychology-based methods with faith-based principles to treat mental health conditions, so believers can continue serving the Lord with a mind filled with peace from the Holy Spirit. Contact our office today to schedule an assessment.

item.title: Do I Need a Grief Counselor?
item.description:
Grief is sometimes obvious. It’s seen in the tears streaming down your face at a funeral. It’s seen in the losses you feel after a divorce. Grief is easy to spot when it’s a direct response to a massive loss. But grief isn’t always so blatant. Sometimes grief shows up in subtle ways or is delayed. Grief can also manifest itself in untraditional and unusual ways, making it hard to identify from anxiety, depression, or even a midlife crisis. You may even wonder if you need a grief counselor.

Begin by considering the feelings you’re experiencing. Are they generalized anxiety or depression, or a byproduct of grief?

What Is Grief?

Grief is complex and multi-layered and can’t be fully explained or understood in a single phrase. But at its core, grief is an emotional response and expression to loss. What that loss is and how grief is processed are all variable, but the core principle is that it is the natural consequence of loss.

Subtle vs. Blatant Grief

When a loss is a singular, identifiable event, like a death, grief is pretty easy to spot. Most people understand if you’re sad after the passing of your mother. And they are sympathetic when your spouse is admitted into hospice. While these big singular events are difficult to live through, there’s often a great deal of support offered. Church families might start a meal train for you, or neighbors might send flowers or a card.

Grief from these identifiable triggers can be horrific, but at least it can be understood. There’s no compelling reason to explain why you feel the way you do because it is relatable. Almost everyone has gone through a similar ordeal and can naturally empathize.

But grief caused by gradual or more subtle losses can often confuse people around you. Maybe you have realized that you’re no longer able to do the things you once could. Perhaps a chronic illness has changed your daily life, or aging has crept up on you and is now preventing you from doing things you love.

Maybe your children have grown up and left home, leaving behind an unfamiliar and off-putting silence. Or perhaps you are trying to come to terms with the realization that a long-held dream is unlikely to happen.

These losses don’t come with sympathy cards or a homemade casserole, but they still produce very real, very painful grief. Not only are they more difficult to identify, but they also often go unsupported for that very reason.

Delayed Grief

Another confusing aspect of grief is that it doesn’t follow a logical or predictable timeline. In the case of a family death, you might feel shock immediately following the event. But then you’re supported by family and friends. While you’re sad, the reality of the tragedy hasn’t quite sunk in.

Maybe you go months without really feeling much of anything. You keep yourself busy and shove the emotions behind a locked emotional door. But then, several months later, things slow down, and you start to feel the impact. You feel sad or lonely or struggle with guilt, and you don’t really know why. “Surely it couldn’t be grief over my loved one? That was months ago, and I’ve been fine,” you might say.

But grief doesn’t follow neat timelines, and it doesn’t adhere to logic. Grief can linger and then surface in the most unexpected moments. It doesn’t always identify itself properly either.

Grief in Disguise

One of the sneakiest aspects of grief is that it doesn’t always present itself in the obvious or expected ways. Of course, it can look like sadness, but it often wears disguises.

Anxiety

Instead of crying, you might find yourself feeling anxious instead. You might worry excessively about your health because of the death of your mother. You might feel constantly on the edge, worrying that yet another relationship will end in betrayal. Is this pure anxiety, or is it part of the grieving process from a major loss?

Depression

Grief can manifest as emotional shutdown. Things that you used to enjoy don’t really matter anymore. You might feel tired, unmotivated, or disconnected from everything that once held meaning. It can look like depression on the outside, but it can also be what grief feels like when shock wears off.

Anger

The common misconception about grief is that it’s synonymous with sadness, but sometimes it exhibits itself as anger. You might feel angry and not even fully know why, or get irritated by things that normally wouldn’t faze you. In these cases, unresolved grief may be to blame.

Busyness

Sometimes grief doesn’t slow you down at all. In fact, it might just speed you up. Sometimes in moments of grief, you pack your schedule so tight that there isn’t much room to think or feel. And that’s the point. Keeping busy is a way of avoiding feelings that you’re not ready to experience. This busyness can be a symptom.

Numbness

Sometimes grief makes you feel nothing. This can be your nervous system in shock or your brain’s way of protecting you from your own emotions. You might go through life, seemingly unfazed, but you might feel dead inside. Not necessarily sad, but truly nothing at all. Even joyful things bring little spike in your emotions when you’re grieving.

How Can You Distinguish These Feelings?

This is the tricky part. But it’s important. In order to resolve some of your bigger emotional issues, you have to trace the origins back to their roots. That can be difficult when emotional responses can mask in different ways and don’t follow predetermined courses. Could it be grief?

Examine Your Losses

When you feel like something isn’t quite right, it’s natural to wonder what’s wrong with you. But maybe the more helpful question would be, “What have I lost?”

This question can be helpful to narrow down possible contributors to your emotional responses. If you only look at what makes you angry, for example, you might be able to list injustices or circumstances that frustrate you. But those are external and environmental forces.

Your reaction to these external and environmental forces is what needs to be examined. You can do this on your own or with the help of a grief counselor. Think about how you feel. Yes, you’re angry and maybe justifiably so, but do those triggers match the severity of your reaction? Could underlying, unresolved grief be at fault? Has a loss in your life made you more susceptible and less resistant to emotional outbursts of anger or bouts of depression?

Ask God

The most important place to bring your questions about grief is to God through prayer. Sometimes people try to sort through their emotions all on their own. They try to analyze everything in an effort to figure out what grief is or what other feelings they have.

Prayer doesn’t always give you an immediate answer, although it can. But it does help you uncover what’s hidden in your life. As you honestly come to the Lord, bringing your confusion, anxiety, or anger, you might find clues in your words. Sometimes in that stillness of prayer, God can bring awareness and clarity. In His presence, truth is revealed.

When you feel overwhelmed by loss or red-hot in anger, God is there. In Psalm 34:18, we are told that God is with the brokenhearted. And that means you. That means you, in your anxiety, anger, and depression.

Talk to a Grief Counselor

Perhaps one of the most practical ways to determine whether your anger, depression, or other negative emotion is a product of grief or something else is to seek therapy. Because grief is so complex and can both mimic other conditions, such as Generalized Anxiety Disorder or Depression, and coexist with them, it can be helpful to have the expertise of a licensed professional on your side.

A grief counselor can not only help you uncover losses that might be negatively impacting your life, but they can also help you find a path to resolution.

If you’re experiencing unexplained anxiety, anger, depression, or any emotion that is interfering with your life or blocking your joy, call us. The reception team can connect you with a grief counselor who can help you identify and resolve grief, even if it’s buried deep in other emotional responses.

item.title: How Circadian Rhythms Shape the Path Through Depression Therapy
item.description:
Sleep can become a complicated thing when depression is present. There are nights when sleep eludes individuals. Sometimes sleep will take over the day and still leave a person feeling hollow, because the rest never reaches the level of tiredness the person feels. For some individuals walking through depression, lack of sleep isn’t just a rough patch of bad nights. The sleep patterns shape nearly every waking hour.

In recent years, it has become clear that depression therapy is connected to the body’s internal clock. Disconnection between depression and the circadian rhythm is biological – and understanding it can change the way depression is healed. As we examine this connection, we can hold onto the promise of Scripture for all of us: “He grants sleep to those he loves.” (Psalm 127:2b, NIV)

When Your Sleep Pattern and Depression Therapy Are Not Working Together

The body’s circadian rhythm is an internal 24-hour cycle. This rhythm regulates some cortisol spikes to get you moving in the morning and, as melatonin rises, helps ease you into sleep at night. Numerous other biological processes are happening beneath the surface, but for most people, this cycle plays out in the background without much thought. However, living with depression, this rhythm is frequently off in a dramatic way.

The difficulty of untangling this challenge is that disrupted sleep and depression reinforce each other in a relentless loop. Poor sleep deepens depressive symptoms, and depressive symptoms make restorative sleep feel out of reach.

The body is unable to understand when it’s supposed to be alert and when it’s supposed to rest. This leads to an emotional toll that compounds quickly and produces a kind of groundlessness in which evening and morning lose their distinctiveness. The result is that every day starts to feel the same shade of gray.

This can produce a particular kind of grief for people of faith. God designed people for rhythm. He gave us rhythms for mornings and evenings, for work and rest, and for seasons of beginnings and endings. When a person feels that this rhythm has been shattered from the inside, they tend to believe it is a personal failing.

That belief is worth examining. What feels like a spiritual shortcoming is often a sign that the body is in genuine distress and that care, not condemnation, is needed. In reality, it is a wound that can be tended with the right care. With help, you can hold onto the promise in Psalm 3:

I lie down and sleep; I wake again, because the LORD sustains me. – Psalm 3:5, NIV

The Biology Behind the Disconnection

The brain holds a suprachiasmatic nucleus that functions as the body’s master clock. This nucleus responds directly to light, especially the light that enters the eyes in the morning. When this happens, the brain suppresses melatonin and ramps up cortisol. And as the day winds down and natural light fades, the process reverses. It is a beautiful system when it works, the way God designed it.

Individuals who deal with depression often have an impaired light response system. Most major forms of depression have a connection to circadian disruption. It isn’t just a symptom of depression. It may be one of the mechanisms driving it. In some cases, the body clock is a contributing factor in depression.

When the internal clock is off, the ripple effect reaches far beyond sleep. Concentration narrows, emotional responses become harder to manage, and the motivation to engage with daily life — including relationships, work, and faith — quietly fades. For someone already carrying the weight of depression, these compounding losses can be difficult to name and even harder to explain.

Sometimes, everyday habits that seem unrelated make this challenge with the circadian rhythm worse. If an individual experiences irregular sleep and wake times, heavy screen exposure at night, spends most of the time indoors, and has a high-stress schedule, it sends competing messages to the internal clock. When the brain receives mixed signals, the consequences manifest emotionally, cognitively, and physically.

We can be honest with God about all these things:

My soul is weary with sorrow; strengthen me according to your word. – Psalm 119:28, NIV

Depression Therapy Approaches That Work with Your Body Clock

When the circadian aspect of this rhythm is understood, there is a door to depression therapy that will work with the body’s biology instead of around it. Light therapy is becoming a common resource to treat individuals who grapple with circadian rhythms and depression.

Light therapy involves sitting in front of a bright light for 20 to 30 minutes in the morning to help reset the body’s internal clock. This leads to measurable reductions in depressive symptoms, especially in seasonal affective disorder. This does not replace the comprehensive care received professionally, but it is a legitimate tool to assist in the approach of treating disconnected rhythms.

Some therapies can be used for sleep interventions. Stimulus control and sleep restriction therapies are used to retrain the sleep-wake cycle. They replace the brain’s association between bed and actual rest instead of the hours of relentless wakefulness associated with depression.

These are not passive treatments. They require consistency and a willingness to work against patterns that depression has reinforced over time. That kind of effort is not easy, but it is also not without hope. Making lifestyle adjustments will support these approaches and give the body a more stable foundation.

The Rhythms God Designed and the Healing He Provides

In Genesis, we see a structure built around days — evening and morning, light and dark, labor and rest. This isn’t a rhythm that God created only in the natural world, but also within us at a fundamental level.

Individuals navigating depression often experience life in terms of fractured sleep and depleted reserves. Rest is not a weakness or a luxury reserved for people whose lives are less demanding. It is a fundamental aspect of how we were designed to function that honors the way God has designed us.

God did not design rest as an afterthought. The rhythm of work and restoration is woven into creation itself, and when that rhythm is broken by depression, it does not mean the design has failed. It means the person needs care that addresses body, mind, and spirit together.

These questions revolve around the grief, the loss of meaning, and the spiritual awareness that depression carries. Healing depression and resetting the circadian rhythm happen when the person is treated holistically. This means that the process is real, even though it isn’t short. We can come to God in this process for the rest we long for. Jesus said, “Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.” (Matthew 11:28, NIV)

You Don’t Have to Figure This Out Alone

Depression steals a lot from individuals when their body’s own rhythm becomes part of what’s working against them. There is a path forward that includes understanding circadian rhythms and their role in depression. This realization expands the picture of what healing looks like, honors the biology God gave us, and the spiritual truth that holds steady.

The connection between an individual’s internal clock and their emotional health is real, and seeking help doesn’t mean choosing between science and faith. Each of these has a place at the table when it comes to sleep, light, and energy as part of treating the whole person.

Christian counselors are trained to approach mental health from the inside as they connect the biological, emotional, and spiritual dimensions of a person’s experience. Christian counselors can identify this intersection in ways that integrate faith and evidence. They create space for whole-person care in the treatment of depression. These counselors walk alongside people as they address the biological challenge and create space for the deeper questions.

There is no need to carry this situation alone. Our reception team is available to take your call and connect you with a counselor who can meet your needs through an integrated program.
