item.title: The Effectiveness and Challenges of DBT for Teens
item.description:
If you have a teen who is struggling in any area of life, you might have considered involving them in DBT, or at least wondered if DBT is right for them. Dialectical Behavioral Therapy (DBT) is an intensive form of talk therapy originally developed to help people with borderline personality disorder.

Now DBT helps people develop skills for managing crises, dealing with strong emotions, and improving communication in relationships. For these reasons, DBT for teens has become increasingly popular in recent years.

DBT is not suitable or effective for everyone. It is comprehensive, highly structured, and can feel demanding for some teens, especially those who are under academic pressure. DBT typically requires at least six months of involvement to see the best results, which is a commitment many teens and their families are not willing or even able to commit to. Still, it can be adapted to suit your needs and is worth considering as a potentially effective form of therapy for a struggling adolescent.

The Building Blocks of DBT

The goal of DBT is to reduce life-threatening behaviors like suicide attempts, self-harm, eating disorders, substance use, or severe emotional dysregulation. It helps by giving you the tools to cope and develop a balanced mindset with regulated emotions. This might sound like a tall order or even an impossible goal, but DBT is developed to help you over a long period of time.

DBT helps you develop skills using mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotional regulation, and interpersonal effectiveness. Firstly, with mindfulness, you are encouraged to be curious about your emotions, thoughts, and responses to the stressors in your life. The key is not to be judgmental of yourselves or others, but to pay gentle attention to your experiences. When you take notice of the things you are thinking and feeling, you have begun to regain control over the chaos in your life.

The next building block of DBT for teens is stress tolerance. There are many crises to navigate as an adolescent, and sometimes it feels as if you are inundated. DBT teaches you how to raise yourself to the surface of the stress, and, over time, to effortlessly navigate difficult situations.

Next, you will learn how to regulate your emotions. This is a vital skill that takes a long time to develop. However, learning how to calm your emotions when they have become overwhelming is a skill that you will carry far into life. Emotional regulation is a vital skill to have and one that you can hone and strengthen over time.

Lastly, DBT will teach you interpersonal effectiveness. This is a blanket term for a host of useful skills, like communicating your needs confidently, setting boundaries, and maintaining self-respect in any relationship. These are things that even adults take decades to learn. DBT could give you a head start as an adolescent in developing skills that you will use for the rest of your life.

The Structure of DBT for Teens

While every therapist is unique, there is a general format for DBT that most therapists will try to follow. Generally, you will attend weekly individual sessions with your therapist where you check in, set goals for your time together, learn or practice skills, and go over homework for the week ahead.

A typical individual session with your therapist will last anywhere between 45 minutes and an hour, after which time you might feel exhausted. Your therapist will also schedule sessions that involve family members, who will also develop skills and receive homework for the coming week.

DBT also typically involves a group therapy session with other teens. These are sort of like a class where you learn and practice new skills together. You might have to do some role-playing exercises and practice communication skills with partners.

A common communication exercise in DBT is DEAR MAN, which stands for Describe, Express, Assert, Reinforce, Mindful, Appear confident, and Negotiate. Another exercise frequently used in DBT for teens is Walking the Middle Path, which helps develop flexible thinking and better problem-solving skills.

Besides the weekly individual session with your therapist and group session, you will also complete homework, which typically involves filling out diary cards and worksheets focusing on your emotions and current experiences. Additionally, your therapist will call you once a week to do a brief coaching session. You might talk about something you are currently facing or a hypothetical situation. The phone session is an opportunity to rehearse a skill you have learned that will apply to the situation.

DBT is not a form of therapy you can approach nonchalantly; it is structured and highly comprehensive. Overall, it takes no less than six months for you to fully incorporate the skills you learn in DBT into your life. You will learn the balance of accepting your emotions in a non-judgmental way, while also changing the way you think and behave in certain situations so that you can cope with stress in healthier ways.

The Challenges of DBT for Teens

While the statistics show just how successful DBT is for teens, it is not a case of one-size-fits-all. Statistics also show high dropout rates and disengagement for teens and their families. Some people never realize how involved this form of therapy is, or else they fail to maintain the momentum required for long-term results.

Sometimes life changes so rapidly that your involvement in the process is hampered. Weeks turn to months, and eventually it’s too hard to pick up from wherever you left off with your therapist. Some people face logistical barriers, too. Intensive therapy is hard for adults, let alone teenagers who have exams, academic pressures, and frequent relationship crises. The things that impact your mental health and necessitate therapy are also the things that steal focus and inhibit your progress.

While some people thrive with the rigid structure and demands of DBT, others find the formal structure clinical and repetitive. People with intellectual disabilities or neurodiverse disorders will likely not gain much from DBT, and it may cause more harm than good in the long run. DBT does not match with some cultures. Certain families will decide that DBT is not a good fit for them at all.

DBT for teens requires regular involvement from parents or primary caregivers and sometimes siblings. They are also required to learn communication and emotional regulation skills, so that the family grows and matures as a unit. However, this can be demanding for certain families who have limited time and demanding schedules. They might have their own unresolved emotional issues, which they are not ready to face. While these factors are legitimate, they also hamper progress.

DBT is as structured, demanding, and intense as it is effective. There are certain issues both teens and adults face that can only be helped by therapies like DBT. Sometimes it is helpful simply knowing that you have options, and that there is a form of therapy specifically designed to impact the specific struggle you are facing. DBT for teens provides an opportunity for a family to learn, heal, and grow together. If you are willing to do the work today, you will reap a harvest tomorrow.

Learn More About DBT for Teens

If you are curious about DBT, if you would like to discuss it with a professional, or if you would like to see if it is available in your area, please get in touch with us. You may speak with our online reception team, who will help connect you to a counselor for more information. We also host an online catalog of counselors whom you can reach out to directly if you would prefer. We hope that we can help you find the form of therapy and counseling that best suits you.

“Teen boy standing alone,” courtesy of Lesli Whitecotton, Unsplash.com, CCO License

item.title: Emotional Abuse and the Invisible Wounds That Run Deep
item.description:
There are times when a person will walk away from a relationship with no visible bruises or physical evidence of harm. Society sees this and says it wasn’t that bad. But there is abuse that doesn’t require physical force to cause real damage. Emotional abuse works gradually through words, silence, manipulation, and control to reshape the way a person sees themselves, the relationship, and their sense of what is normal.

For survivors, the hardest part of this experience is convincing themselves that what happened was real. There may be no photographs of the damage and no visible injuries to point to that clearly mark a line that was crossed. There’s no way to define a single incident that moved into the realm of unacceptable behavior. But something inside of these individuals knows that this abuse was real.

There’s a confusion that comes with this invisible injury, and it is part of the harm. Pain that isn’t seen becomes easy to minimize for others who weren’t there, and for the person who carried it quietly for years.

The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit. – Psalm 34:18, ESV

What Emotional Abuse Actually Looks Like

Emotional abuse does not arrive with a loud voice or an obvious presence. It doesn’t always show up in screaming, in a match, or in clear-cut cruelty. It accumulates slowly in small moments that seem almost manageable.

It could show up as a partner who frames constant criticism as concern or maybe a parent who uses guilt as a primary tool to shape behavior. It may be the friend who dismisses your feelings so consistently that you stop sharing them altogether. These are the patterns that, over time, will produce something in an individual that is deeper than hurt feelings.

Individuals who experience emotional abuse often begin to question their own perception, yet they are right to trust what they sense. Christian counselors are trained to work with individuals who cannot identify what is wrong but do recognize that something is off – feeling depleted, anxious, and small.

Without the presence of a dramatic defining incident, emotional abuse can be harder to name and harder to leave. When there’s no clear moment to point to, doubt fills the space where certainty should be.

For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. – Ephesians 6:12, ESV

The Weight of Words That Stay

Harsh, dismissive words from someone we loved carry disproportionate weight. Our brains are wired for connection, and when people closest to us use that as a point of pressure, the impact is far beyond the surface.

Emotional pain activates the same brain regions as physical pain. Which means the pain people think of as just words or just a difficult personality is actually registered by our nervous system as a genuine threat.

The result of this is a state of chronic vigilance. This is a mindset of always watching, always adjusting, and always trying to stay one step ahead of the next wave of criticism or emotional withdrawal. Society tends to label this as over-sensitivity, but in actuality, it is the natural outcome of living in an environment where safety feels unpredictable and love seems conditional.

The weight of the words spoken isn’t lifted when the relationship ends or when the person is no longer physically present. This weight travels with the survivor long after they have left and surfaces in new relationships, quiet moments, or the way they speak to themselves when no one’s around.

He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. – Psalm 147:3, ESV

How Emotional Abuse Shapes the Way You See Yourself

The most significant and lasting effect of emotional abuse is the damage that occurs to a person’s narrative. It is this running commentary they carry about who they are and what they deserve. Survivors of emotional abuse tend to have an internal voice that sounds remarkably like the person who hurt them.

Some of the effects include second-guessing decisions, apologizing compulsively, or minimizing their own experiences. Each of these actions comes from the place of not knowing the truth after living with so many lies. Christian counselors who are trained in trauma and relational harm define this pattern as an internalized critic. It was placed there by someone else, but the survivor carries it as though it were their own honest assessment.

Untangling this inner voice from its connection to the God-given sense of self is one of the most important parts of emotional abuse recovery. This process becomes deeply sacred as it involves reclaiming an identity that was never the abuser’s to define. This was an identity that was present long before the relationship began, and it remains distorted by emotional abuse.

I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Wonderful are your works; my soul knows it very well. – Psalm 139:14, ESV

Finding Ground Again After the Damage Is Done

The process of healing from relational harm does not follow a clear or predictable timeline. Individuals often encounter setbacks connected to phrases that sound familiar or a wave of grief that arrives without warning. These are signs of a nervous system and spirit that are learning what safety feels like from the inside out. They do not define the individual as a failure or as permanently broken.

The most consistent feature of emotional abuse is isolation. Learning to rebuild community with trusted people and God is one of the most liberating and powerful steps toward broad restoration. Christian counselors help individuals understand that faith does not require minimizing what happened.

Experiencing recovery through honest prayer and lamenting, bringing the weight of the experience to God, are acts of courage, not weakness. Healing from this unseen abuse begins with a single decision to stop dismissing what you lived through.

Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. – Matthew 11:28, ESV

Conclusion

Emotional abuse can leave a mark that the eye cannot see, but the heart and body know it is present. The confusion and self-doubt are not imagined; they are not trivial. These are real injuries that deserve real care and a safe place to heal.

Scripture meets suffering honestly. The God who heals the broken heart and draws near to the crushed is not distant from the person who is still quietly trying to make sense of this unseen abuse. There is no way to rank the pain of emotional wounds beneath physical ones when it comes to what deserves to be addressed.

Individuals who have spent years having their reality questioned and their emotions managed deserve a space to name their experience, be believed, and taken seriously. This space exists, and it is not too late to take that first step toward building their original sense of self.

The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me to bring good news to the poor; he has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are bound. – Isaiah 61:1, ESV

If you are an individual who’s navigating these lasting effects of emotional abuse, reaching out is the first step to gaining strength. Our reception team can help you connect with a counselor who understands and can help you navigate this journey of stepping away from the invisible abuse and walking toward healing. Contact our office today.

item.title: What Are Signs of Bipolar Disorder in Women?
item.description:
The signs of bipolar disorder in women can mimic other conditions or worsen due to stress and hormonal changes. Intense episodes of manic and depressive states can shift quickly, leaving problems in relationships, physical health, work, school, sleep, appetite, and judgment.

Once you know the signs of bipolar disorder in women, you can begin to look for patterns and seek professional help.

Signs of Bipolar Disorder in Women

The signs of bipolar disorder in women can only be diagnosed by a medical professional after assessing symptom persistence, severity, and patterns. You may experience manic episodes that can last from seven days to several months, while depressive episodes can range from 14 days to 6 months or more.

Manic Symptoms

Manic symptoms appear as over-the-top behavior. During a manic episode, the woman may flit from one thing to another, take on more responsibilities than is realistic, and seem uncharacteristically loud and talkative. Manic episodes are just one-half of bipolar disorder in women, followed closely by depressive episodes.

Rapid Movements and Speech

Manic behavior includes rapid movements and speech. The woman with bipolar disorder may move quickly or have jerky movements. She speaks rapidly and loudly, making it hard to interrupt or talk over her. People may need to tell her to slow down or ask her to repeat herself.

Racing Thoughts

Thoughts come at a rapid-fire pace. She may try to tackle too many tasks at once, flitting about from idea to idea. She may leave tasks half-done or stop mid-sentence because a new thought occurred to her. People may struggle to follow her line of thought.

Little Sleep

A woman with bipolar disorder may be able to get away with only three to four hours of sleep per night and feel rested during the day. She may stay up late cleaning house or working on projects, sleep a few hours, then go straight into work.

Grandiose Thinking

Bipolar manic episodes can lead a woman to believe she is invincible and more important than she is at work, in relationships, and to the world at large. She may adopt grandiose thinking and believe she is entitled to certain benefits.

Easily Distracted

As the mind races, the woman with bipolar disorder may struggle to stay focused. She may become easily distracted by others, sounds, and smells. She may interrupt herself to comment on a distraction and lose her train of thought. Others may find this aggravating, especially at work when projects don’t get done, or deadlines aren’t met.

Impulsive Actions

Manic episodes can make people lean towards impulsive actions and rash decisions. They may end relationships, quit jobs, or walk out of conversations. This is also a time when a woman struggling with bipolar disorder may say things she doesn’t mean.

Poor Judgment, Especially with Money

Manic episodes can lead to poor judgment, especially with money. The woman may spend as if there’s no limit, letting bank accounts go into the negative or applying for more credit cards. She may make impulse purchases or buy things to show off.

Depressive Symptoms

Depressive symptoms in bipolar disorder in women can vary, but most notably include persistent sadness that can last for weeks or months. Bipolar depression can last longer if left untreated.

Persistent Sadness

Persistent sadness is the hallmark symptom of depression. This sadness can include feelings of emptiness, numbness, and a nonchalant attitude towards people and situations.

Fatigue and Low Energy

There is a bone-deep weariness that sets in with depression. The woman in a depressive state may feel tired all the time, even after sleeping well during the night. Small tasks may seem like too much effort, such as bathing, grooming, and making meals.

Loss of Interest in Hobbies, Socializing, and Other Things That Brought Pleasure

The woman with depression can lose interest in the things that always brought her pleasure. Hobbies, social events, and even television shows can fall by the wayside.

Rapid Appetite and Weight Changes

Depression can bring about rapid appetite and weight changes. She may not feel like eating due to hunger hormone imbalances, or she may emotionally eat to make herself feel better. Noticeable weight gain or loss can occur during this time.

Trouble Concentrating

Depression can make it difficult to focus on work or other tasks. Brain fog and forgetfulness are common. This can cause problems at work and jeopardize a woman’s job.

Suicide Ideation

Depression can feel like it’s never-ending. This can bring about negative thoughts of self-harm and death. If you are struggling with depression and suicidal thoughts, seek help immediately.

Local Treatment for Bipolar Disorder in Women

Treatment is available for the signs of bipolar disorder in women. You can find our Christian counseling center in your local area for in-person sessions, or you can choose virtual sessions from the comfort of your own home. Since the signs of bipolar disorder in women can mirror other conditions, seek professional help from one of the counselors in our association to overcome the symptoms and break the cycle.

item.title: Christian Perspectives for Anxiety Relief from Hypochondria
item.description:
The constant checking and the endless Google searches create an overwhelming fear that every headache signals some sort of catastrophe. Hypochondria, also known as health anxiety, creates a prison where our mind can become both warden and prisoner. Many Christians struggle and feel isolated because there’s an underlying belief that faith should somehow shield us from these fears.

But the truth is more complex than a simple expectation. Finding genuine anxiety relief requires understanding that even people of deep faith and experience health-related fears. It also requires the acknowledgment that God’s healing can come through both spiritual and practical approaches.

This struggle isn’t about weak faith or insufficient trust in God. Health anxiety affects believers and non-believers in the same way, creating a cycle where physical sensations trigger catastrophic thoughts. These thoughts then create more physical symptoms. The mind and body become trapped in this feedback loop that feels impossible to escape.

However, in the midst of Christian teaching, a framework is set for understanding our humanity and our hope. The first step in this journey toward anxiety relief starts with the acknowledgment that our struggles do not disqualify us from God’s love or healing.

Recognizing the Root of Health Anxiety in Faith Context

Hypochondria often stems from a fundamental misunderstanding of the concepts of control and mortality. Becoming fixated on every bodily sensation causes us to try to manage the unmanageable. This creates an impossible situation, for being vigilant seems necessary for survival. But the same vigilance essentially breeds the anxiety we are trying to avoid.

The contradiction becomes exhausting, and we are left feeling like we failed at something. We should naturally understand. We have an anxiety-driven narrative that our bodies are fragile and unreliable systems that are constantly on the verge of breakdown. Scripture tells us that our physical forms are as God intentionally and wonderfully designed, but we often lose sight of this truth when we are caught up in this cycle of health anxiety.

I praise you because I am fearfully and wonderfully made; your works are wonderful, I know that full well. – Psalm 139:14, NIV

We often see our bodies as enemies rather than gifts. Christian counselors can help us reconnect with this foundational understanding that our physical existence is not a mistake nor a burden to be constantly monitored.

The root of helping anxiety often lies in the illusion that constant vigilance is equal to safety. We have convinced ourselves that if we pay enough attention, do enough research, and check enough, then we can prevent a health disaster.

This is a contradicting mindset of the biblical understanding that God has planned our days, and not our ability to catch every problem that may arise. As we learn to recognize this pattern in this mindset, we are taking the first step toward freedom.

Grounding Yourself in Biblical Truth for Anxiety Relief

When your mind is caught in health anxiety, you find that there are elaborate stories about worst-case scenarios floating around in your thoughts. Every time you have a muscle twitch, your thoughts take you straight to the scenario of a neurological disorder. Every irregular heartbeat brings thoughts of impending cardiac arrest. These thoughts feel real and urgent, seemingly demanding immediate attention and action.

Scripture offers us a different framework for handling these anxious thoughts. It is a thought process that doesn’t dismiss these concerns, but instead helps us find a healthy way of processing them.

Do not be anxious about anything, but in every situation, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. And the peace of God, which transcends all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus. – Philippians 4:6-7, NIV

Scripture doesn’t suggest that we should never feel concerned about health issues; on the contrary, it provides a practical pathway for handling those concerns. God’s instructions for us to present our requests to Him are His acknowledgment that we will have worries and needs.

God’s promise of peace that surpasses understanding offered us something beyond our human logic and medical reassurance. Anxiety relief from this peace doesn’t come from having all the answers, but from trusting the one who does. Practical application involves learning to intercept anxious thoughts before they spiral.

When you have a health concern, rather than immediately turning to the Internet or obsessively checking, your first step in faith-based application is to turn to prayer first. This isn’t to suggest that you should avoid appropriate medical care, but rather choose peace over panic in approaching your health concern. Christian counselors can help you learn this manner of redirection as a fundamental skill for managing hypochondria.

Building Trust Through Surrender and Acceptance

We all have a desire to control our health outcomes that runs deeper than a simple preference. This desire touches on fundamental questions about mortality, purpose, and trust. Health anxiety often masks a deeper struggle with surrendering control to God.

We want to believe that our vigilance, research, and constant monitoring can somehow guarantee our well-being. The result is an impossible burden, where we become responsible for outcomes that were never within our control.

This requires us to learn how to trust God. This doesn’t mean we should become careless or avoid medical care. In fact, it means we recognize the difference between wise stewardship and anxious control. Wise stewardship is evident as we choose to engage in regular check-ups, healthy lifestyle choices, and appropriate attention to symptoms we experience.

Trust in the Lord with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways submit to him, and he will make your paths straight. – Proverbs 3:5-6, NIV

Anxious control involves endless research and constant symptom checking, which is surrounded by the belief that our worry will somehow protect us from harm from any health issue we may face. This creates a feeling that surrender is counterintuitive when dealing with health anxiety because our every instinct screams that we must remain vigilant.

True peace will come from understanding that our health security doesn’t depend on our ability to predict or prevent health issues. The shift from self-protection to God dependence may feel like stepping off a cliff, but it will help you step on the solid ground that was always there.

Creating Healthy Boundaries with Medical Information

This can be helpful for general health education, but it can also become dangerous territory for those who struggle with hypochondria. The endless possibilities provided by the Internet for self-diagnosis lead to information that is more frightening with each search. Learning to create boundaries regarding medical information is essential to maintaining peace and finding anxiety relief.

Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have received from God? You are not your own; you were bought at a price. Therefore honor God with your bodies. – 1 Corinthians 6:19-20, NIV

Rather than viewing our physical form as something to be taken for granted, we should constantly monitor and protect it through our own efforts; according to Scripture, we need to refrain from taking this relationship for granted with our bodies. God has designed our bodies so intricately that he knows how to provide healing in ways we do not see.

Our bodies are a sacred space that belongs to our creator. This belief does not diminish the importance of caring for our bodies properly, but it should change our motivation from fear-based to worship-based stewardship.

Practical boundaries could include limiting health-related Internet searches and avoiding medical websites, except for verified concerns. We should choose to consult healthcare providers rather than online symptom checkers.

It could even be helpful to designate specific times for health-related concerns and not allow them to dominate every moment. Our goal isn’t to become careless, but to create space for peace and trust that will coexist with appropriate health awareness.

From Health Anxiety to Peace

The journey from health anxiety to peace involves learning to trust God’s love and sovereignty, rather than letting health concerns define our experience. Christian counselors can provide guidance in navigating this balance, helping us respond to health concerns with peace rather than panic.

Your local Christian counseling service can connect you with a counselor who will help you navigate reframing your health-anxious thoughts to those of peace. Call our office to speak to a representative and schedule an appointment with a counselor near you.

item.title: Issues Surrounding Aging, Loneliness, and Depression That No One Talks About
item.description:
Many people reach a point in life where it feels like they are sitting alone in a waiting room, with nothing to expect, good or bad. A lot of others find it difficult to say, or even speak aloud, how they feel about growing old/aging with grace, some would say. It would take courage to acknowledge “This getting old sucks.” or even that they are feeling out of sorts.

These thoughts are personal, not to be shared; it’s way too private. One of the reasons this may happen, some older adults have shared feelings and have been denied really being heard, not just listened to. “I’m grieving the loss of my physical health, strength, my spouse, siblings, friends, co-workers, relatives, and my joy.” I feel lost.

Loneliness doesn’t just start at fifty or sixty-five-plus years; that is part of our journey in life. Everyone at some time in life will experience feeling alone. Yet, during the declining years of fifty-plus, there is a change in how we see connections to our support systems. The value of those relationships, as we experience attending the funerals, or hearing of the loss of a relative or longtime friend(s) or acquaintance(s).

It is troubling. When physical and medical challenges increase, it is plausible that depression and loneliness may become a common part of the aging journey, but they don’t have to be. Both can be addressed if you seek help. Life has not truly ended for anyone who has woken up this morning.

Things might look a lot different and less appealing than they once did, but sometimes you need a fresh perspective to see life with a hopeful perspective again. There is a scripture that refers to all things becoming new.

2 Corinthians 5:17 (ESV) “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.” Our mindset has to change. If you acknowledge that Jesus is Lord and Savior, your mindset must change. That is the same with aging.

Why People Don’t See Loneliness and Depression in the Aging Population

If you grew up in a society that condemned or stigmatized things like loneliness and depression, there is little chance that you would ever admit feeling those things yourself. Loneliness was often seen as a kind of weakness, and depression was almost on par with moral failure. People used to gossip in hushed whispers about friends they knew who went to “shrinks,” and therapy was reserved for people with scandalous issues.

Mental health was not a topic people mentioned, except to say what they didn’t believe about it. With values like these, many older people are in denial about their struggles with deep sadness/ depression and fears of being labeled crazy; they brush off any attempt to get help.

It’s easy to mask loneliness and depression behind old age. Depression among people frequently manifests physically, too. It shows in the form of fatigue, memory loss, loss of appetite, difficulty sleeping, and a host of physical ailments and pains.

You might be passing these things off as a part of the regular aging process, and sometimes that’s all they are. However, if you have a general sense of hopelessness and disinterest in life, then these physical symptoms can be manifestations of depression.

If you reach the point in life where you are withdrawing from activities and people, where you spend the majority of your time alone, and where it feels like you have nothing to look forward to, you are likely experiencing loneliness, the outcome of which leads to a depressive mood. This is not a weakness or failure, but something many people experience.

Regardless of your values and belief system, you don’t have to remain feeling this way. It can be hard to communicate with family members about your current state of mind, and often they seem too preoccupied with their own lives to pay attention to any changes you are experiencing.

Unique Challenges That Cause Loneliness and Depression for Older People

You might be feeling like you don’t fit in today’s world because you have had to adjust to a lot of rapid changes; it’s overwhelming. The world changes around you quicker than you can adjust. There is new technology seemingly every day, and at some point, it feels easier to stay out of the loop than to try to keep up.

If you are experiencing the constant feeling of being anxious, not being attended to, what I mean by that is to be seen (facial expressions, eye contact, uncomfortable), heard (are you listening to me when I say how I feel, the words I use), understood (validate my feelings with understanding/ help)

It is overwhelming and lonely to face so much change. In many areas of society, it seems like chaos everywhere, and you don’t understand. It is even worse when there is no one to help explain all the changes to you.

One of the hardest changes to adapt to is when you lose a loved one. If you have lived with and loved someone for most of your life and they aren’t there anymore, that is one of the deepest forms of loneliness and sadness you can face. You may find it difficult to begin living with such a space in your life; a life with its most precious element missing.

If you are grieving the loss of a loved one, you are not alone, and you don’t have to be. Do you fear how you can live without your loved one or that best friend? A counselor can help you process the loss on the journey of grieving. The grief journey is not one to walk alone; you will need support when you are ready to talk about it.

Aging brings a host of issues with it; chief among them is having to deal with a body that is changing, in many ways. Anyone would struggle with having limited mobility, experiencing aches and pains that are unfamiliar.

It’s scary, not just uncomfortable, adapting to new medications and having their independence and wallet impacted by all these things. Ageing well can be difficult for some, but there is help available. “Fear not” is in the Bible multiple times.

Hebrews 13:5 (NIV): “God has said, ‘Never will I leave you; never will I forsake you.’” This verse reminds us of God’s unwavering commitment to His children. He promises to always be with us, never abandoning or forsaking us, even in the midst of challenges and difficulties.

During the changes in our lifestyle due to aging, our hope is that we will have good, positive support. We have to think about what we would consider good support. Preparing ahead of time will make all the difference. Decide who you can consider dependable or not, even in the family, and who is able and willing to help. Guard your heart from disappointment.

Also, consider assistance outside of family through organizations that have excellent reviews. Preparing for the transition of your lifestyle will offer you a sense of peace. If you’re relying on your family for support to any degree, there’s a good chance that you feel as if you’re a burden to them. You may not be a burden, and they would never see you that way if they love you.

Yet we don’t know if they are going to be available. Feeling like a burden can add to depression and hopelessness. That is why we must plan ahead. In our mobile society, many young families have moved away, taken jobs in other areas in the state or other states.

Some families are less involved in their older relatives’ lives. There are few things that are as painful as feeling less important in your loved one’s life. They might think of you regularly, but you won’t know that unless they visit you or call you to prove it.

One of the most unique experiences of aging is a feeling of regret over missed life goals. This is a feeling that you typically only get at a certain age when you take stock of your accomplishments over the years and feel like you missed out on doing important things.

There is a special kind of sadness attached to these feelings, and it’s depressing. It grieves the loss of a perceived opportunity from long ago. Or even a few months ago. You might have run out of resources, motivation, and opportunities, but you haven’t run out of time.

What to Know as a Younger Adult

As a younger person supporting an older family member, there are a few important things to keep in mind and a few practical ways that you can better support your loved ones. The first one is consistency. Life can be demanding, but there will always be excuses until you make up your mind to prioritize someone.

The only thing many senior adults want is your presence. They appreciate your gift of your time with them and couldn’t survive without your practical support. In their last days, all they want is to be with the ones they love.

A practical and straightforward way to support your aging loved one through the aging journey or even their latter days of living is to be attentive and listen to them with understanding. They may repeat the same story for the hundredth time. Their stories and their experiences are like heirlooms, and they have held enormous value for decades. Honor them by treasuring them.

Reassure them that they are loved and a priceless treasure in order to ensure their comfort and happiness. This should go without saying, but it won’t hurt to repeat as often as necessary. Aging family members or friends who are seniors will experience loneliness and some depressive moods.

So much has changed in their physical health, strength, and stamina; with the loss of loved ones and the sorrow of friends who have died, they need to know that they still hold value, that their presence still matters, and that they still have something to impart and teach.

Find out something that they enjoy and ask if they are interested in doing that activity. Allow them to have a voice when you visit. It might be a game or maybe a creative project, like compiling a family tree made of old photographs. You will provide company for them as you craft something together. Equally important is that you also provide a sense of purpose, perhaps even creating something that they can leave behind as their legacy.

Next Steps

Depression is treatable at any age, and it is never too late to get support. If you are caring for a senior or aging family member or friend, you might also need to speak with someone for your sake. Consider meeting with a counselor to share your burdens. Please consult our online catalog or speak with our administration team for further help.

Photos:
“Looking Out the Window”, Unsplash.com, Unsplash+ License; “Grandmother”, Courtesy of Hosein Sediqi, Unsplash.com, CC0 License; “Elderly Woman”, Courtesy of Curated Lifestyle, Unsplash.com, Unsplash+ License; “Still in Love” Courtesy of Junior REIS, Unsplash.com, CC0 License

The post Issues Surrounding Aging, Loneliness, and Depression That No One Talks About appeared first on Tacoma Christian Counseling.

item.title: Dealing with Anxiety: Is an Idle Mind the Devil’s Workshop?
item.description:
There’s an old saying about being idle: “An idle mind is the devil’s workshop.” Some people might swap out hands for mind, but the message is the same. When you’re idle, you give room to the enemy and an environment where unhealthy thoughts can grow.

While keeping your hands busy is good advice for staving off anxious and unhealthy thoughts, the mind is where the real battle often happens. Your thoughts can become dangerous weapons in your mind when they’re unrestrained or unfiltered.

Are you struggling with anxiety? Perhaps you have an idle mind that is working against you. If you are lacking purpose or structure, you may be opening yourself up to endless overthinking or anxiety. The human mind was specifically designed to facilitate a purposeful life. When it sits in an unstructured environment for too long, there can be some unhealthy consequences.

I Thought I Was Supposed to Be Still

The Bible explicitly says to “Be still, and know that I am God.” (Psalm 46:10, ESV) God tells people to slow down numerous times in the Bible. Even He took a break after six days of creation.

Rest isn’t the problem at all. In fact, you should take a break long enough to enjoy the beauty and peace around you. You need time to absorb His love and to meditate on Him. And if you can stay in that wonderful, meditative, and solitary place, then you’re in a good, restful place. You don’t have to concern yourself with your idleness becoming a conduit for Satan’s lies.

But there is a significant difference between purposeful rest and unhealthy idleness. While they might look oddly similar to an outside observer, the internal results are polar opposites.

Rest restores and can help you reconnect with your Creator. It’s the “Be Still” that God lovingly instructed you to do. But unhealthy isolation is entirely different. The same stillness that can bring you peace when done with purpose and directed toward God can also leave you vulnerable to fear and anxiety if done improperly.

Rest vs. Idleness

How do you distinguish between anxious idleness and true rest when they look so similar on the outside? Given time, the distinction will be obvious, but there are some signs you can look for in the early stages of your rest that can help you determine which path you’re walking down.

Are you feeling physically relaxed, or are you holding anxiety in your muscles? If you notice that you’re clenching your jaw or fists, have your shoulders raised, or are curling your toes, chances are, you’re not fully resting.

The true test as to whether you’re resting or simply being idle is to take note of what your mind is doing while your body is sitting still. When you’re at rest, are you intentionally directing your thoughts toward something peaceful or allowing them to drift at will? Are you thinking positive things, or is your mind drifting into anxious territory? If your mind is racing through a series of stressful thoughts, then this time of rest may actually be causing more harm than good.

An Unoccupied Mind

While your body might technically be resting, you may feel mentally untethered and become consumed by fear. When the mind lacks direction or taming, anxiety gladly steps in to fill that void. This is where the enemy loves to operate, in the unchecked corners of your mind.

A single fleeting thought or seemingly benign trigger can turn into ten catastrophic, not-so-benign mental images. And before long, they have taken root in your DNA with no signs of letting go. Maybe these unrelenting mental images develop into new intrusive thoughts. Maybe they give birth to worst-case scenarios. Maybe they are more exhausting to deal with than your average workday.

The Anxiety Spiral

Why does a blank calendar feel like a threat rather than a much-needed break? It’s because anxiety thrives in idleness. When you’re not actively directing your thoughts towards something productive, your brain may default to problem-solving mode, especially if problem-solving is part of your average day. If there isn’t an immediate problem that actually needs solving, anxiety will happily manufacture one.

In those not-so-busy moments, the enemy likes to whisper in your ear. Sometimes the only phrase he needs to drop is a simple, “What if…” to start your internal wheels.

What if that headache is something serious? What if that unanswered text is signaling the end of a relationship? What if you fail to provide for your family and you lose your housing?

A single spark of doubt can quickly spread and morph into a false reality. Soon your heart rate accelerates and your muscles tense. What started as a question in your head has now spread to your nervous system.

Misguided Imagination

Once your mind starts spiraling, it’s very difficult to distinguish between a true threat and an anxiety-induced fear. Anxiety likes to disguise itself as preparation. It is rather convincing when it demands that you rehearse every possible outcome and prepare for every possible loss. But what it’s actually doing is more insidious than you might recognize.

It is taking your gift of creativity that God gave to you and turning it inward as fear. Instead of imagining the creative things God will do in your life, anxiety demands a focus on what might go wrong.

Learning to Rest

How can you learn to rest? To truly rest and be still, you need to cast away everything that might pull you away from God (2 Corinthians 10:5). What are those things that might pull you away from Him?

Doubt and lack of faith can draw you away from God. So can unforgiveness that manifests from dwelling on past pain and injustice. Comparing yourself and your life to others with envy can also interfere with your relationship with God, as ungratefulness takes root.

When you sit down to rest without a deliberate focus, these are the exact entry points that anxiety uses to ruin your peace and potentially your relationship with God.

Taking your thoughts captive is the key to finding peace, and it requires you to actively guard the gateway of your mind. When a critical thought or trigger drifts in, you have to intercept it and ask whether the thought reflects God’s character.

If the answer is no, then you must cast it down by refusing to entertain it. You must rebuke it through the power of Jesus. Consciously hand it over to Christ. And in this act of surrender, you also reclaim that stillness for the purpose God intended.

Therapy Can Help Idleness and Anxiety

Therapy can serve as a bridge, allowing you to transition from unhealthy idleness to purposeful rest. If you are trying to find peace, only to be bombarded with anxiety and intrusive thoughts, then therapy can help.

Therapy allows you to dump all those thoughts that are ruminating in your mind out in the open. Your therapist will allow you the time and opportunity to communicate your fears and confront the intrusive thoughts.

Your Christian therapist can help you learn how to stop spiraling into unhealthy places and help you refocus on your loving Heavenly Father. Scripture calls you to renew your thinking (Romans 12:2) and to take thoughts captive (2 Corinthians 10:5). It reminds you to focus on what is true, not what is fear-driven (Philippians 4:8). Only then can you truly find rest while being still.

If your idle mind is the devil’s workshop, it’s time to learn how to be still and know that God is still in control. Contact this office today. A therapist can help guide you through the process of capturing your anxiety and finding peace in Christ.

item.title: When Compliments Make You Uncomfortable: How Extreme Social Anxiety Breeds Imposter Syndrome
item.description:
Compliments are meant to feel good. Someone notices your effort, your skill, or your character and says something kind. Yet for many people, praise brings tension instead of relief. Instead of soaking in the warmth of kind words, you might feel your stomach twist, or your cheeks flush. You tell yourself the person is being polite, exaggerating, or simply wrong. They said something positive but you know the truth, and you’re embarrassed by it.

Rather than feeling proud, you feel exposed, as if the compliment is actually an accusation that you do not want announced.

This reaction isn’t just modesty. It could be more than your insecurity. It might be a sign of extreme social anxiety quietly shaping how you interpret success. When every compliment feels like a spotlight exposing your flaws, it’s easy to believe you’re living a lie. That’s where imposter syndrome sneaks in. When praise feels like pressure instead of support, imposter syndrome usually follows close behind.

Why Success Doesn’t Silence the Inner Critic

You might think that achieving more, earning promotions, finishing degrees, or receiving recognition would quiet the voice of self-doubt. But for those living with imposter syndrome, success often amplifies it. Each achievement becomes another rung on a ladder you’re terrified of falling from.

These thoughts may sound familiar:

  • If they think I am good at this, expectations rise.
  • If expectations rise, failure feels closer.
  • If I fail, everyone will see who I really am.

This cycle is exhausting. Success doesn’t silence the critic because the critic isn’t rational; it’s fueled by anxiety. And when extreme social anxiety is part of the picture, even small compliments can feel like proof that you’re about to be found out.

How Anxiety Quietly Fuels Imposter Feelings

Many people believe confidence grows with success. More praise should equal more comfort. Yet with imposter syndrome, the opposite happens. It’s as if even mild insecurities are amplified and broadcast.

Each promotion, award, or positive comment feels like borrowed time. Instead of feeling proud, you feel watched. The voice inside says luck played a role. Timing saved you. Someone else deserved this more. You experience guilt for accomplishing something and embarrassed for excelling where others failed, at least when it is acknowledged out in the open.

That feeling has a name: imposter syndrome. It’s not a clinical diagnosis, but it’s a recognized psychological experience that affects millions of people across professions, cultures, and backgrounds. When every compliment feels like a spotlight exposing your flaws, it’s easy to believe you’re undeserving of what you’ve achieved. That’s how imposter syndrome takes root.

Extreme social anxiety feeds that voice simply because anxiety does not argue with logic. It reacts to a threat. As always, you can’t reason with an irrational thought. Together, anxiety and imposter syndrome create a powerful illusion that you’re unworthy, even when reality says otherwise. Praise signals attention, and attention feels unsafe.

You work harder to avoid mistakes, replay conversations in your head, and fear that one wrong move will erase everything you’ve earned.

What Imposter Syndrome Really Is

Imposter syndrome describes the feeling of being a fraud, even when evidence says otherwise. Degrees, experience, and praise fail to register as proof. Instead, your mind searches for reasons those things do not count.

You tell yourself others overestimate you. You wait for someone to point out the truth. You feel like you slipped through the cracks.

This experience appears across ages, jobs, and backgrounds. For people with extreme social anxiety, it feels constant. The fear of judgment blends with self-doubt and creates a steady sense of danger around success.  If there was ever a time to learn to question your feelings, this would be it. “Why does this accomplishment or compliment make me feel worse? Maybe I should talk to someone about this.” I invite you to contact our reception team today to schedule an appointment.

Anxiety doesn’t always announce itself with panic attacks or visible distress. Sometimes it hides in the simplest ways: the knot in your stomach before a meeting, the hesitation to accept praise, the constant replay of conversations in your head.

This quiet anxiety feeds imposter syndrome by:

  • Mistakes feel huge: A small error feels like proof you never belonged. Your mind zooms in on flaws and ignores progress.
  • Success feels discounted: Praise feels undeserved. You credit chance, kindness, or lowered standards rather than effort.
  • Attention feels threatening: Compliments feel like traps. The more people see you, the more exposed you feel.
  • Perfection feels required: You push yourself past exhaustion to avoid giving anyone a reason to doubt you.

When extreme social anxiety is present, these patterns intensify. You may avoid opportunities, downplay your skills, or overwork yourself to earn the place you already deserve.

When praise feels dangerous, deflection becomes protection. You laugh it off, change the subject, point out flaws, and even give credit away. These responses reduce attention in the short term, yet they also teach your brain that praise equals threat. The cycle continues.

You never give yourself time to let kind words land. You move on before they settle. Over time, self-trust weakens, and anxiety grows.

How Common Extreme Social Anxiety Really Is

It’s easy to believe you’re the only one struggling with these thoughts, especially when everyone else seems confident. In truth, many people who appear confident struggle privately with the same thoughts. Leaders, students, artists, and professionals across fields report these feelings. Social anxiety hides well, especially in high achievers.

Seeing this reality helps reduce the sense of isolation that imposter syndrome creates. These thoughts do not mean something is wrong with you. They reflect a nervous system trained to fear judgment.

While counseling is one of the most effective ways to address imposter syndrome and extreme social anxiety, there are small, unconventional practices you can start today to shift your perspective.

Simple Practices that Soften the Fear Around Praise

  • Reframe compliments as data: Instead of rejecting praise, treat it as evidence. If multiple people recognize your skill, that’s proof, not luck.
  • Name the critic: Give your inner critic a silly name. When it pipes up, you can say, “Thanks, but I’m not listening to you today.”
  • Realize that accepting a compliment is not the same as stroking your ego: Being acknowledged for a job well done is just as deserved and equally powerful as being faulted for a mistake or failure. It is a natural, logical outcome that should be received and taken seriously.
  • Practice gratitude for effort, not outcome: Write down what you did well each day, even if the result wasn’t perfect. This builds self-worth on process, not just achievement.
  • Share your doubts with trusted peers: Talking openly about imposter feelings often reveals that others feel the same, reducing isolation.
  • Pause before deflecting praise: When someone compliments you, resist the urge to downplay it. Instead, simply say, Thank you.

These practices do not erase anxiety overnight. They reduce its power slowly and gently.

How Christian Counseling Can Help You See Compliments Differently

While self-help strategies are valuable, counseling offers something deeper: a safe space to explore the roots of your anxiety and imposter feelings.

A counselor listens without judgment and helps trace these patterns back to their roots. Many people with extreme social anxiety learned early that attention brought criticism, pressure, or rejection. Praise now triggers old defenses meant to keep you safe.

Through counseling, you learn to spot distorted thoughts and replace them with grounded ones. You learn how your nervous system reacts and how to calm it. You practice receiving positive feedback in a space where safety is the top priority.

Over time, compliments stop feeling like warnings. They start feeling like a form of recognition.

Counseling also strengthens self-esteem in ways praise alone never could. You learn to trust your effort, your growth, and your value beyond performance.

Living Without the Constant Fear of Being Exposed

Life feels lighter when success no longer feels borrowed. You can feel free to enjoy progress instead of bracing for collapse, accept praise without shrinking, and allow yourself to rest without guilt. From a spiritual perspective, you can rely on the Holy Spirit to comfort you. To resist this is going to distance your relationship with the Lord. Let the Holy Spirit in and allow God to minister to you. He is pleased when you use and succeed using the gifts He has given you.

Extreme social anxiety and imposter syndrome lose their grip when understanding replaces fear. This process takes time and support, yet relief grows with each step.

If compliments make you squirm, if success feels like borrowed time, or if your inner critic never seems to rest, you don’t have to carry that weight alone. Professional depression and anxiety counselors on this site are ready to talk with you. They explore why self-worth feels fragile and guide you toward healthier ways of seeing yourself.

You do not have to live on edge every time someone says something kind. Call the numbers on the screen or schedule a session today. A calmer relationship with success starts with support, and counseling provides that path forward. You have worked hard to accomplish things in your life. Don’t let imposter syndrome take this from you. You deserve the rewards that come with success and the sincere praise from those around you who see it.

item.title: Gaslighting in Relationships and the Road to Healing
item.description:
Some relationships look fine on the surface, but something essential is missing on the inside. The conversations happen, and plans are made, but life keeps moving, and the emotional connection that should anchor it feels out of reach.

It could be a partner, a parent, or an emotionally unavailable sibling, leaving a person questioning their worth, their perception, and their faith. The desire to be truly known and met is not something to be considered prideful. It is, in fact, a human desire for genuine connection that has been wired into us from the very beginning.

God created us with this desire, so He understands when it goes awry and something is missing. For individuals to understand that they must take an honest look at what lies beneath the surface, they often find that their experience goes beyond feeling lonely in a relationship.

Sometimes it is a deeper reckoning with their own emotional needs and a question of whether those needs are valid. This is a difficult thought to process, but it can be the beginning of something meaningful and lasting.

What It Means to Be Emotionally Unavailable

There is a pattern that goes beyond being quiet or reserved. It describes a consistent inability or unwillingness to engage at a meaningful emotional depth within close relationships.

Individuals can be physically present and dependable in practical ways, while at the same time being emotionally distant and avoiding vulnerable conversations and deflecting personal topics. They will maintain surface-level engagement, keeping others at arm’s length. This pattern indicates that some individuals have difficulty expressing feelings and are uncomfortable with intimacy.

The complexity of the situation is that the person is not always aware of what they are doing. Often, the pattern develops gradually as a way of navigating environments where emotional expression is not safe. It is frequently observed that the person learned at a young age to keep things internal so they would be manageable. This became the default, and these are rarely examined until something in life forces the question.

There is a connection in Scripture between the interior life and the health of everything that flows from it. By watching over the heart with diligence, one will find that life flows much more easily. (Proverbs 4:23)

How Emotional Walls Develop Over Time

The walls individuals build are not always deliberate. Most of the time, these are built in response to an experience, such as rejection, abandonment, or unprocessed grief, that has taught a person it is safer to close off than to stay open.

It has been noted that attachment wounds formed in early relationships shape how adults engage emotionally later in life. Those who have had emotional expression met with ridicule, silence, or dismissal in their younger years develop a natural tendency to stop expressing anything. It is a protective instinct that yields a habit that will linger long after the threat has passed.

People often absorb narratives about emotional strength that can influence how they define emotional stability. For these individuals, the idea that vulnerability is weakness or that needing others is a liability leads them to create a relational armor that is difficult to remove. Christian counselors work with individuals who carry these narratives without naming them. They help the individual recognize that the armor once served a purpose but is no longer needed. This recognition can create a pivotal shift in the healing process.

The shift from guarded and closed to something open and alive is a promise found in the Old Testament. God promises to give us a new heart and a new spirit as He removes the heart of stone from our flesh. (Ezekiel 36:26)

Loving Someone Who Is Emotionally Unavailable

Caring deeply for someone unable to meet the same emotional depth can be a disorienting experience. There are patterns of needs getting adjusted downward, silence is interpreted as rejection, and the desire for closeness feels like an unreasonable demand.

When individuals navigate this kind of relational dynamic, they realize the complexity and how it does not follow a simple set of rules. Dynamics require that compassion and self-protection coexist. It will also emphasize that patience and honest boundaries are necessary, as they explore the difference between someone unwilling to engage emotionally and someone who does not know how to.

A healthy relationship requires the person doing the loving to stay grounded in their own emotional reality. It has been noted that, over time, unreciprocated emotional bids can erode a person’s sense of self-worth and make that person feel invisible in the relationship.

Reaching out to Christian counselors can provide much-needed clarity about what is healthy to sustain and what changes may be possible. It also opens up the possibilities of firm boundaries that need to be established to protect both individuals.

Finding Wholeness Through Faith and Support

The process of healing from emotional disconnection, whether the pattern is one’s own or shaped by years of relationships, benefits from both professional care and spiritual grounding. Faith cannot be offered with a clinical framework that cannot fully replicate, which is the assurance that transformation is not only possible but at work.

God consistently points to a promise of drawing near, as He sees what is hidden, and invites the wounded into genuine restoration. This is an invitation that extends to one’s emotional life as much as it does their spiritual life, and these two are rarely as separate as they may seem.

Psychotherapy focuses on attachment patterns, emotional regulation, and relational history, which shows measurable progress for individuals dealing with emotional disconnection. But when faith-informed care becomes integrated into the process, there is a space where the whole person and not just symptoms or behaviors is addressed.

Christian counselors who are familiar with this integrated framework understand that emotional healing and spiritual formation can move together. Individuals often find that as they are willing to open one door, the other opens with it.

When individuals carry this kind of weight in relational disconnection, there is a promise found in Scripture that is not found in a clinical framework alone. It is the invitation given by Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew:

Come to Me, all who are weary and heavy-laden, and I will give you rest. – Matthew 11:28, NASB

The Road to Healing

Emotional unavailability doesn’t have to be the final word on a relationship. For individuals who have spent years behind walls, they didn’t consciously choose to build them, and those who have loved someone through those walls.

Healing is real and reachable. It will require honesty, patience, and the decision to intentionally look beneath the surface at what remains to be addressed. This journey toward emotional wholeness is not linear, and it doesn’t have to be walked alone.

Just as God fashioned the human heart for intimacy, He also restores what has been locked away. Even though it might feel permanently closed, it is not beyond His reach. Choosing to reopen as a movement toward maturity and an honest decision to release what the past has held, and the willingness to step into what the future will hold.

This is an assurance that belongs to every individual who has walked through emotional distance. Whether it was the one living behind the wall or the one waiting at its edge, there is a promise that God sees both sides.

For I know the plans that I have for you, declares the LORD, plans for welfare and not for calamity to give you a future and a hope. – Jeremiah 29:11, NASB

If you find yourself navigating the weight of an emotionally distant relationship, regardless of what side of the wall you are on, you do not have to walk that journey alone. Our reception team can connect you with a counselor who understands the emotional and spiritual dimensions of that dynamic. One phone call can help you start your journey toward tearing down the wall that you never meant to build.

item.title: Understanding Anger Problems in Older Adults
item.description:
In the later years of life, anger is often misunderstood or brushed off as crankiness and stubbornness when something deeper could be at work. Anger problems in older adults are more common than we realize. There is often a frequent signal of unaddressed pain, loss, or fear that goes beyond a simple, bad attitude.

Aging individuals have an emotional weight of declining health, shifting roles, and a growing dependence that builds quietly until it surfaces as frustration, irritability, and sometimes rage. It is vital to understand what drives anger in the elderly in order to offer compassionate and effective support.

What Lies Beneath the Surface

Anger doesn’t exist in isolation. Older adults often exhibit anger problems that are rooted in a layered mix of grief, unresolved emotional wounds, and the loss of control. Retirement and the death of a close friend or spouse, along with physical limitations that require reduced independence, are all significant losses.

Even though these changes are expected, sometimes they trigger grief. If that grief goes unprocessed, it often resurfaces as anger. The loss of independence for older adults is not just an inconvenience. It strikes the core of who they believe themselves to be.

For the man who has always managed his own finances, driven his own car, and provided for his family, finding himself dependent on others for basic tasks brings a new level of frustration that can shift into explosive anger if there is no help to work through the change in lifestyle. A woman who has built her identity around caregiving and now requires care herself can be consumed with an anger that points to the painful reality of how her role has changed.

Recognizing these shifts in lifestyle makes it easier to respond to aging loved ones instead of being defensive. These identity shifts will run deep, and the anger that accompanies them is often a form of grief that has not found words. Families that understand this are better equipped to respond with patience rather than frustration of their own.

The Physical Side of Anger in Older Adults

Anger is not always purely an emotional situation in the elderly. The body can also play a significant role in the way older adults process specific situations. Certain medications can affect mood regulation and make irritability and anger harder to manage.

Chronic pain and sleep disruption are other ways in which the body plays a role in anger issues in the elderly. Dementia and other neurological conditions can damage the brain’s ability to filter emotional responses, which leads to sudden outbursts that the individual doesn’t fully understand or control.

Hormonal changes, thyroid imbalance, and nutritional deficiencies have been linked to mood instability in older adults. The physical dimension becomes important because it means anger in an elderly person should never be dismissed without a medical evaluation.

Family members are encouraged to make a note of changes and be better equipped to advocate for a thorough assessment instead of labeling a loved one as difficult. When the physical contributors are addressed and not overlooked, it removes an unnecessary obstacle to healing.

A Faith Perspective on Anger and Aging

Anger isn’t treated as inherently sinful in Scripture, but it does require believers to handle it carefully. The book of James mentions that we should be slow to anger because it does not produce the righteousness that God desires (James 1:19-20).

An elderly believer who is coping with anger problems can find an invitation for honest self-examination instead of feeling condemned. When anger is acknowledged, named, and right before God, it opens the door to opportunity for growth and closes the door to shame.

Many older adults have carried decades of unexamined emotional patterns. Faith communities can offer safe spaces where these patterns can be addressed as the elderly individual seeks to release the anger and problems.

When an aging believer recognizes the grief, fear, or helplessness that fuels their anger, they may find prayer, Scripture, and a community that cares are powerful anchors. Through honest and prayerful processing of anger in the presence of God, an elderly individual can discover that God is always near the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18).

Supporting an Elderly Loved One Who Faces Anger Problems

Being a caregiver for an older adult who battles with anger problems can become emotionally exhausting. The temptation to respond to anger with anger is real, but it rarely produces anything constructive.

Validating the emotion without reinforcing the behavior is key. Doing this in a calm manner through setting clear boundaries is a practical skill that helps the situation. It can be helpful to remember that an anger outburst is rarely about the moment and instead about something much deeper and heavier.

When families approach the situation with curiosity instead of judgment, they are more likely to connect with the person beneath the frustration. If the anger becomes dangerous or significantly affects the quality of life for everyone, it becomes important to obtain professional support.

Christian counselors who specialize in geriatric mental health can help elderly individuals process emotions that drive their anger. They can help someone who is struggling develop coping strategies rooted in clinical practices and biblical truth to find a peaceful way forward.

For those who walk alongside an angry, elderly loved one, they will often need support of their own. Caregiver fatigue is real. When an individual is absorbing the emotional weight of someone else and their unprocessed pain, it takes a toll. Seeking a counselor as a caregiver is beneficial to the individual as well as the individual receiving the care.

Christian counselors can help family members set appropriate boundaries and process their own frustration. Developing communication strategies that reduce conflict while honoring the older adult’s emotional experience is a meaningful part of this process.

When to Seek Professional Help

When anger becomes frequent, intense, or difficult to de-escalate, it will require more than patience alone. These types of persistent anger problems can damage relationships, contribute to cardiovascular complications, or lead to increased depression and anxiety.

It is important to recognize the need for outside support and understand that it’s not a sign of failure. When a family reaches out for professional help, it is a sign of wisdom based on the love they have for their family member.

Christian counselors are equipped to work with elderly individuals who are navigating the intersection of emotional health, spiritual questions, and physical limitations. Families aren’t required to navigate this difficult situation alone.

Find someone with whom you can have an honest conversation about the older adult in your life grappling with anger that feels out of proportion. Taking that first step towards support for the elderly individual, the caregiver, or both is one of the most loving decisions a family can make.

Finding Peace in the Later Years

We were not meant to live the later years of life to find bitterness or rage, even though we have faced painful circumstances. When handled honestly and with care, anger can become a doorway to deeper healing that many older adults have never had the opportunity to pursue.

The losses were real, the frustrations were valid, and the emotions are not the enemy. Elderly individuals can move from reactive anger towards something closer to peace that passes understanding when they are connected with the right support system. This journey will look different for each individual, but it is worth taking. No stage of life is beyond the reach of grace.

If you have a loved one who is elderly and struggles with anger issues, contact our office today. Our reception team is on hand to answer questions about your next step or schedule an appointment with the right support staff. This is not something you have to face alone.
