Intergenerational trauma, however, refers to the ways the effects of trauma can continue beyond the generation that originally experienced it. Unresolved emotional wounds, learned beliefs, unhealthy coping strategies, relationship patterns, and responses to fear or stress can influence children and later generations, even when they did not experience the original traumatic event themselves.

Intergenerational trauma can occur within families or entire communities and may be passed down in subtle as well as more obvious ways. Over time, these patterns can affect a person’s emotional well-being, relationships, behaviors, and even how they understand themselves and the world around them.

People experiencing intergenerational trauma may struggle with forming healthy relationships, unexplained depression or anxiety, patterns of self-sabotage or fear, or a sense of carrying a burden they struggle to name. These effects can occur in the present even when the original painful or traumatic events happened decades or generations before.

Some Examples of Intergenerational Trauma in Scripture

While the term ‘intergenerational trauma’ is something that has gained currency in recent decades, that does not mean that the reality it names is new. Scripture is quite candid about how sin has consequences; our brokenness and the brokenness of others that we endure, and experience all have consequences, and these can ripple through generations.

Two examples of this can help us. One is to consider the family of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, which we read about from Genesis 12 until the end of the book. In story after story, there are repeated patterns of deeply damaging favoritism, selfishness, and deception, which cause ongoing conflict and shape the dynamics in the family across generations. In Jacob’s story, in particular, the threat of violence looms as he interacts with his brother Esau and his uncle, Laban.

Another example is David, a great king, warrior, and a man with many moral failings. After committing adultery with Bathsheba and arranging to have her husband killed, the Lord warned David that his actions would have lasting consequences in his own family (2 Samuel 11-12). David’s own son sexually assaulted his half-sister, and David did nothing about it. As a result, his family experienced even more violence and betrayal through revenge and a violent civil war.

The cycles of violence, betrayal, deception, and more that affected these families are tied to longstanding patterns of behavior that are rooted even further in the past. While this is true, Scripture also tells us that there is hope in the Lord to break such cycles.

There is the possibility of redemption, restoration, and a brand-new story for those who seek Him and pursue the new life that is possible in Him (Romans 8; 2 Corinthians 5:17).

The Causes and Triggers of Intergenerational Trauma

From what is known, intergenerational trauma has its roots in a traumatic experience a person, family, or community has. A significant event, unresolved pain, or prolonged suffering can be at the root of what goes on to become intergenerational trauma. These events could include abuse, abandonment or loss, poverty, war, forced migration, and familial patterns of violence or addiction.

These various events and experiences operate on several levels. Some of them, like experiences of war, genocide, or forced migration and displacement, are collective events that scar entire communities. Facing systemic oppression and stress from poverty and discrimination can also affect a community that is the target of such measures. There are also family dysfunctions, such as abuse, addiction, neglect, or abandonment, that can become normalized over time in a family unit.

Future generations within a community or family may not experience the original traumatic event. Still, they may inherit emotional and behavioral patterns that were formed as a response to the pain. These patterns would include anxious attachment, aggression, or deep mistrust.

Intergenerational trauma and its effects may become more noticeable during times of stress or transition. These experiences can activate learned emotional and behavioral patterns, attachment wounds, and stress responses that have been shaped by family experiences across generations.

For example, getting married or becoming a parent can trigger unresolved attachment wounds from one’s childhood or resurface old family patterns.

Other situations that may trigger this trauma include conflict situations and situations of loss and injustice that mirror those of past generations. Such conflict situations may trigger inherited anger or fears. Witnessing violence in one’s community or going through financial hardship can also activate a heightened stress response that affects one’s physical and mental well-being.

Some Signs of Intergenerational Trauma to Look Out for

Intergenerational trauma can manifest in various ways. Often, it escapes detection because it can appear as normal, and just the way your family or community does things. To pick up on how certain patterns are rooted in trauma and anything but ‘normal’ requires close examination and the willingness to make changes toward a healthier outlook. Some signs to look out for include the following:

Hypervigilance This is when you are constantly on edge, and you feel unsafe even in safe spaces.

Unhealthy relationship patterns This includes patterns of shame, denial, secrecy, mistrust, and recurring patterns of codependency.

Relational breakdown Patterns of repeated relational breakdowns across generations within the family may also point to intergenerational trauma.

Emotional problems Issues with regulating moods and emotions, persistent anxiety, depression, or emotional numbness may suggest intergenerational trauma. Also, having emotional overreactions to seemingly unrelated events could be the result of reacting to past traumas.

Inherited beliefs Carrying certain unstated or unconscious beliefs that shape your self-understanding could be a sign of intergenerational trauma. These beliefs could include feeling you are not worthy or that the world is a dangerous place. Persistent feelings of guilt or worthlessness without a clear cause may suggest intergenerational trauma.

Physical symptoms These would include insomnia, chronic pain, or stress-related conditions like heart disease.

A list of possible symptoms is a first step to help you identify what you or a loved one may be experiencing. However, various physical, emotional, and mental health challenges carry similar symptoms, and that is why it’s important to see a health professional. They can help you eliminate possible causes so that you can identify the root cause and address it.

Finding Healing from Intergenerational Trauma

This article started by posing a question – can we ever truly escape the past? Your past is your past, and you cannot change it. However, there is always hope for your future to look different, and to lessen the hold of the past on the here and now. There is freedom in Christ (Galatians 5:1), and with help, you can confront the past to step into a new chapter for you and your loved ones.

“So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.” John 8:36 ESV

The path to hope and a new future may include the following:

Acknowledge the pain Healing comes when you identify that there is a problem, a set of patterns of behaviors that are undermining the fullness of life the Lord intends for you. Reflect on your family history, naming the patterns there and recognizing how they have shaped you.

Seek the Lord’s healing You can do this through prayer, reading Scripture, and allowing Him to bring light into the dark spaces in your life. Lament is a powerful way to express your pain to the Lord, and speaking unspoken grief to the Lord in the pattern of the lament Psalms can help you find release.

Forgive and let go Forgiveness does not excuse harm; it helps you break the cycle of resentment and harm as you release the grip of the past on who you are and will be.

Set new patterns Make intentional choices empowered by God’s Spirit and grace to create new family traditions, communicate in a different style, and so on.

Seek counseling A trained Christian counselor can help you identify and unpack the deep wounds and trauma, break harmful patterns of thinking and behavior, and begin building healthier responses to everyday life.

Through faith-based counseling alongside trauma-informed therapies such as internal family systems or cognitive behavioral therapy, your counselor can help you process these deep wounds in a safe environment.

Healing the wounds of the past can start with you today. Reach out to our office or contact our reception team to connect with a counselor who can walk with you on your journey toward healing and wholeness.

References

  • Yehuda, R., & Lehrner, A. (2018). Intergenerational transmission of trauma effects: Putative role of epigenetic mechanisms. World Psychiatry, 17(3), 243–257. https://doi.org/10.1002/wps.20568
  • Isobel, S., Goodyear, M., Furness, T., & Foster, K. (2019). Preventing intergenerational trauma transmission: A critical interpretive synthesis. Journal of Clinical Nursing, 28(7–8), 1100–1113. https://doi.org/10.1111/jocn.14735
  • Narayan, A. J., Lieberman, A. F., & Masten, A. S. (2021). Intergenerational transmission and prevention of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs). Clinical Psychology Review, 85, 101997.

A list of possible symptoms is a first step to help you identify what you or a loved one may be experiencing. However, various physical, emotional, and mental health challenges carry similar symptoms, and that is why it’s important to see a health professional. They can help you eliminate possible causes so that you can identify the root cause and address it.

Finding Healing from Intergenerational Trauma

This article started by posing a question – can we ever truly escape the past? Your past is your past, and you cannot change it. However, there is always hope for your future to look different, and to lessen the hold of the past on the here and now. There is freedom in Christ (Galatians 5:1), and with help, you can confront the past to step into a new chapter for you and your loved ones.

“So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.” John 8:36 ESV

The path to hope and a new future may include the following:

Acknowledge the pain Healing comes when you identify that there is a problem, a set of patterns of behaviors that are undermining the fullness of life the Lord intends for you. Reflect on your family history, naming the patterns there and recognizing how they have shaped you.

Seek the Lord’s healing You can do this through prayer, reading Scripture, and allowing Him to bring light into the dark spaces in your life. Lament is a powerful way to express your pain to the Lord, and speaking unspoken grief to the Lord in the pattern of the lament Psalms can help you find release.

Forgive and let go Forgiveness does not excuse harm; it helps you break the cycle of resentment and harm as you release the grip of the past on who you are and will be.

Set new patterns Make intentional choices empowered by God’s Spirit and grace to create new family traditions, communicate in a different style, and so on.

Seek counseling A trained Christian counselor can help you identify and unpack the deep wounds and trauma, break harmful patterns of thinking and behavior, and begin building healthier responses to everyday life.

Through faith-based counseling alongside trauma-informed therapies such as internal family systems or cognitive behavioral therapy, your counselor can help you process these deep wounds in a safe environment.

Healing the wounds of the past can start with you today. Reach out to our office or contact our reception team to connect with a counselor who can walk with you on your journey toward healing and wholeness.

References

  • Yehuda, R., & Lehrner, A. (2018). Intergenerational transmission of trauma effects: Putative role of epigenetic mechanisms. World Psychiatry, 17(3), 243–257. https://doi.org/10.1002/wps.20568
  • Isobel, S., Goodyear, M., Furness, T., & Foster, K. (2019). Preventing intergenerational trauma transmission: A critical interpretive synthesis. Journal of Clinical Nursing, 28(7–8), 1100–1113. https://doi.org/10.1111/jocn.14735
  • Narayan, A. J., Lieberman, A. F., & Masten, A. S. (2021). Intergenerational transmission and prevention of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs). Clinical Psychology Review, 85, 101997.

item.title: Getting Old: Loving Your Spouse Through Retirement
item.description:
When you hear about couples having marital trouble, you usually think of people in the prime years of their lives. Maybe they’re newly married and trying to adjust to living life as a couple, or perhaps they’ve hit their “seven-year itch” and are starting to drift apart. These times are often stressful for married couples, but marital trouble can hit at any stage and at any age.

Getting older and hitting retirement can be trying for married couples. If you’re married and you or your spouse is approaching retirement, it’s best to be emotionally prepared for the inevitable changes you will be facing.

So Much Togetherness!

You love each other, so spending more time together will be blissful, right? That’s the ideal, but in practical terms, that’s not always the case.

Even if your relationship is rock solid, too much togetherness can put a strain on it. Maybe you get along great now because your time together is limited, and therefore peaceful and purposeful. When you don’t have a lot of time together, which is often the case for couples who work full-time and have families, you are more intentional in the little time you do have.

Where did all this time come from?

When the busyness of work and family obligations fades, you have a lot more time to spend with your spouse. That’s a good thing, but it can also change the way you interact with each other. When your time is limited, you might be more purposeful in your conversations or intentional with your plans. You might schedule intimacy so it fits into both of your calendars, and you may not nitpick your partner’s behaviors because you don’t have time.

When time is no longer an issue, and you abandon your established schedule, things change. You might find that the same rules of conduct that have worked for years no longer shield you from arguments.

Maybe you allow yourself to discuss topics that were previously off-limits because you didn’t want to ruin your limited time together. Or you stop planning intimacy because you assume it will come naturally now that you don’t have a rigid schedule. But without this intentionally blocked-out time, that intimacy may never happen.

Have you always been like this?

When you’ve spent decades working toward the common goals of building a career or raising children, you develop a system, a rhythm of sorts, that works. But retirement can disrupt that. In this new stage, the small habits or preferences that went unnoticed are front and center, 24/7.

You might find yourself wondering if they’ve always chewed so loudly or why they decided that retirement is the perfect time to reorganize the spice rack that you’ve successfully managed for thirty years.

Maybe your spouse wants to sleep in, which never happened except on weekends because they were obligated to a work schedule. But if you’re an early riser, this sudden shift in your partner’s sleep pattern can be off-putting. While they might seem insignificant, these little discoveries can become full-blown resentment.

Who am I? Who are you?

Retirement requires an emotional adjustment. There’s the feeling of finality and the feeling of grief. You’re leaving a career and stepping away from a role. The transitional period from what was to what is and what is to come can be lonely and full of uncertainty and tension.

Even though you are still the same person you were when you were working, you’re no longer defined the same way. And maybe your spouse isn’t either. Having your identity change can affect you deeply. Maybe you no longer feel like the family provider or the nurturer. Maybe you no longer feel needed.

Having a personal identity crisis can magnify the stress of a new schedule and can put a strain on the people who are going through this transition with you.

But I’m still working!

Retirement doesn’t usually happen for both spouses at the same time. If one of you is still working while the other is enjoying a leisurely game of golf, resentment can grow quickly! The working spouse might feel envious of the other’s freedom. The retired spouse might feel guilty for their time off or become demanding of the working spouse’s limited free time.

Intentional Steps

To make your retirement a time of peace and relational growth, you can implement some practical strategies.

Plan “me” time It might sound counterintuitive, but the secret to a happy retirement with your spouse is often spending some time apart. Just because you’re both home for most of the day doesn’t obligate you to be joined at the hip. Some of the healthiest marriages are often the ones where couples maintain separate hobbies or socialize independently of each other.

God made you as an individual before He ever brought you together. Honoring your individuality and personal relationship with God can strengthen your marriage. Keep your book club and standing lunch date with a friend. These independent activities give you both the space you need to maintain your individuality and give you something new to talk about when you do spend time together.

Negotiate domestic duties For years, your household roles were likely dictated by your individual work schedules. Now that these outside obligations are gone, the division of household labor needs to be adjusted. If one spouse stayed home while the other worked, it doesn’t automatically obligate them to continue in that role now that you’re both home.

It’s also important not to treat your spouse like an employee when you do work together on household chores. If you’re used to being the boss, it can be easy to bark out orders and try to manage a spouse. Keep in mind, you’re not managing a department anymore, but being a loving partner.

Create something new Since your old routine is no longer in place, it’s important to create some structure in your life. Without a calendar and routine, days can blend, and a feeling of aimlessness can take root.

To prevent this from happening, create a consistent morning routine that involves prayer or going for a walk with your partner. And to keep the love alive, schedule intentional date nights that don’t include anything from a to-do list.

It’s also wise to find new ways to serve others together. Many couples struggle with finding a purpose after retirement since their primary purpose has always been to take care of a family. Try mentoring a young couple at church or volunteering for a ministry project to help give you a joint purpose.

Talk about difficult topics While it might feel like retirement is a long vacation, it’s more of a major identity shift. Many people feel a sense of loss when they leave their career or their children leave their house, two major events that often happen within a short period of time.

These life shifts can cause an emotional upheaval, and it’s important to understand how these things have impacted each other. Talk with your partner and ask them how they’re handling the transition to retirement. Be quick to listen, and slow to speak. You can also use this season to talk about goals such as traveling or moving closer to grandchildren.

Finances are another sometimes touchy subject. You might want to live it up while your spouse is paralyzed by the fear of running out of money. This spender versus saver conflict can manifest as nitpicking over the grocery bill or the thermostat. To mitigate this, talk with your spouse about your finances in an open and transparent way.

While practicing these ideas with your spouse is a wonderful way to grow closer, it can also be difficult. It’s helpful to discuss them with a licensed, professional therapist, too. A therapist can help you and your spouse grow closer through couples counseling or can help you individually as you manage life’s transitions.

If you’re getting older or are planning for your future retirement, call our office to make an appointment today to help make the most of your golden years.

The post Getting Old: Loving Your Spouse Through Retirement appeared first on Spokane Christian Counseling.

item.title: When to Seek Help for Family Problems
item.description:
Family problems can be a weight pulling you down. It can feel like taking two steps forward and three steps backward. Trying to get everyone on the same page seems fruitless at times. Whether you have babies, toddlers, grade school children, teens, or everyone in between, you want a home full of love, forgiveness, and peace. Why can’t everyone get along?

This is a fallen world, and the enemy knows where to hit the hardest to make a lasting impact: the family. Seeking help for family problems can help you get ahead and prepare you for future issues by equipping you with psychological methods and techniques, as well as faith-based principles.

Common Family Problems

Families have squabbles. Life happens, and sometimes lines are drawn in the household, but it doesn’t have to stay that way. Family problems are inevitable as personalities clash, hormones can take over, and circumstances can change on a dime. The wisdom is to get ahead of it by building a rock-solid foundation with shared beliefs and values, and open communication.

Before reading through the list of common family problems below, consider whether your family has Jesus as the cornerstone. Do you need to speak His name in normal daily conversation? Do you make decisions through a biblical lens, or do you make rash decisions that affect the entire family?

Search your heart for the answers. If you need Jesus to work on your heart and mind, ask for His forgiveness, repent, and lean on God to guide your family as the Head of the Household.

Marital Issues

Marital issues affect everyone in the family, although parents may feel that the problems lie with just the two of them. Children and teens are perceptive, and their moods and behaviors can change in response to growing fears or worries about stability. Marital issues can include emotional distance, betrayal, infidelity, financial concerns, chronic illness, procrastination, unequal household duties, and sexual intimacy problems, among others.

Marriage and family counseling are available for couples who need extra help in navigating life together. If you feel like you are alone in your marriage or that the two of you have become roommates instead of partners, seek help from a counselor.

Communications Within the Family

A communication breakdown can lead to feelings of resentment, anger, bitterness, shame, and regret. One person may push others, trying to get to the bottom of a conflict and trying to bully others to get their own way. Other family members may withdraw, becoming quiet and distant. Miscommunication leads to sibling rivalry and fights, parent-child disputes, and relationship drama between parents.

Family counseling teaches family members how to resolve conflict without insults and blaming. They learn how to manage anger and actively listen to each other. Counseling can also help spark confidence as each family member learns how to advocate for themselves.

Parenting Issues

Parenting issues include disagreements regarding discipline, sibling rivalry and fusses, and children who feel rejected, ignored, or isolated. One parent may feel that the other one contradicts them in front of the children or undermines them. Overwhelmed and stressed parents may feel like they are out of patience as they struggle to find five minutes just to think.

Problems can emerge between the two parents, divorced parents trying to co-parent, stepparents, and between parent and child. Counseling can help if every conversation feels like a struggle, or if you are only talking about surface-level topics with your teens or tweens.

Step-Parenting Adjustments

Blended families tend to have their own issues. An adjustment period is required when a parent remarries, and a new person begins living in the household. The new step-parent may have different rules or a different discipline philosophy. Parents and step-parents need to agree on how to raise the children they share.

Blended families may also include new step-siblings that change the dynamic. Children can feel neglected or ignored when other children are around. Personality clashes can also cause drama and angst in the home. Counseling equips children and parents with skills and techniques to defuse tough situations and express thoughts and emotions without resorting to insults or physical altercations.

Major Life Changes

Major life changes can turn your world upside down, sometimes for good and sometimes not. Life events can include a graduation, wedding, big move, new job, career change, pregnancy, birth of a new baby or adoption, or financial improvement. It can also include illness, death, loss of home or job, natural disaster, bankruptcy, divorce, and estrangement.

Emotional resilience builds as we face obstacles in this fallen world, but at times we may be unable to manage overwhelming blessings on our own. Counseling can help you prioritize your beliefs and values during major shifts.

Addiction

Addiction comes in many forms. You or someone in your home may struggle with addiction to alcohol, illegal drugs, prescription drugs, substances like glue or paint, pornography, sex, food, excessive shopping, or gambling. Anything that you use to fulfill a deeper need can become an addiction.

God created humans to desire Him, but because we have free will, we can reject His love or become confused. We feel an emptiness or numbness, and when we give in to an urge or impulse, we experience a temporary relief, a cascade of feel-good chemicals.

Unfortunately, unless we fill that empty hole with God, we will continue to indulge in addictions that can destroy relationships, jobs, homes, and physical and mental health. Christian counseling helps break the cycle and lean into the very One who created the heart.

Mental Health Disorders

Mental health disorders affect more than just the person experiencing them. Whether you or a family member struggles with any of the following mental health disorders, help is available.

  • Anxiety
  • Depression
  • Bipolar disorder
  • Eating disorders
  • Obsessive-compulsive disorder
  • Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
  • Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder
  • Grief
  • Cognitive disorders
  • Behavioral disorders
  • Abuse and trauma

Christian counseling centers treat families for more than just squabbles. They dive deep into mental health issues and help the family heal as a whole, while addressing their emotional and spiritual health as well.

Poor mental health affects the physical body with unexplained body aches, headaches, digestive issues, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, rapid heart rate, chronic inflammation, and increased risks of heart disease, obesity, Type II diabetes, heart attack, or stroke. Treating mental health disorders while teaching the family how to manage symptoms and work with their family member creates unity and better health.

Why Now is the Time to Seek Christian Counseling

Family problems can rob your home of peace. Now is the time to seek Christian counseling. Even if your family is not experiencing major conflict, counseling can prepare you for the inevitable. When multiple people live at home, personality clashes can arise. Teach your family how to resolve conflict and manage anger before it becomes an issue.

Sometimes families wait to seek professional help due to fear or shame. There was a time when seeking help from a counselor was ridiculed, but psychology and culture have come a long way. More people understand that it’s okay to seek help for family problems, instead of hiding them. When we try to keep problems in the dark, they seem to grow, and in families, this can create emotional distance and estrangement.

If you live in a home with abuse, self-harm, or if someone is having suicidal ideation, seek help immediately. Don’t wait. A home should be a safe haven, and we want to help you in the hard seasons.

Counseling for Family Problems

If you are leaning toward counseling for family problems, you are not alone. Our families are precious to us and deserve the best version of ourselves and to learn about how they can follow Christ while also loving one another. Contact this Christian counseling center today to schedule a session. The counselors want to help you through tough seasons with the grace and mercy of Christ.

item.title: Caring for Others Without Losing Yourself: The Importance of Caregiver Support
item.description:
There is one myth I believe many caregivers unknowingly live by. It is the belief that caring for someone else requires you to lose yourself. At first, this does not seem true. Most caregivers never wake up one morning deciding to abandon their own life. It happens little by little. It happens through responsibility. It happens through love. It happens through necessity. It happened because you took vows, and you are choosing to honor them at all costs.

Caregiving is unique because many people never choose it. It chooses them. One phone call changed everything. A stroke changes everything. It did for me. A diagnosis changes everything. It was for my mom. An accident changes everything. It does for many. Suddenly, the life you knew becomes the life you used to have.

You are no longer simply a husband, a wife, a daughter, a son. You become a caregiver; a grieving, at times confused, overwhelmed, resentful, hurt caregiver. While everyone is watching the person who is sick, few people are watching the one providing the care.

People pity caregivers, but do not support caregivers or the act of caregiving. Due to this, as one who cares for others, it is important to have key things in place to ensure you have a more pleasant experience while staying present.

Caregiving rarely begins with a choice

Most people prepare for careers. They prepare for marriage. They prepare to become parents. Few prepare to become caregivers. But I think there is room for us to start. This is a thought we will explore another time.

For those coming face to face with aging parents, you discover that one doctor’s appointment is turning into several. Hospital visits are becoming too frequent, therefore, normal. Medication schedules are replacing personal routines. Home modifications are now necessary. As the calendar slowly fills with appointments that belong to your mom or dad.

Before long, you have begun measuring each day by the needs of another person. Not to mention that you are not the one who is familiar with the doctors, and now your name is listed on official medical paperwork. You are caregiving, not just being a good son or daughter, husband or wife, friend or neighbor.

This shift happened

When someone you love or care about becomes ill, their health becomes the priority, as it should. Their recovery deserves attention. Their safety deserves protection. Their life deserves every reasonable effort. The challenge is that while their needs move to the front, yours slowly move to the back. Not because you no longer matter.

Because there never seems to be enough room for both. Why? Because family and friends who get thrust into caregiving begin giving out of necessity and panic while the knowledge of needed caregiving organization and balance is unknown to them. A caregiver in this situation does not mean to lose themselves; it just happened.

When The Sick Become the Center

Here is something that you need to know: illness naturally changes the focus of a family. Conversations become centered around symptoms. Decisions become centered around treatments. Finances become centered around medical expenses. Time becomes centered around recovery. Everything else begins to pale in comparison. Nothing seems to be more urgent. Your hobbies get put on hold. Your friendship gets put on pause. Your dreams get halted.

The caregiver often convinces themselves this is only temporary. Yet months become years. Seasons continue to change while the caregiver remains standing in the same place emotionally. This is where losing yourself quietly begins. Not through one major decision. Through thousands of small ones.

My small decisions began with seeing the need in me to bathe daily. It seemed as though when I bathed my husband, that was the most important. My needs were not. At the time of his stroke, we lived in a three-story townhome. We did not go outside for over four months. He was in prison with the punishment of the stroke, so was I.

However, I did not understand until later that he did not need me to live as if I were sick too. He needed to see me live so he could be inspired to get back to living. He wanted to see me beautified as his wife.

The Slow Disappearance of The Caregiver

This is how you know you have lost yourself as a caregiver. Losing yourself is rarely dramatic; it is more often subtle.

  • You stop asking yourself what you need.
  • You stop noticing your own exhaustion.
  • You stop celebrating your own accomplishments.
  • You stop making plans that include your own future.
  • Eventually someone asks how you are doing. Your first response is to talk about the person you care for. You no longer know how to answer the question for yourself.
  • You begin introducing yourself by someone else’s condition instead of your own life.

Watch out for this mislabeling of yourself as a caregiver. Identity is one of the first things to be disrupted as a caregiver.

  • You become the wife of the stroke survivor.
  • The husband of the spouse with cancer.
  • The daughter caring for her aging mother.
  • The son caring for his father.

These descriptions are true. They simply should not become your entire identity. There is honor in caring for others, and I do not want that to go unsaid here. Nevertheless, remember that caring for others requires you to remain able to do so.

This means that emotionally, mentally, and physically, it would be great for you to be in a stable place so that you can help from that same place. A caregiver that is inwardly secure and happy can truly go the distance in care for an individual in a pleasant and effective way. Being a caregiver is one thing; how you give care is another.

What I Wish I Had Known

As a caregiver what I wished I had known is what were some of the key tips that I needed to ensure that it was easier and how to do what was expected of me. I learned how to bathe my husband the hard way. I dressed him the hard way. I helped him use the bathroom the hard way. I fed him the hard way.

Everything I did, I will add “the hard way” because I did not know “how” to do it for a person who was disabled. This would have allowed me to save time and energy which would have helped me not to lose myself so easily in “tying” what was not the best for his condition at the time. Time and method are important.

I mentioned earlier about organization. This tags time and method for me. As a caregiver you won’t be able to get away from the tasks of what is required doctors’ visits, medication runs etc. But how you organize them is up to you. You can use delivery of medication or easier pick-up methods.

Additionally, make sure you have the medication by going to the most convenient pharmacy for you as the caregiver, not the patient. It is also wise to ensure that appointments are synced on the same day as much as possible or sprinkled throughout the week with your errands so that you and the patient are getting what you need.

Organize locations, activities, grocery trips, and leisure outings to ensure everyone gets what they need. As a caregiver, don’t forget our appointments and do not forget to schedule downtime or naps to recharge. You can do that.

Also, do not forget to schedule time to enjoy the relationship with the person and not to emphasize the duty to the person. The relationship is key to nurture while caring for them physically. I wish I had known to protect them a bit more with walks in the park, talks about emotional needs, not just physical or medical, and moments of meaningful physical touch. This includes hugs, hand-holding, kisses, etc.

The person receiving care deserves your best. Your best becomes much more difficult to give when you have nothing remaining inside yourself. Do it for them. Do it for you. Do it for the relationship.

Photos:
“Eating Together”, Courtesy of Getty Images, Unsplash.com, Unsplash+ License; “Tending the Flowers”, Courtesy of Land O’Lakes, Inc., Unsplash.com, CC0 License; 

The post Caring for Others Without Losing Yourself: The Importance of Caregiver Support appeared first on Tacoma Christian Counseling.

The person receiving care deserves your best. Your best becomes much more difficult to give when you have nothing remaining inside yourself. Do it for them. Do it for you. Do it for the relationship.

item.title: Reframing: Changing the Way We See Our Circumstances
item.description:
While working toward my bachelor’s degree in social work, I learned a lot about reframing. “Cognitive reframing,” also known as “cognitive restructuring,” is a psychological technique that involves recognizing unhelpful or distorted thought patterns, evaluating their accuracy, and replacing them with more balanced, realistic perspectives.

In simple terms, reframing means learning to look at a situation from a different perspective. It does not mean ignoring or pretending that something difficult isn’t happening or forcing ourselves to think positively when we are hurting. Instead, it encourages us to slow down, examine the thoughts we are having, and ask whether those thoughts are completely accurate or helpful.

For example, someone might think, “I failed, so I’ll never succeed.” Cognitive reframing encourages them to pause and ask whether that thought is fully true. A more balanced perspective might be, “This setback is disappointing, but it doesn’t define my abilities or my future.”

The circumstances haven’t changed, but the interpretation has, and that shift can significantly affect how we respond to our circumstances and significantly affect our emotional well‑being.

A Brief History of Cognitive Reframing

Aaron T. Beck developed cognitive therapy in the 1960s while working with individuals experiencing depression. Through his work, Beck observed that many of his patients experienced recurring negative thoughts that influenced their emotions and behaviors. He helped patients identify these thought patterns and examine the connection between their thoughts, feelings, and actions.

Beck’s work eventually became the foundation for what is now known as cognitive restructuring. The goal is not simply to eliminate negative thoughts, but to recognize thoughts that are inaccurate, distorted, or unhelpful and replace them with healthier and more realistic perspectives.

In other words, we don’t necessarily have to believe every thought that enters our minds. That concept has always fascinated me, particularly because it connects with something the Bible has been teaching for centuries: the importance of being intentional about what we allow to occupy our minds.

Our Thoughts Matter

I love listening to Dr. Caroline Leaf, a cognitive neuroscientist, communication pathologist, and author who has written extensively about thoughts, emotions, and mental health. Her work has encouraged many people to become more intentional about examining their thoughts and the meaning they assign to their experiences.

One of the ideas she discusses is that we have a choice in how we respond to the information that enters our minds. We are constantly receiving information from the outside world through conversations, social media, news, relationships, and our circumstances. At the same time, we are also dealing with thoughts and memories that we already have.

We cannot always control what thoughts initially enter our minds. A fearful thought may suddenly appear. A painful memory may resurface. Someone may say something hurtful to us. We may experience a setback and immediately begin telling ourselves a story about what that setback means. But we can become more intentional about what we do with those thoughts.

Do we automatically accept the thought as truth? Do we replay it over and over? Or do we stop and examine it? This is where reframing becomes practical.

Taking Our Thoughts Captive

As Christians, we have an additional framework for examining our thoughts. In 2 Corinthians 10:5, Paul reinforces this by urging believers to “take every thought captive to the obedience of Christ.”

We don’t have to allow every thought to run freely through our minds. It is about recognizing when our thoughts drift toward fear, hopelessness, distortion, or self‑condemnation – and intentionally replacing them with what is true. “Fix your thoughts on what is true, and honorable, and right, and pure, and lovely, and admirable. Think about things that are excellent and worthy of praise” Philippians 4:8 (NLT).

We can stop and ask questions such as:

  • Is this thought true?
  • Is this thought helpful?
  • Am I assuming something that I don’t actually know?
  • Does this thought line up with what God says?
  • What would a more balanced perspective look like?

Sometimes our thoughts are based on fear, past experiences, insecurity, or assumptions rather than truth. Reframing gives us a practical way to slow down and examine those thoughts rather than allowing them to control our emotions and behavior.

Renewing Our Minds

The Bible also tells us that we are to renew our minds. Dr. Leaf says if we choose to dwell on thoughts – by analyzing it, meditating on it, or giving it meaning – it becomes part of our memory networks. Once embedded, it must be rebuilt, which she connects to the biblical concept of renewing the mind.

Romans 12:2 says, “Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” What we continually focus on, repeatedly tell, or meditate on matters.

This doesn’t mean that Christians should ignore problems or pretend that life is always good. Scripture certainly doesn’t teach us to deny pain. Instead, it teaches us where to place our attention when we are walking through difficult circumstances.

We can acknowledge, “This is hard,” while also reminding ourselves, “God is with me.” Jesus said, “I have told you these things, so that in me you may have peace. In this world you will have trouble. But take heart! I have overcome the world” (John 16:33, NIV).

We can say, “I don’t know how this is going to work out,” while also saying, “I know I don’t have to face it alone. God will work it out. And even if it doesn’t work out the way I wanted, God will work everything for good (Romans 8:28).” We can recognize disappointment without allowing disappointment to become our identity. That is the difference between simply “thinking positively” and renewing our minds.

A Personal Example

I have experienced the power of reframing in my own life. When my husband and I first moved to Western Washington from Southeast Idaho, I complained about the price of our apartment. Many of my friends back in Idaho were paying approximately the same amount for their mortgages on newly built homes as we were paying in rent for a two-bedroom apartment. I found it difficult to feel content.

Then one night, when I couldn’t sleep, I turned on the television. I was watching a program that showed young families living in extreme poverty. They didn’t have clean water or indoor plumbing, and had little food.

I looked around our apartment. We had clean water. We had indoor plumbing. We had food. We had a comfortable place to sleep. We even had a gas fireplace that I loved to put on at night. Nothing about my circumstances had changed.

The apartment was exactly the same, but suddenly, my perspective was different. God helped me change my perspective. For the first time, instead of focusing on what I didn’t have, I recognized how much I did have. I felt rich.

Over the years, I have had to remind myself to put on my figurative “rose-colored glasses” and look at my circumstances through new eyes. That doesn’t mean ignoring reality. It means intentionally looking for another perspective.

What Are We Choosing to Focus On?

1 Thessalonians 5 encourages us to rejoice, pray continually, and give thanks in all circumstances. That doesn’t mean we will enjoy every circumstance we experience. It means that even in difficult circumstances, we can look for reasons to remain connected to God and practice gratitude. James 1:2 tells us to “count it all joy when you fall into various trials.” The NLT says, “when troubles of any kind come your way.”

This is one reason gratitude can be such a powerful practice.

When we are overwhelmed, our attention can become completely consumed by what is going wrong. Reframing helps us widen the lens.

  • What else is true?
  • What am I overlooking?
  • What am I grateful for? (I often suggest starting a gratitude journal).
  • What does God say about me?
  • What can I learn from this?
  • Where do I see God working?

Sometimes changing our perspective doesn’t change the circumstance. It changes us as we walk through the circumstance.

Second Timothy 1:7 reminds us that God has given us a spirit of power, love, and a sound mind. Philippians 2:3-4 also encourages us to look beyond ourselves and consider the needs of others.

Sometimes the best way to interrupt our own negative thought cycle is to take our eyes off ourselves and refocus them on God and others.

We Can Choose a Different Perspective

We will all experience disappointment, fear, loss, frustration, and circumstances we wish we could change. We will also have thoughts that are discouraging, fearful, or simply untrue. The goal isn’t to never have a negative thought. The goal is to notice it, pause, examine it, and then decide whether it deserves to stay.

Cognitive reframing gives us a practical tool for challenging unhelpful thinking and developing a more balanced perspective. As Christians, we can take that practice one step further by asking whether our thoughts align with the truth of God’s Word.

We may not always be able to choose what happens to us. We may not be able to control every thought that enters our minds. But we can become more intentional about what we dwell on, what we believe, and where we choose to focus our attention.

Next Steps

Changing perspective doesn’t always require changing circumstances. Sometimes, it simply requires seeing those circumstances through new eyes.

If you struggle with negative thoughts, automatic thoughts, or cognitive distortions, we have wonderful Christian counselors who can help you learn how to stop them and replace them. Counselors help overcome cognitive distortions through structured therapeutic approaches like cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and cognitive restructuring.

Photo:
“New Glasses”, Courtesy of Frank Flores, Unsplash.com, Unsplash+ License

The post Reframing: Changing the Way We See Our Circumstances appeared first on Tacoma Christian Counseling.

item.title: How Shame Therapy Can Unmask Issues Surrounding Self-Esteem
item.description:
In every episode of the classic cartoon Scooby-Doo, there is a supernatural monster that commits a crime and causes havoc in unsuspecting communities. A gang of young characters must follow the clues to solve these mysteries. They always end up exposing the villain to be an ordinary person in an elaborate costume. Similarly, shame therapy can expose the beliefs behind and beneath some of your greatest struggles and character flaws, if you are brave enough to allow it to do so.

Shame is one of the most complex emotions a person can feel, and it most often begins in childhood. No child can fully understand or process their emotions, even when they are pleasant, much less when they are attached to trauma, neglect, or abuse. People learn from a young age to push shame deep below the surface, out of sight, so that it won’t affect them.

Unfortunately, shame affects you potentially more than any other emotion, even when hidden behind a mask. It is only with shame therapy that you can begin to follow the clues that will eventually result in you unmasking and apprehending shame in your life.

Cracked Foundations

To use another metaphor, sometimes shame is like a seemingly harmless crack that appears in the walls of a building, spreading slowly across the entire wall over time. What might seem like a superficial problem that is easily covered with plaster and paint often tells of a more serious issue deep below the ground.

The appearance of a crack in the walls shows that the foundations have begun to shift or sink, potentially compromising the structural integrity of the entire building and signaling danger to its occupants. Similarly, a person’s behavior can show that they have an issue with their foundational self-beliefs and that their behaviors may be rooted in shame.

This is apparent in men who become violently angry at others for seemingly no reason. They move around life as balls of pent-up aggression and hostility, attacking anyone who dares challenge their identity or values. Like the crack that forms on the wall, their attitude and behavior suggest that they have some serious structural damage at the foundation of their identity.

Shame therapy might expose that they feel inferior because of an aspect of their personality that they feel helpless to resolve, like their height, weight, stature, or masculinity. These core components of their self-worth are so shrouded by guilt, shame, and fear that they default to displays of aggression and intimidation, rather than begin the difficult work of processing their damaged emotions.

How Shame Therapy Works

Shame therapy takes you back to your foundational experiences, to the times when you first felt cast aside, rejected, overlooked, bullied, or abused. These were the moments when your childlike mind could not understand why you were being treated a certain way and defaulted to taking the blame for the injustice.

You told yourself, maybe not with words but with beliefs, that you deserved the beating, that it was your fault the once-trusted adult did that to you, or that you were ignored all day by the parents who could do no wrong in your eyes. As a child, you were surviving.

There was no way you could understand any of these events, so you tried your best to forget them. Over time, their memory got buried underground, where you thought it would eventually be forgotten for good. What remained, however, was the narrative surrounding each of these moments. Kids might not be able to process complex emotions, but they do know how to tell a story. The stories you told yourself about the things you went through became foundational to your identity, and as foundational as the memories you buried. Shame therapy attempts to uncover and expose as many of these beliefs and stories as possible, to confront them, and to contradict them.

For example, you might have been punished by your parents when you were a child for being lazy. In a shame therapy session, you may relive that exact moment with your therapist and uncover the emotions behind the memory, even though they were buried because they were difficult to deal with. Now, in a safe place as an adult with a trusted friend, you can look at that memory again, confront it, and contradict it.

You might remember your father beating you because you hadn’t done your homework. He called you lazy, and you have had that memory in your head every time you relaxed or did not complete a task. Not only do you remember the words your father used in that moment, but you remember the fear you felt, the surprise at your father’s sudden aggression, and most of all, the guilt and shame you felt. Lazy became an identity marker for you after that because you believed what your dad told you, because, in your young eyes, he could not lie.

In shame therapy, you will be asked to think of all the times you were not lazy. You will recall each achievement, even if there are few. You will be asked if you think of other people as lazy when you see them resting, or if you would beat your own child for not finishing their homework. The likely answer is that no, you don’t think of other people as lazy, and you wouldn’t ever beat your child. Simply admitting this is a confrontation with a shame-rooted belief that has been affecting you your entire life.

By reliving painful memories like this, you are waking them and bringing them to the surface, where you can properly address them. Though they might cause you pain to remember them, or make you wince with embarrassment, those emotions begin to dissolve as you expose them to logic, truth, and self-kindness.

Sometimes your therapist will ask you to remember a powerful, emotional memory that contradicts the shameful one, such as a time when you were praised, celebrated, and felt loved. If the fruit of shame is low self-esteem, then the opposite of shame is self-kindness and self-acceptance.

A Safe Place

Everyone has unconscious beliefs about themselves and others that they have carried from childhood, sometimes into old age. You might not know that you have these beliefs, where they came from, or just how incorrect they may be. These are things that get exposed in shame therapy.

Somewhere in your youth, you heard something about yourself, you believed it, and you internalized it. It sank down to become a stone in the foundation of your identity. Now it lies there hidden, but an essential aspect of your identity and worldview.

Now you must learn that it is safe to disagree with these things, even if they have been a crucial part of how you understand the world. Sometimes in shame therapy, you will be guided through remembering a particular shameful memory, and your therapist will ask you to imagine having a friend there with you in that moment. Instantly, the idea of having a loved one there with you in that moment may flood you with warmth and a feeling of safety.

You will be asked to imagine your friend’s response to the situation, or what they would do to protect you. Ultimately, you will feel safe remembering that event because now you have attached that memory to someone who loves you, accepts you, and would protect you if necessary.

Shame is a complex emotion to process and a powerful emotion to harbor, but it is life-changing to overcome. There is no memory too deeply rooted or experience too traumatic to heal. You are not forever defined by the words someone spoke to you decades ago. When your tormentor is unmasked, you will find that you were an equal match for him the entire time.

You can find a counselor to process past trauma and shame with, if that is something you would like to do. You may consult the online catalog of counselors to find someone to meet with. The reception team can also help you if you would prefer. Contact the office today to learn more about how a therapist can help you overcome shame.

Photo:
“Women talking,” courtesy of Christina @ wocintechchat.com M, Unsplash.com, CCO License

The post How Shame Therapy Can Unmask Issues Surrounding Self-Esteem appeared first on Bothell Christian Counseling.

item.title: Confronting and Letting Go of Toxic Shame
item.description:
Some of us grew up in families where we felt invisible and unimportant, regardless of what we tried to do to get attention and affection. Some of us had terrible experiences with people who should have loved and protected us, but instead hurt us and exploited us. Some of us were bullied, rejected, and ridiculed for things that we couldn’t help, by peers or by people old enough to know better. The painful memories from these experiences stayed with us in the form of toxic shame.

Toxic shame hides in our hearts. It tells us that we’re not good enough, that there is something wrong with us, that we’ll never amount to anything more than what we are now. It may even tell us that we are fundamentally unlovable.

These are sentences that we don’t necessarily hear. They are ideas and beliefs that we probably don’t repeat out loud, but they still affect our self-image. These are the beliefs that lie at our foundation, brought into being by the shame surrounding our most painful experiences.

At some point, though, we will encounter the opposite of what we’re used to. We will meet someone who wants to accept us, to cherish us, to love us, and to enjoy our company. When this happens, we will have no choice but to confront the toxic shame that shields us from accepting this love, and to heal it from the inside out. There is a long life ahead of us, filled with wonderful opportunities, but to advance, we must heal the hurt that lies beneath toxic shame.

We Accept the Love We Think We Deserve

Everyone has a baseline of the kind of treatment they think they deserve, and this is called our norm. It is our past experiences, both painful and positive, that determine our norms. When we get less than what we are used to, or when we are treated below our level of norm, our default emotion is anger. Imagine receiving your monthly paycheck, and it is significantly less than you are used to receiving each month. You will feel disbelief, you will want an explanation, and you will be outraged at the injustice of getting less than what you are used to.

When we get more than our norm, and when we have toxic shame, our response is guilt.

If someone else looked at their monthly paycheck and noticed significantly more money there than they are used to, they might also respond with disbelief. When they followed up about it and discovered that the amount was not a mistake, they would be delighted and grateful.

The person with toxic shame in this same scenario, however, would feel guilty and unworthy. They would reflect on their failures and human moments, and they would think of these moments as the reasons why they are disqualified from getting a pay raise.

Everyone evaluates their self-worth based on the way they were treated in their earliest memories, to the way they were treated through their childhood and teen years. The way others treated them dictates their value and sets the baseline norm of how they expect to be treated.

If they were neglected, abused, mistreated, or bullied, they will carry toxic shame as if they were to blame for those experiences. Their baseline norm for receiving love is low, and they feel guilty or ashamed each time they receive more love or when they are treated kinder than they are used to. This is what the phrase “We accept the love we think we deserve” truly means.

People who carry toxic shame purposely make it difficult for others to love them. In the Bible, we are told that Adam and Eve had a close friendship with their Creator, and the author even tells us that they were naked and had no shame. As soon as they do what they were told not to do, they become aware of their nakedness, they cover themselves, and they withdraw from God, hiding from Him as He comes to look for them. (Genesis 3)

Adam and Eve covering up, withdrawing, and hiding is a perfect picture of what toxic shame does to us. We put up emotional barriers and create distance from those looking to connect with us because we feel unworthy, exposed, or broken beyond repair.

Letting Go of Toxic Shame

Many of us spend our lives oblivious to our emotions and the thoughts behind them. Similar to the physical foundations of a building, we all have unseen thoughts and beliefs that form the foundation of our identity; it is the essence of how we feel about ourselves. A teacher might have scolded us in front of the class, telling us that we’re hopeless because we never listen to instructions. That simple sentence might go on to form the foundation of our identity, magnifying one of our struggles to the point that it becomes a defining feature.

Some of us were never told anything in our young lives, positive or negative. We were left alone for vast stretches of time, our achievements unnoticed, our needs unmet, and our painful emotions ignored. Neglected children grow up believing that they are unlovable and unworthy of praise, based on the affection that they never received.

This is toxic shame because it causes someone to feel guilty even when they were a victim. The same goes for children who were mistreated and abused. They carry toxic shame as if they caused bad things to happen to them.

It’s not simple, but it is possible to heal and release toxic shame. We are spiritual beings in a physical body, with minds and emotions. We must learn to reach and speak to every part of ourselves, leaving no broken area unaddressed. There are physical exercises that heal our nervous system, and there are affirmations to speak to our damaged mind and emotions. God has spoken loving truths to our spirits, and we must hear them and accept them to be healed within.

The further we go into dealing with our past and toxic shame, the more we will realize that some things are impossible to do alone. Many of us were hurt by others, and those same hurts can only be healed by others, as uncomfortable and scary as that idea might be.

One of the central parts of healing toxic shame lies in learning to become vulnerable with others, in the way God wanted Adam and Eve to be vulnerable with Him. Not everyone can be trusted, but we must find the ones who can. Healing will only come when we allow others to see our shame and love us anyway.

You might look at yourself in the mirror now and struggle to comprehend how anyone could love you. You have never needed to earn love, and you have never needed to make yourself lovable. Toxic shame has had you believing all kinds of things about yourself that have never been true.

It can be scary and deeply uncomfortable to confront your past and to let go of the beliefs you have been clinging to. It is only when you can let go of the handfuls of shame that you have been holding that you can have a free hand to receive and accept the love that you have always been deserving of and that the people around you have been desperate for you to receive.

Perhaps you don’t have someone that you can trust with details of your past. When you speak with a counselor, you are in a safe place, with someone who will keep your confidence. You can meet with as many counselors as it takes for you to feel safe and comfortable enough to open up to the right person. To get started, please consult our online catalog of counselors or speak with our reception team. We trust that you will find someone and begin the healing process soon.

Photo:
“Woman in forest,” courtesy of John Lord Vicente, Unsplash.com, CCO License

The post Confronting and Letting Go of Toxic Shame appeared first on Tacoma Christian Counseling.

item.title: How to Define OCD: Three Areas That Are Helped By Counseling
item.description:
The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders defines obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) as:

“…the presence of obsessions and /or compulsions. Obsessions are recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted, whereas compulsions are repetitive behaviors or mental acts that an individual feels driven to perform in response to an obsession or according to rules that must be applied rigidly” – American Psychiatric Association, 2022

Although concise, this definition can be made more understandable by breaking down different elements of this disorder. The two main components of this disorder are obsessions and compulsions.

Obsessions/Intrusive Thoughts

Obsessions are consistent thoughts, impulsive feelings or mental pictures that take place repeatedly in one’s mind. They take place without the person causing them and without the person wanting them to be there; this is where the term intrusive comes from. The thought, image, or urge intrudes on a person.

There are all sorts of obsessions that one might have, and they are as varied as people are. One person might experience an obsession as an intrusive thought that they have committed a sin, but that is only the beginning for someone with OCD. The thought of possibly committing a sin won’t leave their mind, and they find themself thinking about it over and over again, even when they don’t want to. This category would be called religious OCD or scrupulosity.

Another example of an obsession might be someone who feels an intrusive impulse (urge) to harm someone in some way and they are horrified by the realization. They continue to experience it over and over again, feeling more horror and more shame with each experience of it. This category is called harm OCD.

Yet another example might be someone who has intrusive mental images of sexual acts. This person does not want these images and is disgusted and horrified by them but cannot seem to get them out of their head. This would fall under the category of sexual OCD.

Because clinicians have noticed patterns among those who are diagnosed with OCD, obsessions have been grouped into particular categories, such as the ones used in the examples above. Other categories include but are not limited to hoarding/saving, symmetry/order, contamination, somatic (having to do with the body), and relationships.

Compulsions

It is often the case that both obsessions and compulsions are present in an individual who is diagnosed with OCD; however, only one of these needs to be present to meet the criteria for an OCD diagnosis.

The other component to a diagnosis of OCD is compulsions. Compulsions are physical or mental actions repeated over and over. These actions are characterized by an urge to complete them or by a particular and precise way of completing them. Compulsions are sometimes called “safety behaviors.” They are called this because one forms a belief that if they complete the behavior, they will be or feel safe.

For example, think of someone who has a contamination obsession. This person might obsess about the spread of germs. Their compulsion might be to clean everything that might have come in contact with germs. The compulsion might make them feel “safe” from germs, but only temporarily.

The trouble is that as the person uses the compulsion (cleaning) to temporarily feel safe, they are inadvertently training their mind that cleaning must happen to relieve the fear of germs spreading. The more one completes the compulsion, the stronger their belief that the compulsion will keep them safe from spreading germs.

You may see where this is going. The compulsions require more and more from the sufferer because it is not possible to be safe from all germs, and somewhere in their mind, they are aware of that. This awareness drives them to continue to try to fix the problem of germs being a danger. The solution to this is not to be or feel entirely safe from the effects of germs, as this is impossible. However, the OCD sufferer believes that this is the solution.

The Goal of OCD Treatment

In reality, the solution to symptoms of OCD is to build up the capacity to tolerate the discomfort and fear that comes with the thought of germs. The more this tolerance is built up, the less the compulsion will feel needed.

The same is true for any category of OCD: the OCD sufferer has convinced himself that the compulsion brings safety, but the reality is that it does not bring safety but demands continued engagement in the compulsions and mounting fear that drives the obsession. There are specific fears behind every obsession, and the goal for treatment of OCD is to build up a tolerance and a capacity to live with those fears.

Ways That Counseling Can Help

Sharing Obsessions and Intrusive Thoughts

Many people with OCD find the intrusive thoughts, obsessions, and compulsions they experience as frightening or shameful. This often leads to suffering in silence and fear, without knowing these are symptoms of OCD and without knowing that there are people who can offer help and support.

In particular, those who suffer from harm and sexual OCD symptoms often believe that they are bad people for having these unwanted and intrusive thoughts or compulsions. The word intrusive means that the thought is unwanted, uninvited, and unexpected. As you may be able to imagine, having sexual images suddenly come into your mind or unexpectedly thinking about harming another person would be quite disturbing!

This is common in those who suffer from OCD. The truth is that all people experience thoughts that are unwanted. Those who do not have OCD move past these thoughts without forming any judgments about themselves or the thoughts. Those with OCD have thoughts about these thoughts, which often lead to compulsions to get rid of these disturbances.

Meeting with a counselor and sharing these thoughts, obsessions, or compulsions with them can offer great relief from shame. Counseling can offer a place where someone can share these things that disturb them, and they will not be met with judgment but with compassion and help.

This is an important step for those who suffer from OCD. Being able to share this part of their life with another person who does not believe that they are “bad” for any of these things can bring a profound sense of relief and a starting point for continued treatment of OCD.

Tolerating Discomfort and Fear with Support

Once a person has been able to share these disturbing obsessions and compulsions with a caring counselor who does not respond with judgment, support and treatment can be discussed. The most common and efficacious treatment for OCD is called Exposure Response Prevention (ERP).

The first step is exposing the person to the fear behind the obsession. There are many ways to do this. Some people can use real-world exposures, and some can use imagining different scenarios as an exposure. This is done in the presence of a counselor, and the individual will share their emotional experience with the counselor.

It is important to note that the process of exposure causes great anxiety and fear to emerge in the individual. The purpose of this is to reform the brain processes to allow the person to not engage in a compulsion when they normally would and to teach themself that they do have the ability to tolerate the fear and discomfort they are attempting to avoid.

Response prevention involves the individual refraining from engaging in the compulsion or safety behavior, whatever that might look like. The point of refraining from the safety behavior is to train the brain and body to tolerate the discomfort of the fear or anxiety experienced when not engaging in the compulsion.

Eventually, the intensity of discomfort will subside, and the exposure will be over. This can be an overwhelming and scary experience, and this is why it is important to do it with a trained and caring counselor. The goal is for the individual to grow skilled at doing this so that they can practice it outside of their treatment with a counselor and eventually be able to do it on their own.

Identifying Unhelpful Thinking Patterns

An important part of treatment for OCD is identifying different thinking patterns that are not helpful. All of us experience what we might call automatic thoughts. These are generally based on different beliefs that we have about the world or ourselves.

For example, one person might experience an urge to floor the gas pedal as they are stopped in rush hour traffic. An automatic thought from someone who does not suffer from OCD might be “Wow, that’s a weird urge to have” or “That’s kind of funny that urge just showed up in my mind.” Someone who suffers from OCD might have the thought of “I’m a terrible person who cannot be trusted to operate a vehicle!”

The automatic thought of the person who suffers from OCD could bring up feelings of guilt, fear, shame, etc. If one can identify this automatic thought, one can then decide if they truly believe that thought. More often than not, these automatic thoughts contain errors in logic.

In this example, one of the errors in logic might be that the person is confusing feelings with facts. The person feels terrible for having that image come into their head, but that doesn’t mean that they are terrible for having that image come into their head. Slowly, with time and support from a trained counselor, these automatic thoughts can be identified and examined for alignment with the truth.

In summary, obsessions and/or compulsions are the components that are the diagnostic makeup of obsessive-compulsive disorder. As with all mental disorders, for one to be diagnosed, the symptoms must cause significant difficulty in functioning. In other words, the mere presence of obsessions or compulsions in one’s life does not mean that one meets the criteria for an OCD diagnosis. It is when it gets in the way of functioning that it becomes a mental disorder.

There are three significant ways that counseling can help one who suffers from OCD: sharing obsessions, intrusive thoughts, or compulsions with a non-judgmental and skilled counselor; engaging in ERP treatment; and learning to identify and slowly change unhelpful thought patterns.

There are many other ways that counseling can help those who suffer from OCD; this list is not exhaustive. Those with OCD need not suffer in silence nor continue to be bound by OCD; there is hope and people who want to support you in healing!

References:
